claims.quote: More fundamentally, these data reveal additional morphogenetic competencies of cells which could have implications for evolutionary developmental biology, as evolution of anatomical and functional features could be affected by the ability of the same genome to produce very diverse forms in different environments.
claims.work: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells
claims.chapter: Gumuskaya G 2024, Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells › Conclusion

claims.label: A collective's perceptual field and ability to find alternative paths grow with its size
claims.statement: Extending William James' definition of intelligence (reaching the same goal by different means) to collectives via the perceptual field, the region of space and time an agent can survey for alternative paths to a goal, the authors propose that as a collective grows its perceptual field increases, improving its ability to find variant paths.
claims.quote: As the size of a collective increases its perceptual field increases, improving its ability to find variant paths.
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction

claims.label: Neural unification into a self is a pivot of earlier morphogenetic cell communication
claims.statement: It has been hypothesized, and the authors adopt, that the ability of neurons to unify into a centralized self is an evolutionary pivot of earlier cell-communication strategies that first solved problems in anatomical morphospace, a domain also requiring information processing above the single-cell level.
claims.quote: Indeed it has been hypothesized that the remarkable ability of neurons to unify toward a centralized self – the emergent agent that is the subject of memories, preferences, and goals which are not assignable to any of the individual components – is an evolutionary pivot of far earlier cell communication strategies that first solved problems in navigating another domain that requires information processing above the single cell level: anatomical morphospace70.
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction

claims.label: The number of embryos a blastoderm forms is not fixed by genetics
claims.statement: The number of individuals formed by an embryonic blastoderm is not fixed at one by the genome: temporarily introducing breaks that informationally isolate islands of cells yields twins, triplets and so on, showing the blastoderm is an excitable medium in which several coherent embryos can self-organize.
claims.quote: Indeed, the question of how many individuals are present in an embryonic blastoderm is not fixed at 1 by the genetics, because temporary introduction of breaks in the blastoderm (leading to informational isolation of islands of cell masses) results in twins, triplets, etc103.
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction › Development: transition to multicellularity

claims.label: Keratocyte fragments migrate to the anode while whole keratocytes migrate to the cathode
claims.statement: In an electric field, whole keratocytes migrate toward the cathode while fragments of keratocytes migrate toward the anode, so the collective (an intact cell) has the opposite taxis to its parts, illustrating that collective behaviour can be a hard-to-predict function of component tendencies.
claims.quote: In an electric field, keratocytes migrate to the cathode, but fragments of keratocytes migrate to the anode104.
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction › Cell migration: the group does not go where each of the parts wants to go

claims.label: Targeting instructor-cell voltage converts tadpole melanocytes to a melanoma-like state
claims.statement: In Xenopus tadpoles, briefly targeting the bioelectric state of a small population of instructor cells (with a chloride channel activator or a GlyCl mutant), in the absence of carcinogens, oncogenes or DNA damage, converts melanocytes throughout the animal, including distant ones, into an over-proliferative, invasive melanoma-like phenotype via disruption of serotonergic signalling.
claims.quote: This could be achieved in the absence of classical carcinogens, oncogenes, or DNA damage, by brief exposure to chemical (chloride ion channel activator drug) or molecular-genetic (GlyCl mutant) targeting of the bioelectric state of a specific cell population: instructor cells which normally keep the melanocytes in their healthy state via serotonergic signaling118.
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction › From normal melanocytes to a melanoma phenotype: a collective decision

claims.label: Melanocyte conversion is all-or-none per animal, stochastic only across the cohort
claims.statement: Melanocyte conversion after instructor-cell depolarization is a collective, all-or-none decision: different reagents give different incidences in a cohort (e.g. 70% converted), but each animal is either fully converted or fully normal; a computational model fitted to these incidences predicted interventions (two drugs and a dominant-negative construct) that were then confirmed to produce the first partially converted animals.
claims.quote: Using different reagents could induce different incidences of hyperpigmentation (conversion) in a cohort of animals, but this was a population-level phenotype: for example, 70% of the animals could be converted, but any given animal was either fully converted or fully normal (Fig. 4a, b).
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction › From normal melanocytes to a melanoma phenotype: a collective decision

claims.label: Head-versus-tail choice at a planarian cut cannot be made locally
claims.statement: When a planarian is cut once, cells that were adjacent neighbours at the same positional-information value make a head on one side and a tail on the other, so this anatomical decision cannot be made locally: wound cells must coordinate with the rest of the fragment to learn where they are, which way they face and what structures remain.
claims.quote: In other words, it is actually impossible for an anatomical decision like this to be made locally – the cells of the wound must coordinate with the remaining fragment to get information about where they are located, which way they are facing, and what other structures exist121,122, in order to make adaptive decisions about large-scale growth and form that enable regeneration of normal worms.
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction › Left/right, head/tail: random, but collective anatomical decisions

claims.label: Cryptic planaria randomize head number per animal, not per cell
claims.statement: Perturbing the planarian bioelectric control circuit produces 'Cryptic' destabilized worms whose fragments, even from the same parent, regenerate one-headed and two-headed forms at a set frequency of about 1:2, yet each animal has clear heads and tails rather than mixed tissue, so the randomized bioelectric state is interpreted by collectives rather than by individual cells.
claims.quote: More specifically, several perturbations targeting the bioelectric control circuit (Fig. 5e) have shown randomization of outcome: such Cryptic planaria are destabilized, and fragments (even from the same parent worm) will form 1-head and 2-head forms at a set frequency of ~1:2130 (Fig. 5f).
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction › Left/right, head/tail: random, but collective anatomical decisions

claims.label: Left-right randomization is concordant within an embryo except after VANGL knockdown
claims.statement: Bioelectric and biochemical perturbations of vertebrate left-right patterning randomize laterality only at the level of whole embryos (each embryo's cells agree on L and R identity); the only known perturbation that breaks this concordance is down-regulation of planar-polarity VANGL signalling, which produces speckled L/R marker expression on both sides of the midline.
claims.quote: In all of the many studies on perturbation of the LR pathway, we are aware of only one that actually breaks the concordance: disruption of the planar polarity pathway by down-regulating VANGL signaling149 leads to a speckling on both sides of the midline, consistent with individual cells within a single lateral domain disagreeing on whether they should have L or R identity (Fig. 6a–d).
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction › Left/right, head/tail: random, but collective anatomical decisions

claims.label: Grafted groups of neural crest cells keep their identity; single grafted cells do not
claims.statement: Single neural crest cells transposed to a different anterior-posterior axial domain change their gene expression to match their neighbours, whereas groups of transposed cells keep their original gene expression, which the authors interpret as collectives having greater positional memory (a perceptual field extending further into the past) than individual cells.
claims.quote: Individual cells transposed from one anterior-posterior axial domain to another will change their gene expression to match their neighbors159,161,162. In contrast, groups of cells transposed along the anterior-posterior axis maintain their original gene expression, thus resisting the inductive effects of the surrounding tissue159,161,162.
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction › Neural crest intelligence is collective

claims.label: The segmentation clock needs a cell collective to oscillate and entrains grafted cells
claims.statement: The vertebrate segmentation clock depends on collectivity: presomitic mesoderm cells do not oscillate when cultured individually but resume oscillating when cultured together, wild-type cells grafted into non-cycling mutant fish express her1 without cycling, and cells grafted into tissue at a different clock phase synchronize to their neighbours' phase.
claims.quote: Similarly, pre-somitic mesoderm cells do not oscillate when cultured independently, but will resume oscillating when cultured collectively169.
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Introduction › Segmentation intelligence is collective

claims.label: Frog embryo brain gene expression is driven by voltage differences, not absolute values
claims.statement: In the frog embryo brain, downstream gene expression is driven by the spatial difference in membrane voltage between regions rather than the absolute voltage of any cells, so cells must read patterns over whole cell fields: collectivity appears in the input as well as the output of cell-group behaviour.
claims.quote: For example, in the frog embryo brain, it is the spatial difference in voltage between regions that drives downstream gene expression, not the absolute value of any cells186,187.
claims.work: Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates
claims.chapter: McMillen P 2024, Collective intelligence: A unifying concept for integrating biology across scales and substrates › Conclusion

claims.label: Biological memory preserves salience rather than fidelity
claims.statement: Levin proposes that memory, across scales from cells to societies, is best understood as preserving salience (what matters for the agent's future) rather than fidelity to the details of the original data.
claims.quote: Using examples from developmental biology, evolution, and synthetic bioengineering, in addition to neuroscience, I propose that a perspective on memory as preserving salience, not fidelity, is applicable to many phenomena on scales from cells to societies.
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › Abstract

claims.label: Adaptive confabulation resolves the persistence paradox for individuals and lineages
claims.statement: Levin argues that the paradox that a changing agent or species ceases to be itself while an unchanging one dies out is resolved by continuous commitment to creative, adaptive confabulation (reinterpretation of memories and information) at levels from molecular to behavioural, in individuals and whole lineages.
claims.quote: Continuous commitment to creative, adaptive confabulation, from the molecular to the behavioral levels, is the answer to the persistence paradox as it applies to individuals and whole lineages.
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › Abstract

claims.label: Memories may be active agents in the sense-making process
claims.statement: Levin speculates that, on a substrate-independent, processual view of life and mind, memories, as patterns in the excitable medium of cognitive systems, could be seen as minimally agential participants that help shape their own reinterpretation, blurring the line between thoughts and thinkers.
claims.quote: I also speculate that a substrate-independent, processual view of life and mind suggests that memories, as patterns in the excitable medium of cognitive systems, could be seen as active agents in the sense-making process.
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › Abstract

claims.label: Reinterpreting non-local memories is a cognitive glue that makes Selves
claims.statement: Levin proposes that mnemonic improvisation, the ability to modify, remap and interpret non-local memories onto new media and contexts, is one of the kinds of cognitive glue that binds parts into a Self at every scale.
claims.quote: Thus, I propose that the ability to modify and interpret non-local memories is one of the kinds of cognitive glue that reifies Selves (at all scales) [23,24,25].
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 1. Introduction and Overview

claims.label: Memories surviving metamorphosis are remapped to stay salient in the new body
claims.statement: In insects whose memories survive metamorphosis (caterpillar to butterfly), recall does not carry over specific caterpillar memories but generalizes and remaps them (e.g. from leaves to food) so that the learned relationship keeps its salience in the new body and environment.
claims.quote: The process of memory and recall not only functionally generalizes (abstracts20) the information (not leaves, but “food”), but most importantly, remaps21 it in a way that the basic relationship learned maintains its salience in a new body and environment.
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 3. Remapping Memories: Beyond Storage and Simple Modification

claims.label: Engrams act more like prompts decoded by an intelligent receiver than like encodings
claims.statement: From examples such as frogs that seek out an odorant injected into the egg they developed from, Levin argues that engrams behave less like encoded memories and more like prompts, with much of the work (detecting novelty, remapping across scales, contextualizing and generalizing) done by the encoding and decoding process.
claims.quote: The engrams seem less like encoded memories29, and more like a kind of prompt, with a lot of the hard work being carried out through the encoding/decoding process, which adds interpretation, context sensitivity, and generalization (i.e., intelligence) to the process.
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 3. Remapping Memories: Beyond Storage and Simple Modification

claims.label: The same bioelectric trigger is reinterpreted by context (monensin: tails vs legs)
claims.statement: Low-information bioelectric triggers are interpreted by competent tissues according to context: the voltage-modifying reagent monensin induces tail regrowth in tadpoles but leg regrowth in froglets, never the reverse, preserving high-level information such as 'build whatever normally goes at this location'.
claims.quote: Here, the same bioelectric stimulus is functionally reinterpreted based on the specific context, preserving salient, high-level information like “build whatever normally goes at this location” (in the case of the appendage regeneration trigger).
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 4. Beyond the Brain: Bowties Everywhere

claims.label: Polyploid newts build normal tubules by switching molecular mechanisms
claims.statement: Engineered polyploid newts with much larger cells keep kidney tubule diameter normal by using fewer cells and, with truly enormous cells, a single cell bending around itself, showing that tissues call up different molecular mechanisms (cytoskeletal bending instead of cell–cell communication) to reach the same anatomical goal state.
claims.quote: This requires using a different molecular mechanism (cytoskeletal bending instead of cell–cell communication of tubulogenesis)—calling up different modular subroutines to accomplish their high-level goal state as needed, while circumstances (indeed, their inner components) change unexpectedly34.
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 4. Beyond the Brain: Bowties Everywhere

claims.label: Bowtie compression is common in biochemical, bioelectric and mechanical pathways
claims.statement: Levin argues that a bowtie architecture, which compresses data to a generative kernel that must later be re-inflated and reinterpreted, is common at the subcellular scale in biochemical, bioelectrical and biomechanical pathways, as well as in the egg stage of the metazoan life cycle and in learning.
claims.quote: Note that this bowtie architecture—which forces a compression36 of data to a generative kernel that then has to be re-inflated and elaborated—is also a common feature of biochemical, bioelectrical, and biomechanical pathways (Figure 7), that is, at the subcellular scale;
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 4. Beyond the Brain: Bowties Everywhere

claims.label: Anatomical plasticity across species reflects willingness to confabulate in morphospace
claims.statement: Levin proposes that the spectrum from hardwired, mosaic C. elegans through intermediately plastic amphibians and embryonic mammals to extremely plastic planaria reflects a strategic parameter: the willingness to confabulate in anatomical space, i.e. to rely on pattern extraction and completion rather than taking genetic priors too seriously.
claims.quote: What underlying parameter is represented by the spectrum ranging from the hardwired, mosaic C. elegans to the intermediately plastic amphibia and (embryonic) mammals, and to the extreme plasticity of planaria? I propose it is the willingness to confabulate in anatomical space
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 4. Beyond the Brain: Bowties Everywhere

claims.label: Planaria resist cancer and ageing despite noisy genomes via pattern completion
claims.statement: In silico simulations show how lineages such as planarian flatworms can become extremely resistant to transgenesis, ageing, cancer and injury despite very noisy genomes because they commit to a strategy that overrides genetic details with large-scale pattern completion.
claims.quote: In silico simulation results [176] show how this kind of process can give rise to remarkable lineages, such as planarian flatworms, which are extremely resistant to transgenesis, aging, cancer, and injury despite40 their incredibly noisy genome because they have fully committed to a strategy that overrides genetic details with large-scale pattern completion [176].
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 4. Beyond the Brain: Bowties Everywhere

claims.label: Substrate unreliability is the reason, not an obstacle, for biological intelligence
claims.statement: Levin argues that the noise and unreliability of biological matter is a feature rather than a bug: morphological and behavioural intelligence arose because of, not in spite of, the vulnerability of the substrate, as suggested by planaria having the noisiest genome and the best regeneration and cancer resistance.
claims.quote: It seems that the underlying noise and unreliability of biological matter is not a bug but a feature: we obtained morphological (and behavioral) intelligence because of, not in spite of, the vulnerability of the substrate45.
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 6. What It Means, and What Next: A Research Program for Further Development

claims.label: Cellular competency hides genome quality from selection, driving an intelligence ratchet
claims.statement: Because competent biological material compensates for defects, selection cannot see genome quality clearly, so more evolutionary change accrues in competency mechanisms than in structural components, producing a positive-feedback intelligence ratchet based on remapping information to new contexts.
claims.quote: The competency of our material means that selection cannot see the quality of genomes clearly46. More evolutionary work thus has to be conducted on the competency mechanisms, not the structural components, leading to a positive feedback loop—an intelligence ratchet based on the remapping of information to new contexts47.
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 6. What It Means, and What Next: A Research Program for Further Development

claims.label: There is no single substrate for memory; all components can serve as scratchpads
claims.statement: Levin hypothesizes that there is no single substrate for memory: every component of a living system can use everything in its environment, including the high-dimensional reservoir of subcellular structure, as an interpretable scratchpad, rather than engrams residing only in synapses.
claims.quote: My current hypothesis, driven by the above multi-scale perspective [218], is that there is no single substrate for memory49.
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 6. What It Means, and What Next: A Research Program for Further Development

claims.label: Training associative memories may increase integration of composite systems
claims.statement: Levin proposes that memories belonging to a collective (e.g. a rat's lever–reward association, which no single cell experiences) may help reify the collective Self, and that training associative memories into gene regulatory networks should be tested for increases in integrated information (self-coherence).
claims.quote: This is currently being investigated in the context of our training of associative memories into gene-regulatory networks and other substrates, with measures of integrated information to determine if the forming of memories increases the self-coherence of composite systems.
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 7. A Continuum: From Thoughts to Thinkers

claims.label: Consciousness may be palpated uncertainty about one's own memories
claims.statement: Extending Solms's idea that consciousness is palpated uncertainty about the outside world, Levin hypothesizes that consciousness is palpated uncertainty about one's own memories and internal states.
claims.quote: I propose to expand this idea, with the hypothesis that consciousness is palpated uncertainty about your own memories and internal states.
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 7. A Continuum: From Thoughts to Thinkers

claims.label: Behavioural intelligence evolved from morphogenetic problem-solving
claims.statement: Levin proposes that behavioural intelligence in 3D space evolved from morphogenetic problem-solving competencies in anatomical space, which were themselves required by the inevitability of mutation and injury.
claims.quote: Behavioral intelligence in 3D space evolved from morphogenetic problem-solving competencies in anatomical space [97,124].
claims.work: Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue
claims.chapter: Levin M 2024, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue › 8. Conclusions

claims.label: Planaria have chaotic genomes yet regenerate, resist cancer and do not age
claims.statement: Planaria, despite chaotic mixoploid genomes from ~400 million years of asexual reproduction and large numbers of plastic proliferative stem cells, are champions of regeneration, cancer resistant and apparently do not age, the opposite of what a 'genome drives function' paradigm would predict.
claims.quote: Despite that, they are champions of regeneration, are cancer resistant, and apparently do not age. This is the polar opposite of the outcome that the current paradigm of “genome drives function” would predict for the animal with the messiest genome, full of undifferentiated cells in the adult stage.
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Introduction

claims.label: The body is a collective intelligence, so behavioural tools should beat micromanagement
claims.statement: Levin's central hypothesis is that the body is a collective intelligence behaving in anatomical, physiological and transcriptional spaces, so behavioural-science tools developed to collaborate with complex systems should provide therapeutic advantages over biochemical micromanagement of molecular components.
claims.quote: The central hypothesis is that the body is a collective intelligence behaving in anatomical, physiological, and transcriptional spaces [13]. Thus, behavioral science tools developed to collaborate with complex systems should provide therapeutic advantages over biochemical micromanagement.
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Introduction › BOX 1

claims.label: Intelligence is reaching the same goal by different means, including in morphogenesis
claims.statement: Levin defines intelligence, following William James, as the ability to reach the same goal by different means; for tissues this is the problem-solving competency to adapt to conditions in order to construct and repair a specific morphology or function, a functional definition that lets intelligence be studied in non-neural substrates.
claims.quote: I define intelligence here in William James’ [22] sense as the ability to reach the same goal by different means: the focus is on problem‐solving competency, which in this case is the ability to adapt to conditions to construct and repair a specific morphology or function.
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Intelligence Below the Cellular Level

claims.label: Gene regulatory network models show habituation, sensitization and Pavlovian learning
claims.statement: When standard behavioural-training protocols are applied to even simple models of gene regulatory networks and molecular pathways, the models show habituation, sensitization and Pavlovian (associative) conditioning, a dynamical state memory that requires no change to network topology or edge strengths.
claims.quote: By applying standard approaches from behavioral theory [17], it was seen that even simple models of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and molecular pathways show several different kinds of learning, including habituation, sensitization, and Pavlovian (associative) conditioning [23, 24].
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Intelligence Below the Cellular Level › The Inner Life of Active Matter

claims.label: Planarian heads degenerated by barium regenerate adapted to it via a handful of genes
claims.statement: Planarian flatworms exposed to barium, a nonspecific potassium channel blocker, lose their heads but soon regenerate new heads completely adapted to barium, and transcriptomic analysis shows only a handful of genes up- or down-regulated, which Levin interprets as cells solving a problem in high-dimensional transcriptional space without an evolved response to barium.
claims.quote: Remarkably, they soon regenerate new heads which are completely adapted to the presence of barium [66]. Transcriptomic analysis reveals just a handful of genes that have been up‐ and down‐regulated to enable this feat of morphological and physiological homeostasis.
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Intelligence Below the Cellular Level › The Inner Life of Active Matter

claims.label: Morphogenesis is behaviour of cell collectives navigating anatomical morphospace
claims.statement: Morphogenesis can be viewed as behaviour in anatomical morphospace: cellular collectives actively navigate from various starting states to the region corresponding to the species-specific target morphology, with competency ranging from a constrained random walk to advanced problem-solving, a framing Levin presents as a useful metaphor for importing tools from behavioural and cognitive science.
claims.quote: We previously argued that morphogenesis can be viewed as behavior in anatomical morphospace [13]; on this model, cellular collectives are systems that actively navigate from various starting states to a region corresponding to the species‐specific target morphology (Figure 2).
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › The Collective Intelligence of Cell Groups › Morphogenesis as Behavior in Anatomical Space

claims.label: Anatomical homeostasis uses large-scale feedback loops that reduce error from a target
claims.statement: Morphogenetic problem-solving cases indicate that anatomical development is not entirely open-loop: large-scale feedback loops measure distance from a target anatomical state and execute diverse molecular steps to reduce the error, and such networks can store setpoints that are complex data structures rather than simple scalars.
claims.quote: These examples indicate that these processes are not entirely open‐loop: large‐scale feedback loops exist that measure distance from a given target state and execute diverse molecular steps to implement those goals (reduce error).
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › The Collective Intelligence of Cell Groups › The Competencies of Anatomical Homeostasis

claims.label: Channelopathies that cause patterning defects link developmental biology and neuroscience
claims.statement: The deep symmetry between developmental biology and neuroscience is shown by the many ion-channel diseases (channelopathies) that produce patterning defects, and by the applicability of neuroscience tools, from drugs to optogenetics to training protocols, to morphogenetic decisions.
claims.quote: It can be seen in numerous channelopathies that result in patterning defects (see Table 1 in [110], and [111, 112, 113]), and in the applicability of the tools of neuroscience—from drugs to optogenetics to training protocols—to morphogenetic decisions.
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Bioelectricity as the Interface to Multicellularity › Thinking Beyond the Brain

claims.label: An endogenous electric face of resting potentials determines vertebrate face patterning
claims.statement: An endogenous spatial distribution of resting membrane potentials (the 'electric face') determines gene expression and anatomical regionalization of the vertebrate face; manipulating it by pharmacology, optogenetics or ion channel misexpression predictably changes craniofacial development and explains why ion channel mutations cause craniofacial phenotypes from frog to human.
claims.quote: One example is the electric face (Figure 4B)—an endogenous distribution of resting potentials that determines the gene expression and anatomical regionalization of the vertebrate face [118].
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Bioelectricity as the Interface to Multicellularity › Applications: Modulating Endogenous Bioelectric Cues

claims.label: A membrane-voltage change can induce eyes almost anywhere in the Xenopus body
claims.statement: In Xenopus laevis, misexpressing potassium channels to change membrane voltage induces ectopic eyes in many posterior regions including the gut, showing that cells outside the anterior neural field are competent to build eyes when given a higher-level bioelectric signal, contrary to conclusions drawn from prompting cells with the 'master eye gene' Pax6.
claims.quote: It was always thought that cells outside the anterior neural field in vertebrates were not competent to build eyes. But prior studies prompted cells with the so‐called master eye gene Pax6 [123]. It turns out that a higher‐level signal (V mem change) can induce eyes almost anywhere in the body.
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Bioelectricity as the Interface to Multicellularity › Applications: Modulating Endogenous Bioelectric Cues

claims.label: Many ectopic eye spots but one eye reflect competing goals of neighbouring cell groups
claims.statement: In Xenopus embryos injected with a potassium channel, many ectopic eye spots appear early but typically only one new eye forms; Levin interprets this as bidirectional signalling between channel-induced cells pushed toward an eye setpoint, which recruit neighbours, and uninjected neighbours whose setpoint is still 'gut', which signal to maintain normal fate.
claims.quote: At early stages in embryos injected with the potassium channel, many ectopic eye spots are detected, but just one new eye tends to appear at the end. This is the consequence of conversation between morphogenetic agents with different goals.
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Bioelectricity as the Interface to Multicellularity › Applications: Modulating Endogenous Bioelectric Cues

claims.label: Restoring the neural-plate bioelectric prepattern rescues teratogen and Notch defects
claims.statement: Normal brain morphogenesis in vertebrate (frog) embryos depends on a specific bioelectric prepattern that chemical or genetic teratogens alter; forcing a return to the correct prepattern in the neural plate, for example by activating the HCN2 channel, corrects brain morphology, gene expression and learning capacity in animals exposed to alcohol, nicotine or a dominant Notch mutation.
claims.quote: Forcing a return to the correct prepattern in the neural plate can correct brain morphology, gene expression, and learning capacity in animals exposed to alcohol, nicotine, or even mutations of the critical neurogenesis gene Notch [124, 125, 126].
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Bioelectricity as the Interface to Multicellularity › Birth Defect Repair and Limb Regeneration

claims.label: Cancer cells are not more selfish; they have smaller selves
claims.statement: On the cognitive light cone model of cancer, in which the 'cognitive light cone' is the spatiotemporal size of the homeodynamic goal states a system can pursue, cancer is a pathological rolling back to small cell-level goals: cancer cells are not more selfish but have smaller selves, treating the rest of the body as external environment.
claims.quote: But more specifically, the cognitive light cone model suggests that cancer cells are not more selfish; they just have smaller selves.
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Cancer and the Scaling of the Self

claims.label: Gap-junction closure in transformation is a positive feedback loop of isolation
claims.statement: Cells may physiologically disconnect from the tissue network (e.g. closing gap junctions under prolonged stress), and each reduction in connectivity makes local computation easier and further gap-junction closure more likely, a positive feedback loop of dissociation that makes tissue-level goals ever harder to achieve; Levin presents this as consistent with gap-junction closure in early transformation and with tumours induced by non-carcinogenic geometric barriers.
claims.quote: Each reduction in physiological connectivity makes it easier for cells to perform computations at the local level. This makes it easier for cells to close off gap junctions even more, driving a positive feedback loop—a cycle of dissociation and isolation that makes it ever harder to achieve large‐scale cell collective goals (maintaining complex anatomical structure).
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Cancer and the Scaling of the Self

claims.label: Oncogene-induced cancer can be detected early by bioelectrical imaging
claims.statement: Cancer induced in vivo by human oncogenes can be detected early by bioelectrical (membrane-voltage) imaging, as predicted by the view of cancer as a failure of bioelectric 'cognitive glue'.
claims.quote: It has now been shown that (a) cancer induced by human oncogenes in vivo can be detected early by bioelectrical imaging [175]
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Cancer and the Scaling of the Self

claims.label: Transient bioelectric and serotonergic perturbation induces a melanoma-like phenotype
claims.statement: Transient perturbation of bioelectrical and serotonergic signalling among cells can induce a melanoma-like phenotype in the absence of carcinogens, oncogenes or DNA damage.
claims.quote: (b) transient perturbation of bioelectrical and serotonergic signaling among cells can induce a melanoma‐like phenotype in the absence of carcinogens, oncogenes, or DNA damage [176, 177, 178]
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Cancer and the Scaling of the Self

claims.label: Oncogene-induced tumours can be prevented and normalized by managing bioelectric state
claims.statement: Tumours induced by powerful human oncogenes can be prevented and normalized by managing their bioelectric state (e.g. forcing hyperpolarization), without correcting the oncogene.
claims.quote: (c) tumors induced by powerful human oncogenes can be prevented and normalized by managing their bioelectric state [175, 179, 180, 181]
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Cancer and the Scaling of the Self

claims.label: Physiological information processing, not genetic hardware, dominates cancer outcomes
claims.statement: Levin interprets the ability to normalize oncogene-driven tumours by restoring bioelectric connectivity (reinflating cells' cognitive light cone) as showing that physiological information processing, not genetic hardware, dominates cancer outcomes, suggesting a clinical roadmap different from chemotherapy.
claims.quote: This ability to reinflate the cognitive light cone of cells shows that physiological information processing, not genetic hardware, dominates outcomes and suggests a clinical roadmap quite different from the chemotherapy that dominates the field today [165, 168, 182].
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Cancer and the Scaling of the Self

claims.label: Embryos in large groups form a 'hyperembryo' that resists teratogens better
claims.statement: Individual embryos raised in large groups form a kind of 'hyperembryo' with its own distinct transcriptome and an ability to resist teratogenic challenges far better than individual embryos or small groups.
claims.quote: For example, the hypothesis of scale‐free biology [196] has led to the discovery that individual embryos in large groups form a kind of “hyperembryo” with its own unique transcriptome and an ability to solve teratogenic challenges far better than individual embryos (or small groups) exhibit [197].
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Applications and a Roadmap Toward a Radical Regenerative Medicine › Top‐Down Control Exploits Agential Materials by Pushing Complexity from the Engineer onto the System Itself

claims.label: The same electroceutical, monensin, induces tails at tail wounds and legs at leg wounds
claims.statement: Applied systemically, the same bioelectric-modifying drug (monensin) triggers tail regeneration at tail wounds and leg regeneration at leg wounds, showing that the specificity of the regenerative response lies in the responding cell collective rather than in the reagent.
claims.quote: Even more remarkably, the exact same electroceutical—monensin—triggers tails in tail wounds and legs at leg wounds: the specificity in all of these cases is in the cell collective that responds to the stimulus [128, 200].
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Applications and a Roadmap Toward a Radical Regenerative Medicine › Top‐Down Control Exploits Agential Materials by Pushing Complexity from the Engineer onto the System Itself

claims.label: Aging may result from degraded bioelectric pattern memories that maintain tissue order
claims.statement: Levin proposes that aging is due to the degradation of endogenous bioelectric pattern memories required throughout life to maintain tissue order, so that solutions to aging need to target this information scaffold as well as cell-level rejuvenation (e.g. Yamanaka factors).
claims.quote: we have previously proposed that aging is due to the degradation of important endogenous (bioelectric) pattern memories that are required throughout the lifespan to maintain tissue order [146, 147].
claims.work: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine
claims.chapter: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Applications and a Roadmap Toward a Radical Regenerative Medicine › A Better Understanding of Disease: From Molecular Markers to Physiological Patterns

claims.label: Animal parts are either uniform (homogeneous) or composite
claims.statement: The parts of animals are of two kinds: simple parts, which divide into parts like themselves (as flesh into flesh), and composite parts, which do not (a hand does not divide into hands).
claims.quote: Of the parts of animals some are simple: to wit, all such as divide into parts uniform with themselves, as flesh into flesh; others are composite, such as divide into parts not uniform with themselves
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 1

claims.label: Parts of different genera can correspond only by analogy, as feather to scale
claims.statement: Animals of different genera may have parts that are the same only by analogy: bone corresponds to fish-bone, nail to hoof, hand to claw, and the feather of a bird to the scale of a fish.
claims.quote: they are the same only in the way of analogy, as, for instance, bone is only analogous to fish-bone, nail to hoof, hand to claw, and scale to feather; for what the feather is in a bird, the scale is in a fish.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 1

claims.label: The gadfly develops from river worms that leave the water
claims.statement: Some animals live first in water and later change their shape and live out of water; the gadfly develops from river worms in this way.
claims.quote: Some animals at first live in water, and by and by change their shape and live out of water, as is the case with river worms, for out of these the gadfly develops.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 1

claims.label: No bird with crooked talons is gregarious
claims.statement: No bird with crooked talons (a bird of prey) lives in flocks.
claims.quote: no bird furnished with crooked talons is gregarious
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 1

claims.label: Every domesticated kind of animal also exists in a wild form
claims.statement: Whenever a kind of animal is found domesticated, the same kind is always also found wild, as with horses, cattle, swine, sheep, goats and dogs.
claims.quote: whenever a race of animals is found domesticated, the same is always to be found in a wild condition; as we find to be the case with horses, kine, swine, (men), sheep, goats, and dogs.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 1

claims.label: An animal with a bladder always has an intestine, but not conversely
claims.statement: Every animal that has a bladder for wet residue also has an intestine for dry residue, but an animal may have an intestine without a bladder.
claims.quote: In other words, an animal has a bowel or intestine if it have a bladder; but an animal may have a bowel and be without a bladder.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 2

claims.label: Touch is the only sense common to all animals
claims.statement: Touch is the one and only sense that all animals possess.
claims.quote: One sense, and one alone, is common to all animals-the sense of touch.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 3

claims.label: Animals with more than four feet are bloodless
claims.statement: All animals with more than four feet are bloodless, as are the bee, the wasp, the cuttlefish and the crawfish, while animals with blood have no feet, two feet or four feet.
claims.quote: other animals are bloodless, such as the bee and the wasp, and, of marine animals, the cuttle-fish, the crawfish, and all such animals as have more than four feet.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 4

claims.label: In an egg the embryo forms from part of it, the rest being food
claims.statement: In an egg the embryo arises from only part of the egg, and the rest serves as food for the developing embryo, whereas a grub develops into the animal as a whole.
claims.quote: in respect to its primitive germ it comes from part only of the egg, while the rest serves for food as the germ develops.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 5

claims.label: Sharks hatch eggs inside their own bodies
claims.statement: Some viviparous animals, such as the sharks, hatch eggs inside their own bodies, while others, such as man and the horse, carry a live foetus.
claims.quote: Of viviparous animals, some hatch eggs in their own interior, as creatures of the shark kind; others engender in their interior a live foetus, as man and the horse.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 5

claims.label: Bloodless animals are largest in mild climates and in the sea
claims.statement: Among bloodless animals, the largest kinds live in milder climates, and those living in the sea are larger than those living on land or in fresh water.
claims.quote: And of these bloodless genera, those are the largest that dwell in milder climates, and those that inhabit the sea are larger than those living on dry land or in fresh water.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 5

claims.label: All hair-coated animals are viviparous
claims.statement: Every animal with a coat of hair (counting the spines of hedgehogs and porcupines as hair) bears live young.
claims.quote: All animals, however, that are hair-coated are viviparous.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 6

claims.label: Women's skulls have one circular suture, men's usually three meeting
claims.statement: The skull of a woman has one circular suture, while the skull of a man, as a general rule, has three sutures meeting at a point.
claims.quote: The skull has sutures: one, of circular form, in the case of women; in the case of men, as a general rule, three meeting at a point.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 7

claims.label: The mole has stunted eyes hidden under the skin
claims.statement: The mole cannot see and has no externally visible eyes, but beneath its skin lie the eye region and the dark parts of the eyes, stunted and overgrown by skin; it is the only viviparous animal without eyes.
claims.quote: For in point of absolute fact it cannot see, and has no eyes visible externally; but when the outer skin is removed, it is found to have the place where eyes are usually situated, and the black parts of the eyes rightly situated
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 9

claims.label: Man is the only, or nearly only, animal with varied eye colours
claims.statement: Man is the only, or nearly the only, animal whose eyes vary in colour between individuals; other animals as a rule have eyes of a single colour, though some horses have blue eyes.
claims.quote: Man is the only, or nearly the only, creature, that has eyes of diverse colours. Animals, as a rule, have eyes of one colour only.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 10

claims.label: The inner ear connects to the palate, not to the brain
claims.statement: The inner cavity of the ear has no passage to the brain but does have a passage to the palate.
claims.quote: This receptacle does not communicate by any passage with the brain, but does so with the palate
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 11

claims.label: Man is the only animal with ears that cannot move them
claims.statement: Of all animals that have ears, man is the only one that cannot move them.
claims.quote: Of animals possessed of ears man is the only one that cannot move this organ.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 11

claims.label: The crocodile alone moves its upper jaw instead of its lower
claims.statement: All animals move the lower jaw except the river crocodile, which moves only its upper jaw.
claims.quote: All animals move the lower jaw, with the exception of the river crocodile; this creature moves the upper jaw only.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 11

claims.label: Man has eight ribs on each side
claims.statement: The human trunk has eight ribs on each side.
claims.quote: Common to the upper and lower part of the trunk are the 'ribs', eight on either side
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 15

claims.label: Man has the largest and moistest brain for his size
claims.statement: Relative to body size, man has the largest and the moistest brain of any animal.
claims.quote: But, taking size for size of animal, the largest brain, and the moistest, is that of man.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 16

claims.label: The brain is bloodless, has no veins and is cold
claims.statement: In all animals the brain is bloodless, has no veins in it and is naturally cold to the touch.
claims.quote: The brain in all animals is bloodless, devoid of veins, and naturally cold to the touch
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 16

claims.label: The heart has three cavities, the right largest and the left smallest
claims.statement: The heart has three cavities: the right-hand one is the largest, the left-hand one the smallest, and the middle one intermediate in size.
claims.quote: It has three cavities, as has been said: the right-hand one the largest of the three, the left-hand one the least, and the middle one intermediate in size.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 17

claims.label: The lung is the organ most richly supplied with blood
claims.statement: In animals that have a lung and bear live young, the lung is the organ most richly supplied with blood, being spongy and reached at every pore by branches of the great vein; it is not empty, as some suppose.
claims.quote: the lung is of all organs the most richly supplied with blood; for the lung is throughout spongy in texture, and along by every single pore in it go branches from the great vein.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 17

claims.label: The right kidney lies higher than the left in all animals
claims.statement: In all animals that have kidneys, the right kidney lies higher in the body than the left.
claims.quote: In all animals that are provided with this organ, the right kidney is situated higher up than the other.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book I, Part 17

claims.label: The lion's neck is a single bone without vertebrae
claims.statement: The lion's neck consists of a single bone instead of vertebrae.
claims.quote: The lion has its neck composed of one single bone instead of vertebrae
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 1

claims.label: The elephant sleeps lying on its side, not standing
claims.statement: The elephant does not sleep standing; it bends its legs, settles down and sleeps lying on one side.
claims.quote: The elephant does not sleep standing, as some were wont to assert, but it bends its legs and settles down
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 1

claims.label: Horned animals are mostly cloven-hoofed; none is solid-hoofed with two horns
claims.statement: The great majority of horned animals are cloven-hoofed, and no solid-hoofed animal with a pair of horns has ever been found.
claims.quote: The great majority of the horned animals are cloven-footed, as the ox, the stag, the goat; and a solid-hooved animal with a pair of horns has never yet been met with.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 1

claims.label: Only the deer sheds its horns, annually after age two
claims.statement: The deer is the only animal that sheds its horns; it does so every year after reaching the age of two and grows them again.
claims.quote: The deer is the only animal that sheds its horns, and it does so annually, after reaching the age of two years, and again renews them.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 1

claims.label: The fox, wolf, marten and weasel have a bony penis
claims.statement: In some animals the penis is bony, as in the fox, the wolf, the marten and the weasel.
claims.quote: in other cases it is bony, as with the fox, the wolf, the marten, and the weasel; for this organ in the weasel has a bone.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 1

claims.label: No animal has both tusks and horns, nor does any saw-toothed animal
claims.statement: No animal has both tusks and horns, and no animal with interlocking pointed (saw-like) teeth has either tusks or horns.
claims.quote: No animal is there that possesses both tusks and horns, nor yet do either of these structures exist in any animal possessed of 'saw-teeth'.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 1

claims.label: No animal sheds its molars, and the pig sheds no teeth at all
claims.statement: Man sheds his front teeth, but no animal sheds its molars, and the pig sheds none of its teeth at all.
claims.quote: And man sheds his front teeth; but there is no instance of an animal that sheds its molars. The pig sheds none of its teeth at all.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 1

claims.label: Teeth blacken with age except in the horse, whose teeth whiten
claims.statement: As animals grow older their teeth generally become blacker, but the horse's teeth become whiter with age.
claims.quote: for, generally speaking, as animals grow older their teeth get blacker, but the horse's teeth grow whiter with age.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 3

claims.label: Males have more teeth than females in man, sheep, goats and swine
claims.statement: In men, sheep, goats and swine, males have more teeth than females.
claims.quote: Males have more teeth than females in the case of men, sheep, goats, and swine
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 3

claims.label: Animals with more teeth live longer, as a rule
claims.statement: As a rule, animals with more teeth live longer, and those with fewer and more thinly set teeth are correspondingly short-lived.
claims.quote: the more teeth they have the more long-lived are they, as a rule, while those are short-lived in proportion that have teeth fewer in number and thinly set.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 3

claims.label: Oviparous quadrupeds lack external ears, breasts and a copulatory organ
claims.statement: Oviparous blooded quadrupeds have no external ears but only an auditory passage, no breasts, no copulatory organ, and no external testicles, only internal ones.
claims.quote: Again, oviparous blooded quadrupeds are unprovided with ears, but possess only the passage for hearing; neither have they breasts, nor a copulatory organ, nor external testicles, but internal ones only
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 10

claims.label: River crocodiles spend the day on land and the night in water
claims.statement: As a rule, river crocodiles spend the daytime on land and the night in the water.
claims.quote: As a rule, they pass the day-time on land and the nighttime in the water
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 10

claims.label: Crocodiles enter water at night because it is then warmer than the air
claims.statement: Crocodiles spend the night in the water because at night the water is warmer than the open air.
claims.quote: for the temperature of the water is at night-time more genial than that of the open air.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 10

claims.label: The chameleon changes colour when it inflates itself with air
claims.statement: The chameleon changes colour when it is inflated with air, turning black, or green with black spots, over its whole body including the eyes and tail.
claims.quote: The change in its colour takes place when it is inflated with air; it is then black, not unlike the crocodile, or green like the lizard but black-spotted like the pard.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 11

claims.label: High-flying birds are four-toed, most three-forward one-back
claims.statement: Birds that fly high are all four-toed; most have three toes in front and one behind, and a few, such as the wryneck, have two in front and two behind.
claims.quote: Birds that fly high in air are in all cases four-toed: that is, the greater part have three toes in front and one behind in place of a heel; some few have two in front and two behind, as the wryneck.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 12

claims.label: No fish has a neck, limbs, testicles or breasts
claims.statement: No fish has a neck, any limb, testicles (internal or external), or breasts.
claims.quote: No fish has a neck, or any limb, or testicles at all, within or without, or breasts.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 13

claims.label: The dolphin has two breasts near its genitals
claims.statement: The dolphin bears live young directly and has two breasts placed near its genitals rather than high up, with no visible teats but two slits from which milk flows.
claims.quote: Thus the dolphin is directly viviparous, and accordingly we find it furnished with two breasts, not situated high up, but in the neighbourhood of the genitals.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 13

claims.label: Fishes have no organs or passages for hearing or smell
claims.statement: Of the sense organs fishes have only eyes; they have neither the organs of hearing and smell nor any passages for them.
claims.quote: with regard to the organs connected with the other senses, hearing and smell, they are devoid alike of the organs themselves and of passages indicative of them.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 13

claims.label: Scaly fish lay eggs; cartilaginous fish bear live young
claims.statement: Scaly fishes are always oviparous, and cartilaginous fishes are all viviparous except the fishing-frog.
claims.quote: scaly fish are invariably oviparous, but cartilaginous fishes are all viviparous, with the single exception of the fishing-frog.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 13

claims.label: Some oxen and the horse have a bone inside the heart
claims.statement: In one kind of ox, though not in every individual, a bone is found inside the heart, and the horse's heart also has a bone in it.
claims.quote: there is one species of ox where, though not in all cases, a bone is found inside the heart. And, by the way, the horse's heart also has a bone inside it.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 15

claims.label: Deer, horse, mule, ass, seal and some pigs lack a gall-bladder
claims.statement: Among viviparous quadrupeds the deer, the roe, the horse, the mule, the ass, the seal and some kinds of pig have no gall-bladder.
claims.quote: Of viviparous quadrupeds the deer is without the organ, as also the roe, the horse, the mule, the ass, the seal, and some kinds of pigs.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 15

claims.label: Stags always have about twenty maggots inside the head
claims.statement: Without exception, stags have maggots living inside the head, in the hollow beneath the root of the tongue and near the first vertebra, usually about twenty in a cluster.
claims.quote: However, without any exception, stags are found to have maggots living inside the head
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 15

claims.label: No fish or bird has kidneys or a bladder
claims.statement: No oviparous animal that is not a quadruped, whether fish or bird, is known to have kidneys or a bladder.
claims.quote: Of the ovipara that are not quadrupedal there is no instance known of an animal, whether fish or bird, provided with these organs.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 16

claims.label: Horned animals lacking upper front teeth have four stomachs and ruminate
claims.statement: Horned quadrupeds that lack a full set of teeth in both jaws have a stomach of four chambers, and these are the animals that chew the cud.
claims.quote: such of the horned animals as are not equally furnished with teeth in both jaws are furnished with four such chambers. These animals, by the way, are those that are said to chew the cud.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 17

claims.label: Serpents have thirty ribs, as many as the days of a month
claims.statement: Serpents have thirty ribs.
claims.quote: Their ribs are as numerous as the days of the month; in other words, they are thirty in number.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book II, Part 17

claims.label: Fishes, gilled animals and serpents have no testicles
claims.statement: No fish, no other gill-bearing animal and no serpent has testicles; nor does any footless animal except those that are viviparous within themselves.
claims.quote: No fish is furnished with testicles, nor any other creature that has gills, nor any serpent whatever: nor, in short, any animal devoid of feet, save such only as are viviparous within themselves.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 1

claims.label: Birds, oviparous quadrupeds and the hedgehog have internal testicles near the loin
claims.statement: Birds have testicles placed internally close to the loin, as do oviparous quadrupeds such as the lizard, the tortoise and the crocodile, and among viviparous animals the hedgehog.
claims.quote: Birds are furnished with testicles, but these are internally situated, close to the loin. The case is similar with oviparous quadrupeds, such as the lizard, the tortoise and the crocodile; and among the viviparous animals this peculiarity is found in the hedgehog.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 1

claims.label: Bird testicles enlarge greatly in the breeding season
claims.statement: Before the breeding season the testicles of birds are small or invisible, but during the breeding season they become greatly enlarged in all birds.
claims.quote: before the breeding season the organ is small in some birds and quite invisible in others, but during the season the organ in all cases is greatly enlarged.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 1

claims.label: Selachians are internally oviparous and externally viviparous
claims.statement: The dogfish and the other selachians (footless gilled animals that bear live young) produce eggs inside the body, and the eggs turn into young within the womb before birth.
claims.quote: With animals devoid of feet that are internally oviparous and viviparous externally, as is the case with the dogfish and the other so-called Selachians
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 1

claims.label: The viper is the only viviparous serpent
claims.statement: Serpents as a rule lay eggs; the viper is the only serpent that bears live young, and it does so by first producing eggs internally.
claims.quote: Serpents as a rule are oviparous, the viper being the only viviparous member of the genus. The viper is, previously to external parturition, oviparous internally
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 1

claims.label: Horned animals, hare, mouse and bat have cotyledons in the pregnant womb
claims.statement: Pregnant females of horned animals lacking upper front teeth have cotyledons in the womb, as do the hare, the mouse and the bat; all other viviparous footed animals with teeth in both jaws have a smooth womb with the embryo attached directly to it.
claims.quote: the females of horned nonambidental animals are furnished with cotyledons in the womb when they are pregnant, and such is the case, among ambidentals, with the hare, the mouse, and the bat
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 1

claims.label: The great blood-vessels originate in the heart, not the head
claims.statement: The two great blood-vessels (the great vein and the aorta) have their origin in the heart, not, as earlier writers held, in the head or brain.
claims.quote: These blood-vessels have their origins in the heart, for they traverse the other viscera, in whatever direction they happen to run, without in any way losing their distinctive characteristic as blood-vessels
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 3

claims.label: The heart has three chambers, all visible only in the largest animals
claims.statement: The heart has three chambers; in small animals even the largest chamber is scarcely visible, in medium-sized animals the second is scarcely visible, and only in the largest animals are all three distinctly seen.
claims.quote: In the case of the smaller animals even the largest of the chambers is scarcely discernible; the second larger is scarcely discernible in animals of medium size; but in the largest animals all three chambers are distinctly seen.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 3

claims.label: The brain contains no blood and no vein
claims.statement: In all animals the brain itself is bloodless, and no vein, large or small, runs within it; veins end in the membrane around the brain.
claims.quote: The brain itself in all animals is destitute of blood, and no vein, great or small, holds its course therein.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 3

claims.label: Fibres in the blood cause it to coagulate
claims.statement: Blood coagulates because of a fibrous matter it contains; if the fibre is left in, the blood coagulates, and if it is removed, the blood cannot coagulate.
claims.quote: If this fibre be left in the blood, the blood will coagulate; if it be removed or extracted, the blood is found to be incapable of coagulation.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 6

claims.label: Deer, roe and antelope blood lacks fibre and clots weakly
claims.statement: The blood of the deer, the roe, the antelope and some other animals lacks the coagulating fibre, and so does not coagulate as firmly as the blood of other animals.
claims.quote: we fail to find it in the blood of the deer, the roe, the antelope, and some other animals; and, owing to this deficiency of the fibrous tissue, the blood of these animals does not coagulate to the extent observed in the blood of other animals.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 6

claims.label: The crocodile is the only animal that moves its upper jaw
claims.statement: Animals in general move the lower jaw; the river crocodile is the only animal that moves the upper jaw.
claims.quote: Animals in general move the lower jaw; the river crocodile is the only animal that moves the upper one.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 7

claims.label: The dolphin has true bone, not fish-spine
claims.statement: The dolphin's skeleton is made of bone, like that of viviparous quadrupeds, not of fish-spine.
claims.quote: The dolphin has bones, and not fish-spine.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 7

claims.label: Only the stag has solid branching horns, shed annually unless castrated
claims.statement: Of all animals only the stag has horns that are solid throughout and branched, and only the deer sheds its horns, annually, unless it has been castrated.
claims.quote: In the case of the stag alone of all animals the horns are solid throughout, and ramify into branches (or antlers). And, whereas no other animal is known to shed its horns, the deer sheds its horns annually, unless it has been castrated
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 9

claims.label: All toed animals have nails except the elephant
claims.statement: All animals that have feet with toes have nails, except the elephant, whose toes are undivided and slightly jointed and which has no nails at all.
claims.quote: all animals have nails that have toes, and toes that have feet, except the elephant; and the elephant has toes undivided and slightly articulated, but has no nails whatsoever
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 9

claims.label: Viviparous footed animals have hair, oviparous footed have scutes, fishes scales
claims.statement: All viviparous animals with feet have hair; all oviparous animals with feet have horny plates; and fishes, and only fishes, have scales.
claims.quote: All viviparous animals furnished with feet have hair; all oviparous animals furnished with feet have horn-like tessellates; fishes, and fishes only, have scales
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 10

claims.label: Grey hairs are mostly white from the start, so greying is not withering
claims.statement: Hair greys from the tip back toward the root, but most grey hairs are white from the beginning, which shows that greying is not a withering or decrepitude of the hair.
claims.quote: Hair turns grey from the point backwards to the roots. But, in the majority of cases, grey hairs are white from the beginning; and this is a proof that greyness of hair does not, as some believe to be the case, imply withering or decrepitude
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book III, Part 11

claims.label: Boys, women and castrated men never go bald
claims.statement: No boy, no woman and no castrated man ever becomes bald, and a man castrated before puberty never grows the later hair (pubic, axillary, beard).
