claims.statement: Many birds do not migrate to warmer countries but hide where they are in winter; swallows have often been found in holes without feathers, and the kite, stork, turtle-dove, lark and others go into hiding.
claims.quote: A great number of birds also go into hiding; they do not all migrate, as is generally supposed, to warmer countries.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 16

claims.label: The she-bear gives birth during winter concealment and emerges in spring
claims.statement: The she-bear gives birth while in winter concealment and stays hidden until she brings the cubs out in spring, about three months after the winter solstice; bears eat nothing while hidden.
claims.quote: The female brings forth her young at this time, and remains in concealment until it is time to bring the cubs out; and she brings them out in spring, about three months after the winter solstice.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 17

claims.label: Crustaceans moult not once but repeatedly
claims.statement: Crabs, crawfish and lobsters slough their shells, becoming soft all over, and they do so not once for all but over and over again.
claims.quote: These animals also do not cast their skins once and for all, but over and over again.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 17

claims.label: Fishes have no pestilential diseases like those of man and livestock
claims.statement: No pestilential (epidemic) disease is known to attack fishes as such diseases attack man, horses and oxen, although individual fishes do appear to fall sick.
claims.quote: We know of no pestilential malady attacking fishes, such as those which attack man, and horses and oxen among the quadrupedal vivipara
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 19

claims.label: The purple murex dies within a day of tasting fresh water
claims.statement: Shellfish generally benefit from rain, but the purple murex is an exception: placed near a river mouth, it dies within a day of tasting fresh water.
claims.quote: if it be placed on a shore near to where a river discharges, it will die within a day after tasting the fresh water.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 20

claims.label: The pig is the only animal known to get measles
claims.statement: The pig is the only animal known to suffer from 'measles' (pimples in the flesh, seen especially under the tongue), and pigs never get it while still sucklings.
claims.quote: The pig is the only animal known to be subject to measles.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 21

claims.label: Rabies passes to every animal bitten by a mad dog except man
claims.statement: Rabies drives dogs mad and is fatal to them, and any animal bitten by a rabid dog catches it and dies, with the exception of man.
claims.quote: ary animal whatever, excepting man, will take the disease if bitten by a dog so afflicted; the disease is fatal to the dog itself, and to any animal it may bite, man excepted.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 22

claims.label: The ass tolerates cold least and is absent from Scythia
claims.statement: Of all animals of its kind the ass is least able to endure extreme cold, which is why it is not found on the shores of the Black Sea or in Scythia.
claims.quote: Of all animals on its of its kind it is the least capable of enduring extreme cold, which circumstance will account for the fact that the animal is not found on the shores of the Euxine, nor in Scythia.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 25

claims.label: All insects die when smeared with oil
claims.statement: All insects without exception die if smeared with oil, and die faster if the head is smeared and they are laid in the sun.
claims.quote: All insects, without exception, die if they be smeared over with oil; and they die all the more rapidly if you smear their head with the oil and lay them out in the sun.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 27

claims.label: The leopard is absent from Europe while lions live in part of Greece
claims.statement: Lions are more numerous in Libya and in the part of Europe between the Achelous and the Nessus rivers; the leopard is more abundant in Asia Minor and is not found in Europe at all.
claims.quote: lions are more numerous in Libya, and in that district of Europe that lies between the Achelous and the Nessus; the leopard is more abundant in Asia Minor, and is not found in Europe at all.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 28

claims.label: Different species breed together if similar in size and gestation length
claims.statement: In Libya animals of different species meet at watering places and pair, and such pairs often breed if they are nearly the same size and have gestation periods of the same length.
claims.quote: such pairs will often breed if they be nearly of the same size and have periods of gestation of the same length.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 28

claims.label: Wolves and dogs interbreed, and the Laconian hound is a fox–dog cross
claims.statement: Animals of different kinds produce hybrids: in Cyrene the wolf and the bitch couple and breed, and the Laconian hound is a cross between the fox and the dog.
claims.quote: Elsewhere also bastard-animals are born to heterogeneous pairs; thus in Cyrene the wolf and the bitch will couple and breed; and the Laconian hound is a cross between the fox and the dog.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 28

claims.label: A scaly fish's age can be told from the size and hardness of its scales
claims.statement: The age of a scaly fish can be told from the size and hardness of its scales.
claims.quote: The age of a scaly fish may be told by the size and the hardness of its scales.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book VIII, Part 30

claims.label: Females are less spirited than males, except in the bear and leopard
claims.statement: In all animals with separate sexes the female is less spirited (less courageous) than the male, except in the bear and the leopard, where the female is the more courageous.
claims.quote: In all cases, excepting those of the bear and leopard, the female is less spirited than the male; in regard to the two exceptional cases, the superiority in courage rests with the female.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 1

claims.label: Animals sharing a locality or food are enemies
claims.statement: Animals that live in the same localities or feed on the same food are enemies, and when food runs short animals of the same kind fight one another.
claims.quote: There is enmity between such animals as dwell in the same localities or subsist on the food. If the means of subsistence run short, creatures of like kind will fight together.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 1

claims.label: With unlimited food, wild animals would be tame to man and each other
claims.statement: If there were no shortage of food, animals that are now wild or afraid of man would become tame towards man and peaceable towards one another, as fed animals in Egypt show.
claims.quote: One may go so far as to say that if there were no lack or stint of food, then those animals that are now afraid of man or are wild by nature would be tame and familiar with him, and in like manner with one another.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 1

claims.label: Stag antler points increase yearly until about six years old
claims.statement: Stags grow no horns in their first year, unbranched spikes in their second, two-pointed antlers in the third and three-pointed in the fourth, increasing in complexity until about six years old, after which antlers no longer indicate age.
claims.quote: In the third year the antlers are bifurcate; in the fourth year they grow trifurcate; and so they go on increasing in complexity until the creature is six years old: after this they grow their horns without any specific differentiation, so that you cannot by observation of them tell the animal's age.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 5

claims.label: Hinds swallow the afterbirth immediately after giving birth
claims.statement: After giving birth, the hind (female deer) at once swallows the afterbirth, catching it before it falls to the ground.
claims.quote: The hinds after parturition at once swallow the afterbirth, and it is impossible to secure it, for the hind catches it before it falls to the ground
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 5

claims.label: Sick animals treat themselves, e.g. dogs eat grass to vomit
claims.statement: Many quadrupeds treat their own ailments: dogs, when ill, eat a kind of grass that makes them vomit.
claims.quote: Many other quadrupeds help themselves in clever ways. Wild goats in Crete are said, when wounded by arrows, to go in search of dittany, which is supposed to have the property of ejecting arrows in the body. Dogs, when they are ill, eat some kind of grass and produce vomiting.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 6

claims.label: The trochilus cleans the crocodile's teeth
claims.statement: When the crocodile gapes, a small bird, the trochilus, enters its mouth and cleans its teeth, feeding itself thereby, and the crocodile does not harm it.
claims.quote: When the crocodile yawns, the trochilus flies into his mouth and cleans his teeth. The trochilus gets his food thereby, and the crocodile gets ease and comfort; it makes no attempt to injure its little friend
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 6

claims.label: Pigeons pair for life
claims.statement: Pigeons pair with the same mate until one of the pair dies, though occasionally a female mates with a bird other than her mate.
claims.quote: In pairing the same male and the same female keep together; and the union is only broken by the death of one of the two parties.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 7

claims.label: Heavy-bodied birds like quails and partridges build no nests
claims.statement: Heavy-bodied birds such as quails and partridges build no nests but lay in a scraped hollow on level ground, since nest building would be of no use to birds that cannot fly well.
claims.quote: Birds of a heavy build, such as quails, partridges, and the like, build no nests; indeed, where they are incapable of flight, it would be of no use if they could do so.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 8

claims.label: Partridge hens feign lameness to lure intruders from the brood
claims.statement: When a man comes upon a partridge brood, the hen rolls in front of him pretending to be lame, drawing him away until the young have escaped, then returns and calls them back.
claims.quote: When a man comes by chance upon a young brood, and tries to catch them, the hen-bird rolls in front of the hunter, pretending to be lame: the man every moment thinks he is on the point of catching her, and so she draws him on and on, until every one of her brood has had time to escape
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 8

claims.label: Web-footed birds all live near water
claims.statement: All web-footed birds live near the sea, rivers or pools, because they resort to places suited to their structure.
claims.quote: Web-footed birds without exception live near the sea or rivers or pools, as they naturally resort to places adapted to their structure.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 12

claims.label: Swans sing chiefly as they approach death
claims.statement: Swans are musical and sing chiefly at the approach of death, flying out to sea at that time.
claims.quote: They are musical, and sing chiefly at the approach of death; at this time they fly out to sea, and men, when sailing past the coast of Libya, have fallen in with many of them out at sea singing in mournful strains
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 12

claims.label: The cuckoo lays a single egg in another bird's nest and does not hatch it
claims.statement: The cuckoo builds no nest, lays only one egg in the nest of another bird, and leaves the foster mother to hatch and rear it.
claims.quote: it lays only one egg and does not hatch it itself, but the mother-bird in whose nest it has deposited it hatches and rears it
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 29

claims.label: Cuckoos lay in others' nests because of their own cowardice
claims.statement: The cuckoo places its young in another bird's nest because it is the most cowardly of birds and could not defend its young in an emergency.
claims.quote: The cuckoo shows great sagacity in the disposal of its progeny; the fact is, the mother cuckoo is quite conscious of her own cowardice and of the fact that she could never help her young one in an emergency
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 29

claims.label: A pair of eagles needs a large territory and drives other birds away
claims.statement: A pair of eagles needs an extensive area to maintain itself, so it expels its fledged young from the neighbourhood and does not allow other birds to settle nearby.
claims.quote: The fact is that a pair of eagles demands an extensive space for its maintenance, and consequently cannot allow other birds to quarter themselves in close neighbourhood.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 32

claims.label: The sea-eagle makes its young stare at the sun and kills those that cannot
claims.statement: Before its young are fledged the sea-eagle makes them stare at the sun, beats any that refuse, and kills one whose eyes water.
claims.quote: the sea-eagle is very keen-sighted, and before its young are fledged tries to make them stare at the sun, and beats the one that refuses to do so, and twists him back in the sun's direction; and if one of them gets watery eyes in the process, it kills him, and rears the other.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 34

claims.label: The fishing-frog lures prey with filaments in front of its eyes
claims.statement: The fishing-frog (angler) has long thin filaments with rounded tips in front of its eyes which it raises as bait while hidden in sand and mud, drawing small fish that touch them into its mouth.
claims.quote: The fishing-frog has a set of filaments that project in front of its eyes; they are long and thin like hairs, and are round at the tips; they lie on either side, and are used as baits.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: The torpedo stuns its prey with a shock from its body
claims.statement: The torpedo (electric ray) catches its prey by numbing it with a shock residing in its body, and can numb humans too.
claims.quote: The torpedo narcotizes the creatures that it wants to catch, overpowering them by the power of shock that is resident in its body, and feeds upon them
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: The male sheat-fish guards the spawn for forty to fifty days
claims.statement: In the sheat-fish the female leaves after spawning while the male guards the spawn and fry, driving off small fish, for forty or fifty days until the young can escape on their own.
claims.quote: contenting himself with keeping off all other little fishes that might steal the spawn or fry, and this he does for forty or fifty days, until the young are sufficiently grown to make away from the other fishes for themselves.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: All fish are carnivorous except a few, and carnivorous fish wander most
claims.statement: All fish are carnivorous except a few such as the grey mullet, the saupe, the red mullet and the chalcis, and the carnivorous fish wander most.
claims.quote: Carnivorous fish wander most; and all fish are carnivorous with the exception of a few, such as the mullet, the saupe, the red mullet, and the chalcis.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: Only the sepia uses its ink for concealment; octopus and squid ink from fear
claims.statement: Among cephalopods the sepia (cuttlefish) alone discharges its ink for concealment as well as from fear, while the octopus and calamary (squid) discharge it only from fear.
claims.quote: Of molluscs the sepia is the most cunning, and is the only species that employs its dark liquid for the sake of concealment as well as from fear: the octopus and calamary make the discharge solely from fear.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: The octopus changes colour to match nearby stones
claims.statement: The octopus hunts by changing its colour to match the adjacent stones, and does so also when alarmed.
claims.quote: It seeks its prey by so changing its colour as to render it like the colour of the stones adjacent to it; it does so also when alarmed.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: The octopus as a rule does not live beyond one year
claims.statement: The octopus as a rule does not live a full year, and after spawning the female in particular becomes weak, stupid and wastes away.
claims.quote: The octopus as a rule does not live the year out.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: The argonaut uses its web as a sail and arms as oars
claims.statement: The nautilus (argonaut) rises to the surface and, when a breeze blows, uses a thin web between its arms as a sail and lets down some arms as rudder-oars.
claims.quote: It uses this structure, when a breeze is blowing, for a sail, and lets down some of its feelers alongside as rudder-oars.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 37

claims.label: Spiders spin from the surface of the body, not from an excretion
claims.statement: Spiders can spin from birth, and their thread comes off the body like bark rather than from inside as a superfluity or excretion, contrary to Democritus.
claims.quote: Spiders can spin webs from the time of their birth, not from their interior as a superfluity or excretion, as Democritus avers, but off their body as a kind of tree-bark
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 39

claims.label: On each trip a bee visits flowers of only one kind
claims.statement: On each foraging trip a bee goes from flower to flower of one kind only and does not visit another kind until it has returned to the hive.
claims.quote: On each expedition the bee does not fly from a flower of one kind to a flower of another, but flies from one violet, say, to another violet, and never meddles with another flower until it has got back to the hive
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 40

claims.label: Bees kill most of their kings to prevent the hive splitting
claims.statement: Worker bees kill most of their kings, especially inferior ones, to prevent a multiplicity of kings from splitting the hive, and destroy royal cells when no swarm is intended.
claims.quote: These bees also kill without mercy most of their kings, and especially kings of the inferior sort; and this they do for fear a multiplicity of kings should lead to a dismemberment of the hive.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 40

claims.label: A bee that stings dies because it loses its gut with the sting
claims.statement: A bee that stings dies because it cannot withdraw its sting without tearing out its intestines; once it loses its sting it must die.
claims.quote: Bees that sting die from their inability to extract the sting without at the same time extracting their intestines.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 40

claims.label: Older bees work indoors, younger bees forage outside
claims.statement: Older bees do the work inside the hive and are rough and hairy from staying indoors, while young bees do the carrying outside and are comparatively smooth.
claims.quote: The elder bees do the indoor work, and are rough and hairy from staying indoors; the young bees do the outer carrying, and are comparatively smooth.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 40

claims.label: Bees carry a stone as ballast in high wind
claims.statement: In a high wind bees carry a stone as ballast to steady their flight.
claims.quote: In a high wind they carry a stone by way of ballast to steady them.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 40

claims.label: Worker wasps all die in winter; only the mother-wasps overwinter
claims.statement: Worker wasps do not survive into a second year but all die as winter comes on, while the larger mother-wasps survive the winter in holes underground.
claims.quote: The workers do not live over into a second year, but all die when winter comes on; and this can be proved, for at the commencement of winter the workers become drowsy, and about the time of the winter solstice they are never seen at all.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 41

claims.label: Lions attack humans when old and their teeth are diseased
claims.statement: Lions invade cattle-folds and attack humans when old age and diseased teeth prevent them from catching their usual prey.
claims.quote: They invade the cattle-folds and attack human beings when they are grown old and so by reason of old age and the diseased condition of their teeth are unable to pursue their wonted prey.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 44

claims.label: The elephant breathes through its trunk to cross water
claims.statement: The elephant can make its way through water as long as the tip of its trunk is above the surface, because it breathes through its trunk.
claims.quote: he can make his way through water, as long as the tip of his trunk can be above the surface, for he blows with his trunk and breathes through it.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 46

claims.label: Hens that beat a cock become cock-like, even growing spurs
claims.statement: Hens that have beaten the cock in a fight crow like a cock, try to tread him, raise a crest and tail-feathers, and sometimes grow small spurs.
claims.quote: Hens, for instance, when they have beaten the cock in a fight, will crow like the cock and endeavour to tread him; the crest rises up on their head and the tail-feathers on the rump, so that it becomes difficult to recognize that they are hens; in some cases there is a growth of small spurs.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 49

claims.label: Castrated cocks lose their crest colour, crowing and sexual drive
claims.statement: A full-grown cock castrated by cauterizing the rump loses the colour of its crest, stops crowing and loses sexual desire; if castrated young, it never develops these male traits.
claims.quote: If you burn this twice or thrice with hot irons, then, if the bird be full-grown, his crest grows sallow, he ceases to crow, and foregoes sexual passion; but if you cauterize the bird when young, none of these male attributes propensities will come to him as he grows up.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: Boys castrated before puberty keep a high voice; eunuchs never go bald
claims.statement: Men castrated in boyhood never grow the later hair and keep a high-pitched voice, and a eunuch never goes bald.
claims.quote: if you mutilate them in boyhood, the later-growing hair never comes, and the voice never changes but remains high-pitched
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: Stags castrated before growing horns never grow them
claims.statement: Stags castrated before they have horns never grow horns, and stags castrated when they have horns keep them unchanged in size and do not shed them.
claims.quote: If stags be mutilated, when, by reason of their age, they have as yet no horns, they never grow horns at all; if they be mutilated when they have horns, the horns remain unchanged in size, and the animal does not lose them.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: Animals lacking upper teeth are the ones that ruminate
claims.statement: The animals that ruminate are those lacking upper (front) teeth, such as cattle, sheep and goats, though a few with teeth in both jaws also ruminate.
claims.quote: It is the animals that lack the upper teeth that ruminate, such as kine, sheep, and goats.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: Many birds change plumage colour and song with the seasons
claims.statement: Many birds change the colour of their plumage and their song with the season; for example, the blackbird turns yellow instead of black and its song changes.
claims.quote: A considerable number of birds change according to season the colour of their plumage and their note; as, for instance, the owsel becomes yellow instead of black, and its note gets altered
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: The redbreast and the redstart are one bird in two seasonal forms
claims.statement: The robin (a winter bird) and the redstart (a summer bird) change into one another and differ only in plumage colour; likewise the beccafico and the blackcap.
claims.quote: The erithacus (or redbreast) and the so-called redstart change into one another; the former is a winter bird, the latter a summer one, and the difference between them is practically limited to the coloration of their plumage.
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: Ground birds dust-bathe; waterside birds water-bathe
claims.statement: Birds that do not fly but live on the ground take dust-baths, waterside birds and some straight-taloned birds take water-baths, and most crooked-taloned birds take neither.
claims.quote: Birds that do not fly but keep on the ground take the dust-bath, as for instance the hen, the partridge, the francolin, the crested lark, the pheasant; some of the straight-taloned birds, and such as live on the banks of a river, in marshes, or by the sea, take a water-bath
claims.chapter: The History of Animals, Book IX, Part 50

claims.label: The final cause comes before the motor cause in explaining nature
claims.statement: Of the causes at work in the generation of natural things, the final cause (the end or purpose) is prior to the motor cause, in nature as in art.
claims.quote: Plainly, however, that cause is the first which we call the final one. For this is the Reason, and the Reason forms the starting-point, alike in the works of art and in works of nature.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 1

claims.label: The vertebrae are not formed by accidental breaking of the foetal backbone
claims.statement: The division of the backbone into vertebrae is not, as Empedocles held, the result of the backbone being broken by the contorted position of the foetus in the womb, nor are animal characters in general mere incidents of development.
claims.quote: Empedocles, then, was in error when he said that many of the characters presented by animals were merely the results of incidental occurrences during their development; for instance, that the backbone was divided as it is into vertebrae, because it happened to be broken owing to the contorted position of the foetus in the womb.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 1

claims.label: Like begets like: the parent's characters determine the offspring's
claims.statement: Man is generated from man, and it is the possession of certain characters by the parent that determines the development of like characters in the offspring.
claims.quote: For man is generated from man; and thus it is the possession of certain characters by the parent that determines the development of like characters in the child.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 1

claims.label: Only man has intellect, though other animals move themselves
claims.statement: Other animals besides man have the power of locomotion, but none but man has intellect.
claims.quote: I say not the intellectual part; for other animals than man have the power of locomotion, but in none but him is there intellect.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 1

claims.label: Respiration is driven by an alternation of heat and cooling
claims.statement: Breathing exists for the alternate discharge and re-entry of heat, and the alternation of heating and cooling in the body necessarily produces the alternate intake and discharge of outer air.
claims.quote: For the alternate discharge and re-entrance of heat and the inflow of air are necessary if we are to live. Here we have at once a necessity in the former of the two senses. But the alternation of heat and refrigeration produces of necessity an alternate admission and discharge of the outer air, and this is a necessity of the second kind.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 1

claims.label: Some ants fly and others do not
claims.statement: Among ants some fly and others do not, so Flying versus Walking cannot be used to divide animal kinds.
claims.quote: For some groups, Ants for instance, fall under both divisions, some ants flying while others do not.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 3

claims.label: Groups such as Wild and Tame cannot divide species, since tame kinds also occur wild
claims.statement: In almost all kinds of animal of which some members are tame, other members are wild, so wildness and tameness are not specific differences.
claims.quote: For in almost all species in which some members are tame, there are other members that are wild. Such, for example, is the case with Men, Horses, Oxen, Dogs in India, Pigs, Goats, Sheep
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 3

claims.label: Natural groups are marked by many differentiae, not by dichotomy
claims.statement: Animals should be classified into the natural groups that mankind instinctively recognizes, such as Birds and Fishes, each defined by many differentiae together, and not by successive two-way division on a single character.
claims.quote: The method then that we must adopt is to attempt to recognize the natural groups, following the indications afforded by the instincts of mankind, which led them for instance to form the class of Birds and the class of Fishes, each of which groups combines a multitude of differentiae, and is not defined by a single one as in dichotomy.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 3

claims.label: Within a class animals differ by degree; across classes their parts are only analogous
claims.statement: Animals within one class differ only by degree (more and less of the same part), while different classes agree only in having analogous organs, as the bird's feather corresponds to the fish's scale.
claims.quote: For instance, bird differs from bird by gradation, or by excess and defect; some birds have long feathers, others short ones, but all are feathered. Bird and Fish are more remote and only agree in having analogous organs; for what in the bird is feather, in the fish is scale.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 4

claims.label: Groups lacking lungs or blood have analogous organs and fluids in their place
claims.statement: Some groups of animals have lungs and others have instead an organ analogous to a lung; some have blood and others have instead a fluid analogous to blood with the same office.
claims.quote: For instance, some groups have lungs, others have no lung, but an organ analogous to a lung in its place; some have blood, others have no blood, but a fluid analogous to blood, and with the same office.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 5

claims.label: The body exists for the soul and each part for its function
claims.statement: As each instrument serves some action, the body is made for the soul and each part of the body for some subordinate function to which it is adapted.
claims.quote: Thus the saw is made for sawing, for sawing is a function, and not sawing for the saw. Similarly, the body too must somehow or other be made for the soul, and each part of it for some subordinate function, to which it is adapted.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Part 5

claims.label: Homogeneous tissues exist for the sake of the heterogeneous organs
claims.statement: Animals are composed of homogeneous parts (such as bone and flesh) and heterogeneous parts (such as face and hand), and the homogeneous parts exist for the sake of the heterogeneous ones, which carry on the body's functions.
claims.quote: Animals, then, are composed of homogeneous parts, and are also composed of heterogeneous parts. The former, however, exist for the sake of the latter. For the active functions and operations of the body are carried on by these; that is, by the heterogeneous parts, such as the eye, the nostril, the whole face, the fingers, the hand, and the whole arm.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 1

claims.label: The heart is the seat of sensation, motion and nutrition in blooded animals
claims.statement: The sensory, motor and nutritive faculties are lodged in one central part, which in animals with blood is the heart and in bloodless animals the part that takes the place of a heart.
claims.quote: For this reason it is the heart which in sanguineous animals constitutes this central part, and in bloodless animals it is that which takes the place of a heart.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 1

claims.label: Thick hot blood gives strength; thin cool blood gives sensation and intelligence
claims.statement: The thicker and hotter an animal's blood, the more it conduces to strength; the thinner and colder, the better suited it is to sensation and intelligence; those with hot, thin and clear blood are best for both courage and intelligence.
claims.quote: As regards the results of such differences, the thicker and the hotter blood is, the more conducive is it to strength, while in proportion to its thinness and its coldness is its suitability for sensation and intelligence.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 2

claims.label: Blood solidifies outside the body, yellow bile becomes more fluid
claims.statement: Blood is hot and fluid in the living body but becomes cold and coagulates when separated from it, whereas yellow bile becomes more fluid when separated.
claims.quote: Of the former blood is an example, of the latter bile; for while blood solidifies when thus separated, yellow bile under the same circumstances becomes more fluid.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 3

claims.label: Nearly all animals, and all that move about, have a stomach
claims.statement: Animals, with scarcely an exception and conspicuously all those capable of locomotion, have a stomach-sac that serves them as an internal substitute for the earth from which plants draw food.
claims.quote: But animals, with scarcely an exception, and conspicuously all such as are capable of locomotion, are provided with a stomachal sac, which is as it were an internal substitute for the earth.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 3

claims.label: Blood is the final nutriment and its quantity follows food intake
claims.statement: Blood is the final nutritive material of the body in animals that have it; it diminishes in quantity when no food is taken, increases when much is eaten, and is healthy or unhealthy according to the food.
claims.quote: This explains why the blood diminishes in quantity when no food is taken, and increases when much is consumed, and also why it becomes healthy and unhealthy according as the food is of the one or the other character.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 3

claims.label: Deer and roe blood has no fibres and never coagulates
claims.statement: The blood of deer and of roe deer contains no fibres and for this reason never coagulates.
claims.quote: There are none, for instance, in the blood of deer and of roes; and for this reason the blood of such animals as these never coagulates.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 4

claims.label: Bloodless animals are more timorous, freezing and discharging excretions when frightened
claims.statement: Bloodless animals are, as a general rule, more timorous than animals with blood: when frightened they stay motionless, discharge their excretions and in some cases change colour.
claims.quote: This also explains why bloodless animals are, as a general rule, more timorous than such as have blood, so that they remain motionless, when frightened, and discharge their excretions, and in some instances change colour.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 4

claims.label: Bull's blood coagulates faster than any other animal's
claims.statement: Bulls and boars have blood exceedingly rich in fibres, and the bull's blood coagulates more rapidly than that of any other animal.
claims.quote: This explains why bulls and boars are so choleric and so passionate. For their blood is exceedingly rich in fibres, and the bull's at any rate coagulates more rapidly than that of any other animal.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 4

claims.label: Horned animals lacking upper front teeth have suet; others have lard
claims.statement: Horned animals without front teeth in the upper jaw have fat in the form of suet, whereas hornless animals with front teeth in both jaws and toed feet have lard, which neither coagulates nor dries into a friable mass.
claims.quote: Thus it is that in those horned animals that have no front teeth in the upper jaw the fat consists of suet.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 5

claims.label: Fat animals are less prolific
claims.statement: Fat animals are less prolific than others, because the blood that should form semen is used up in making lard and suet.
claims.quote: For the same reason fat animals are less prolific than others. For that part of the blood which should go to form semen and seed is used up in the production of lard and suet
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 5

claims.label: The lion's bones have almost no marrow
claims.statement: Animals with strong and solid bones, such as the lion, have hardly any marrow, the lion's being so insignificant that its bones look as though they had none.
claims.quote: There are some animals that can hardly be said to have any marrow. These are those whose bones are strong and solid, as is the case with the lion. For in this animal the marrow is so utterly insignificant that the bones look as though they had none at all.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 6

claims.label: The brain is the coldest part of the body and bloodless in its substance
claims.statement: Of all parts of the body none is as cold as the brain, which is cold to the touch and has no blood in its proper substance.
claims.quote: The coldness of the brain is also manifest enough. For in the first place it is cold even to the touch; and, secondly, of all the fluid parts of the body it is the driest and the one that has the least blood; for in fact it has no blood at all in its proper substance.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 7

claims.label: The brain exists to cool the heat of the heart
claims.statement: Nature has made the brain, a compound of earth and water, as a counterpoise to the heat of the region of the heart, to moderate it.
claims.quote: nature has contrived the brain as a counterpoise to the region of the heart with its contained heat, and has given it to animals to moderate the latter, combining in it the properties of earth and water.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 7

claims.label: Every animal with blood has a brain; no bloodless animal has one
claims.statement: Every animal with blood has a brain, whereas no bloodless animal has such an organ, except by analogy, as in the poulp (octopus).
claims.quote: For this reason it is, that every sanguineous animal has a brain; whereas no bloodless creature has such an organ, unless indeed it be, as the Poulp, by analogy.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 7

claims.label: The brain causes sleep by chilling the blood rising after food
claims.statement: The brain, or its analogue, is the cause of sleep: by chilling the blood that streams upward after food it produces heaviness in the head and drives the heat downward with the blood.
claims.quote: It is the brain again-or, in animals that have no brain, the part analogous to it-which is the cause of sleep. For either by chilling the blood that streams upwards after food, or by some other similar influences, it produces heaviness in the region in which it lies
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 7

claims.label: Man has the largest brain for his size, and men larger than women
claims.statement: Of all animals, man has the largest brain in proportion to his size, and the brain is larger in men than in women.
claims.quote: Of all animals, man has the largest brain in proportion to his size; and it is larger in men than in women.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 7

claims.label: Only in man does the bregma solidify last
claims.statement: In man the cranial bone called the bregma is the last to become solidified, because evaporation continues through it under the influence of heat; man is the only animal with blood in which this happens.
claims.quote: it is again owing to this superabundance that the cranial bone, which some call the Bregma, is the last to become solidified; so long does evaporation continue to occur through it under the influence of heat. Man is the only sanguineous animal in which this takes place.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 7

claims.label: Man has more skull sutures than any animal, males more than females
claims.statement: Man has more sutures in his skull than any other animal, and the male more than the female, because the larger brain requires more ventilation.
claims.quote: Man, again, has more sutures in his skull than any other animal, and the male more than the female.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 7

claims.label: Crustaceans and testaceans have their hard supporting part outside
claims.statement: In all crustaceans and testaceans the fleshy substance is within and the hard earthy matter is outside, and the shell both holds the soft parts together and keeps in their scanty natural heat.
claims.quote: For in all these animals the fleshy substance is within, and the earthy matter, which holds the soft parts together and keeps them from injury, is on the outside. For the shell not only enables the soft parts to hold together, but also, as the animal is bloodless and so has but little natural warmth, surrounds it
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 8

claims.label: Cuttlefish and squid have an internal shell; the octopus has none
claims.statement: Cuttlefishes have an internal hard part (the os sepiae) and calamaries (squids) the gladius, but poulps (octopuses) have no such part because their body-sac is short.
claims.quote: For instance, in the Cuttle-fishes there is what is known as the os sepiae, and in the Calamaries there is the so-called gladius. In the Poulps, on the other hand, there is no such internal part
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 8

claims.label: The belly wall is boneless in all animals
claims.statement: The walls of the belly are in all animals devoid of bones, so as not to hinder its expansion after a meal or the growth of the foetus in females.
claims.quote: The walls of this are in all animals devoid of bones; in order that there may be no hindrance to the expansion which necessarily occurs in this part after a meal, nor, in females, any interference with the growth of the foetus, which is lodged here.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 9

claims.label: Males' bones are harder than females', carnivores' harder than herbivores'
claims.statement: The bones of males are harder than those of females, and the bones of carnivores that get their food by fighting are harder than those of herbivores.
claims.quote: Thus it is that the bones of males are harder than those of females; and the bones of flesh-eaters, that get their food by fighting, are harder than those of Herbivora.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 9

claims.label: The lion's bones are so hard they give off sparks when struck
claims.statement: The lion's bones are so hard that when struck they give off sparks, as though they were stones.
claims.quote: Of this the Lion is an example; for so hard are its bones, that, when struck, they give off sparks, as though they were stones.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 9

claims.label: The dolphin, being viviparous, has bones rather than fish-spines
claims.statement: The dolphin, being viviparous, has bones and not fish-spines.
claims.quote: It may be mentioned also that the Dolphin, in as much as it is viviparous, is provided with bones and not with fish-spines.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 9

claims.label: Selachians have cartilage instead of fish-spine, for undulating movement
claims.statement: In selachians (cartilaginous fishes) the fish-spines are replaced by cartilage, because their undulating movement requires a pliable rather than brittle supporting framework.
claims.quote: Lastly, in the Selachia, as they are called, the fish-spines are replaced by cartilage. For it is necessary that the movements of these animals shall be of an undulating character; and this again requires the framework that supports the body to be made of a pliable and not of a brittle substance.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 9

claims.label: Neither cartilage nor bone grows again once cut off
claims.statement: Cartilage and bone differ only in degree, and neither cartilage nor bone grows again once cut off.
claims.quote: Cartilage and bone are indeed fundamentally the same thing, the differences between them being merely matters of degree. Thus neither cartilage nor bone, when once cut off, grows again.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 9

claims.label: The brain is insensible and not the cause of sensation
claims.statement: The brain cannot be the cause of any sensation, being itself as without feeling as any of the excretions; the sensory centre is the region of the heart.
claims.quote: and, as to the other half of their statement, the brain cannot be the cause of any of the sensations, seeing that it is itself as utterly without feeling as any one of the excretions.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 10

claims.label: Birds and scaly oviparous quadrupeds have no external ears
claims.statement: Birds have no ears but only the auditory passages, because their skin is hard and they have feathers instead of hair; the same is true of oviparous quadrupeds clad in scaly plates.
claims.quote: In birds, on the other hand, there are no ears, but only the auditory passages. This is because their skin is hard and because they have feathers instead of hairs, so that they have not got the proper material for the formation of ears.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 12

claims.label: The seal has no external ears, only auditory passages
claims.statement: The seal, alone among viviparous quadrupeds, has no ears but only the auditory passages, being a quadruped of stunted formation.
claims.quote: There is also one of the viviparous quadrupeds, namely the seal, that has no ears but only the auditory passages. The explanation of this is that the seal, though a quadruped, is a quadruped of stunted formation.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 12

claims.label: Some animals close the eye with the lower lid; birds blink with a membrane
claims.statement: Viviparous animals have two eyelids and use both to close and to blink; oviparous quadrupeds and heavy-bodied birds close the eye with the lower lid only, while birds blink with a membrane issuing from the corner of the eye.
claims.quote: whereas the oviparous quadrupeds, and the heavy-bodied birds as well as some others, use only the lower lid to close the eye; while birds blink by means of a membrane that issues from the canthus.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 13

claims.label: Birds of prey are sharp-sighted, ground fowl are not
claims.statement: Birds with talons, which search for prey by eye from aloft and soar higher than other birds, are sharp-sighted, while common fowls and similar ground-living birds have no such keenness of vision.
claims.quote: This too explains why birds with talons, that have to search for prey by eye from aloft, and therefore soar to greater heights than other birds, are sharpsighted; while common fowls and the like, that live on the ground and are not made for flight, have no such keenness of vision.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 13

claims.label: Fishes, insects and crustaceans have no eyelids
claims.statement: Fishes, insects and hard-skinned crustaceans have no eyelids; insects and still more crustaceans compensate for their hard eyes by having movable eyes.
claims.quote: Fishes and Insects and the hard-skinned Crustacea present certain differences in their eyes, but so far resemble each other as that none of them have eyelids.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 13

claims.label: All hairy animals have eyelashes; birds and scaly animals lack them, except the ostrich
claims.statement: All animals with hair on the body have eyelashes, while birds and animals with scaly plates, being hairless, have none; the Libyan ostrich is an exception, having eyelashes though a bird.
claims.quote: All animals that have hairs on the body have lashes on the eyelids; but birds and animals with scale-like plates, being hairless, have none. The Libyan ostrich, indeed, forms an exception; for, though a bird, it is furnished with eyelashes.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 14

claims.label: Only man has lashes on both eyelids; no quadruped has a lower eyelash
claims.statement: Of hairy animals, man alone has lashes on both eyelids; no quadruped has a lower eyelash, though some have a few scattered hairs under the lower lid.
claims.quote: Of hairy animals, man alone has lashes on both lids.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 14

claims.label: The elephant uses its nostril as a hand
claims.statement: The elephant's proboscis is a nostril which it uses as a hand, conveying food and drink to its mouth and tearing up trees by coiling it round their stems.
claims.quote: For the elephant uses its nostril as a hand; this being the instrument with which it conveys food, fluid and solid alike, to its mouth. With it, too, it tears up trees, coiling it round their stems.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 16

claims.label: Elephants breathe through the raised trunk when crossing water
claims.statement: Elephants, being both land and swamp animals, have a lengthened nostril which, when they traverse water, they lift above the surface and breathe through, like a diver's breathing instrument.
claims.quote: so also have elephants been furnished by nature with their lengthened nostril; and, whenever they have to traverse the water, they lift this up above the surface and breathe through it.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 16

claims.label: Birds that pronounce letters best have the broadest tongues
claims.statement: Among birds, those most capable of pronouncing letters have the broadest tongues, whereas viviparous quadrupeds, whose tongue is hard, thick and not free, have very limited vocal articulation.
claims.quote: What has been said explains why, among birds, those that are most capable of pronouncing letters are such as have the broadest tongues; and why the viviparous and sanguineous quadrupeds, where the tongue is hard and thick and not free in its motions, have a very limited vocal articulation.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 17

claims.label: All birds communicate with their tongues, some seeming to teach one another
claims.statement: All birds use their tongues to communicate with each other, some more than others, so that in some cases it seems as though actual instruction passes from one bird to another.
claims.quote: All birds use their tongues to communicate with each other. But some do this in a greater degree than the rest; so that in some cases it even seems as though actual instruction were imparted from one to another by its agency.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 17

claims.label: Serpents and lizards have long forked tongues suited to taste
claims.statement: Land-dwelling oviparous animals with blood mostly have a tongue tied down and hard, but in serpents and lizards it is long and forked, suiting it to the perception of savours.
claims.quote: As to those oviparous and sanguineous animals that live not in the air but on the earth, their tongue in most cases is tied down and hard, and is therefore useless for vocal purposes; in the serpents, however, and in the lizards it is long and forked, so as to be suited for the perception of savours.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 17

claims.label: The crocodile moves its upper jaw and its tongue adheres to the lower
claims.statement: The crocodile's tongue is adherent to the lower jaw, which is immobile; in the crocodile it is the upper jaw that moves, the reverse of other animals.
claims.quote: For the crocodile's tongue is adherent to the lower jaw. For its upper and lower jaws are, as it were, inverted, it being the upper jaw which in other animals is the immovable one.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 17

claims.label: Purple snails bore through shells with their tongue
claims.statement: In the purpurae (purple snails) the tongue-like part is so strong that it bores holes through the shells of other shellfish, such as the spiral snails used as bait to catch them.
claims.quote: In the Purpurae, for instance, so strong is this part that it enables them to bore holes through the hard covering of shell-fish, of the spiral snails, for example, that are used as bait to catch them.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book II, Part 17

claims.label: Sharp interlocking teeth and tusks never occur together
claims.statement: No animal that has sharp, interlocking (saw-like) teeth also has tusks; tusks go to animals that strike in fighting and saw-teeth to those that bite.
claims.quote: No animal that has sharp interfitting teeth is at the same time furnished with tusks. For nature never makes anything superfluous or in vain.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 1

claims.label: Nature gives each weapon only, or most fully, to animals that can use it
claims.statement: Nature allots each offensive or defensive weapon (sting, spur, horn, tusk) only, or in a more developed form, to the animals that can use it, and in its most perfect form to those that can use it best.
claims.quote: Nature allots each weapon, offensive and defensive alike, to those animals alone that can use it; or, if not to them alone, to them in a more marked degree; and she allots it in its most perfect state to those that can use it best
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 1

claims.label: Weapons such as horns and spurs are confined to or larger in males
claims.statement: Because males are stronger and more spirited than females, weapons such as horns, tusks and spurs are found only in males in some species and are more fully developed in males in others (e.g. stags have horns and hinds none; hens often lack the spurs of cocks).
claims.quote: Thus as males are stronger and more choleric than females, it is in males that such parts as those just mentioned are found, either exclusively, as in some species, or more fully developed, as in others.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 1

claims.label: All fishes have saw-like teeth except the parrot-fish (Scarus)
claims.statement: All fishes have sharp, serrated (saw-like) teeth, with the single exception of the Scarus (parrot-fish).
claims.quote: All fishes have teeth of the serrated form, with the single exception of the fish known as the Scarus.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 1

claims.label: Hook-clawed birds have hooked beaks and eat no vegetable food
claims.statement: Birds with crooked talons (birds of prey) invariably have a hooked beak, because they are carnivorous and eat no vegetable food at all.
claims.quote: Thus in those birds that are called Crooked-clawed it is invariably hooked, inasmuch as these birds are carnivorous, and eat no kind of vegetable food whatsoever.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 1

claims.label: True horns occur only in viviparous animals
claims.statement: True horns exist only in viviparous animals; what are called horns in some egg-laying animals are horns only by metaphor and are never used for fighting.
claims.quote: They exist in none but viviparous animals; though in some ovipara certain parts are metaphorically spoken of as horns, in virtue of a certain resemblance.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 2

claims.label: Deer alone have solid horns and alone shed them
claims.statement: Deer are the only animals whose horns are solid throughout, and the only animals that shed their horns.
claims.quote: Deer are the only animals in which the horns are solid throughout, and are also the only animals that cast them.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 2

claims.label: No horned animal has front teeth in the upper jaw
claims.statement: No horned animal has front teeth in both jaws; the upper front teeth are lacking, because the material taken from the teeth is added to the horns.
claims.quote: Thus it is that no animal that has horns has also front teeth in both jaws, those in the upper jaw being deficient. For nature by subtracting from the teeth adds to the horns
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 2

claims.label: Animals without a lung have no neck
claims.statement: An animal that has no lung has no neck, the neck existing for the windpipe; fishes are an example.
claims.quote: Therefore it is that, when there is no lung, there is also no neck. Of this condition the Fishes are an example.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 3

claims.label: Only hairy, lunged animals have an epiglottis
claims.statement: An epiglottis is found only in animals with blood that have a lung and a hairy skin; animals covered with scaly plates or feathers have none, the larynx itself closing instead.
claims.quote: This part is not found in all sanguineous animals, but only in such of them as have a lung; nor in all of these, but only in such as at the same time have their skin covered with hairs, and not either with scaly plates or with feathers.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 3

claims.label: Only animals with blood have viscera
claims.statement: Viscera (heart, lung, liver, spleen, kidneys) are found only in animals with blood; no bloodless animal has any viscera at all.
claims.quote: These are peculiar to sanguineous animals, some of which have all of them, others only a part, while no bloodless animals have any at all.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 4

claims.label: The heart is the first part formed and at once contains blood
claims.statement: In animals with blood the heart is the first of all the parts to be formed in the embryo, and it contains blood as soon as it is formed.
claims.quote: For the heart is the first of all the parts to be formed; and no sooner is it formed than it contains blood.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 4

claims.label: The heart is the source of all sensation, pain and pleasure
claims.statement: The motions of pain, pleasure and all sensation have their source in the heart and end there; the heart, not the head, is the primary seat of sensation.
claims.quote: Moreover, the motions of pain and pleasure, and generally of all sensation, plainly have their source in the heart, and find in it their ultimate termination.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 4

claims.label: Only in man does the heart lie to the left of centre
claims.statement: In every animal except man the heart lies in the middle of the chest; in man it inclines a little to the left, to counterbalance the coldness of that side.
claims.quote: In all animals but man the heart is placed in the centre of the pectoral region; but in man it inclines a little towards the left, so that it may counterbalance the chilliness of that side.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 4

claims.label: Only the horse and a kind of ox have a bone in the heart
claims.statement: No animal has a bone in its heart except the horse and a certain kind of ox, where the large heart needs a bony support.
claims.quote: In no animals does the heart contain a bone, certainly in none of those that we have ourselves inspected, with the exception of the horse and a certain kind of ox.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 4

claims.label: Large animals' hearts have three cavities, smaller ones two
claims.statement: In animals of great size the heart has three cavities, in smaller animals two, and in every animal at least one.
claims.quote: In animals of great size the heart has three cavities; in smaller animals it has two; and in all has at least one
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 4

claims.label: Animals with a large heart are timid, with a small heart courageous
claims.statement: An animal with a large heart is timid and one with a smaller, moderate heart is more courageous; the hare, deer, mouse, hyena, ass, leopard and marten have large hearts.
claims.quote: So also when the heart is of large size the animal is timorous, while it is more courageous if the organ be smaller and of moderate bulk.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 4

claims.label: Blood is the material from which the whole body is built
claims.statement: Blood is the material from which every part of the body is made, which is why nature has laid down vessels like irrigation channels throughout the whole body.
claims.quote: Now just after the same fashion has nature laid down channels for the conveyance of the blood throughout the whole body, because this blood is the material out of which the whole fabric is made.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 5

claims.label: Breathing serves to cool; fishes are cooled by water and have gills, not a lung
claims.statement: Animals with blood must be cooled from outside, by air or by water; fishes are cooled by water and therefore never have a lung but have gills in its place.
claims.quote: The external cooling agent must be either air or water. In fishes the agent is water. Fishes therefore never have a lung, but have gills in its place
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 6

claims.label: Viviparous animals have large blood-rich lungs, oviparous ones small dry lungs
claims.statement: In viviparous animals the lung is large and full of blood because of their natural heat, while in egg-laying animals (oviparous quadrupeds and birds) it is small, dry and spongy but can expand greatly when inflated.
claims.quote: In the vivipara it is large and rich in blood, because of their natural heat; while in the ovipara it is small and dry but capable of expanding to a vast extent when inflated.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 6

claims.label: Heart and liver, and only these, are found in every animal with blood
claims.statement: Every animal with blood has a heart and a liver, and these are the only two viscera invariably present in all of them.
claims.quote: All sanguineous animals, then, need these two parts; and this explains why these two viscera, and these two alone, are invariably found in them all.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 7

claims.label: Feathered and scaly animals lack a bladder, tortoises excepted
claims.statement: Animals covered with feathers, scales or scaly plates have no urinary bladder, the tortoises being the only exception.
claims.quote: all these animals, owing to the small amount of fluid which they imbibe, and owing also to such residue as there may be being converted into feathers and the like, are invariably without a bladder. The Tortoises, which are comprised among animals with scaly plates, form the only exception
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 8

claims.label: Feathered and scaly animals have no kidneys, tortoises excepted
claims.statement: Kidneys are lacking in all animals clad with feathers, scales or scaly plates, the sea and land tortoises being the only exception; some birds have only flattened kidney-like bodies.
claims.quote: For these also are wanting in all animals that are clad with feathers or with scales or with scale-like plates; the sea and land tortoises forming the only exception.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 9

claims.label: The right kidney always lies higher than the left
claims.statement: In all animals that have kidneys, the right kidney is placed higher than the left.
claims.quote: In all animals that have kidneys, that on the right is placed higher than that on the left.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 9

claims.label: Man is the only animal that laughs
claims.statement: Man is the only animal that laughs, and therefore the only animal that is affected by tickling.
claims.quote: That man alone is affected by tickling is due firstly to the delicacy of his skin, and secondly to his being the only animal that laughs.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 10

claims.label: Viviparous animals with front teeth in both jaws have a single stomach
claims.statement: The stomach is single in all viviparous animals with blood that have front teeth in both jaws, such as man, dog, lion, horse, mule, ass and pig.
claims.quote: Thus the stomach is single in all such sanguineous and viviparous animals as have teeth in front of both jaws.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 14

claims.label: Horned animals have several stomachs because they lack upper front teeth
claims.statement: Horned animals (sheep, ox, goat, deer and the like) have several stomachs, because they lack front teeth in the upper jaw and the stomachs make up for the imperfect chewing.
claims.quote: A similar multiplicity of stomachs exists also in the horned animals; the reason being that horn-bearing animals have no front teeth in the upper jaw.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 14

claims.label: The parrot-fish alone among fishes ruminates
claims.statement: The Scarus (parrot-fish) apparently ruminates, though no other fish does.
claims.quote: And this is probably the reason why this fish apparently ruminates, though no other fishes do so.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 14

claims.label: Rennet occurs in all multi-stomached animals and, among others, in the hare
claims.statement: Rennet is found in all animals with a multiple stomach and, among single-stomached animals, in the hare.
claims.quote: What is known as rennet is found in all animals that have a multiple stomach, and in the hare among animals whose stomach is single.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book III, Part 15

claims.label: Vipers and selachians produce eggs internally and bear live young
claims.statement: Vipers among serpents, like the selachians (cartilaginous fishes) among fishes, first produce eggs internally and then bring forth live young.
claims.quote: For both these and vipers are externally viviparous, but previously produce ova internally.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 1

claims.label: All fishes have a gall-bladder, mostly attached to the intestine
claims.statement: All fishes have a gall-bladder, and in most of them it is attached to the intestine rather than to the liver.
claims.quote: For all fishes have a gall-bladder; and in most of them it is attached to the intestine
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 2

claims.label: Horse, mule, ass, deer and roe have no gall-bladder
claims.statement: Some animals have no gall-bladder at all, among them the horse, mule, ass, deer and roe; the camel has only small biliary vessels, and the seal and dolphin have none.
claims.quote: For in some animals there is absolutely no gall-bladder at all--in the horse, for instance, the mule, the ass, the deer, and the roe
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 2

claims.label: Gall-bladder size in sheep and goats varies by locality
claims.statement: Sheep and goats usually have a gall-bladder, but in some localities (Naxos) it is enormously large and in others (a district of Chalcis in Euboea) it is altogether absent.
claims.quote: For these animals usually have a gall-bladder; but, while in some localities it is so enormously big as to appear a monstrosity, as is the case in Naxos, in others it is altogether wanting
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 2

claims.label: Animals without a gall-bladder are long-lived
claims.statement: Animals without a gall-bladder, such as deer, solid-hoofed animals, the camel and the dolphin, are long-lived.
claims.quote: For such have no gall-bladder and live long. But besides these there are other animals that have no gall-bladder, though those old writers had not noticed the fact, such as the camel and the dolphin; and these also are, as it happens, long-lived.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 2

claims.label: All cephalopods have ink, the cuttlefish most
claims.statement: All cephalopods have ink, and the cuttlefish (Sepia) has more of it than any other.
claims.quote: All Cephalopoda alike have this characteristic ink, but chief of all the Sepia, where it is more abundant than in the rest.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 5

claims.label: Crayfish and some crabs have a second set of teeth in the stomach
claims.statement: In the Carabi (spiny lobsters and the like) and some crabs the stomach has a second set of teeth, because the front teeth are not enough to chew the food properly.
claims.quote: and then a stomach, which in the Carabi and some of the Crabs is furnished with a second set of teeth, the anterior teeth being insufficient for adequate mastication.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 5

claims.label: Sea-urchin 'eggs' grow largest at full moon
claims.statement: The so-called eggs of sea-urchins become larger than usual at the time of the full moon, because the nights are then warmer from the moonlight, not because the urchins eat more.
claims.quote: yet they acquire a greater size than usual at the time of full moon; not, as some think, because sea-urchins eat more at that season, but because the nights are then warmer, owing to the moonlight.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 5

claims.label: Every sea-urchin has five 'eggs', five teeth and five stomachs
claims.statement: The number of so-called eggs is the same in all sea-urchins and is odd: five, matching their five teeth and five stomach compartments.
claims.quote: The number of the ova is the same in all sea-urchins, and is an odd one. For there are five ova, just as there are also five teeth and five stomachs
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 5

claims.label: Nature passes from lifeless things to animals by unbroken gradation
claims.statement: Nature passes from lifeless things to animals in an unbroken sequence, with living things that are not animals between them, so that neighbouring groups scarcely differ.
claims.quote: For nature passes from lifeless objects to animals in such unbroken sequence, interposing between them beings which live and yet are not animals, that scarcely any difference seems to exist between two neighbouring groups owing to their close proximity.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 5

claims.label: Cicadas live on moisture deposited from the air
claims.statement: Cicadas find enough to live on in the moisture deposited from the air, insects in general being small eaters because of their cold nature.
claims.quote: In no insects is this so conspicuous as in these Cicadae. For they find enough to live on in the moisture which is deposited from the air.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 5

claims.label: Very small flying insects have only two wings
claims.statement: Flying insects that are very small have only two wings, as flies do, while larger ones such as bees have four.
claims.quote: When, however, such insects are of very small bulk, their feathers are reduced to two, as is the case with flies.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 6

claims.label: In crabs and spiny lobsters the right claw is always the larger
claims.statement: In the Carabi (spiny lobsters and crayfish) and in crabs the right claw is invariably the larger and stronger; only in the lobster is it a matter of chance which claw is larger.
claims.quote: In the Carabi and in the Crabs the right claw is invariably the larger and the stronger.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 8

claims.label: All cephalopods have eight feet, short in cuttlefish and squid, long in octopus
claims.statement: All cephalopods have eight feet, which are short in cuttlefish and squid and longer in the octopus.
claims.quote: Again, though the number of feet is the same in all the Cephalopoda, namely eight, their length varies in different kinds, being short in the Sepias and the Calamaries, but greater in the Poulps.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 9

claims.label: Wolves and lions have a neck made of a single bone
claims.statement: In all other animals the neck is flexible and has several vertebrae, but in wolves and lions it consists of a single bone.
claims.quote: In all other animals this neck is flexible and contains several vertebrae; but in wolves and lions it contains only a single bone.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 10

claims.label: Foals are nearly as tall as grown horses, with relatively long legs
claims.statement: In solid- and cloven-hoofed quadrupeds the lower parts are largest in youth, so that foals are scarcely shorter than full-grown horses and can touch their heads with their hind legs, which adults cannot.
claims.quote: Thus it is that colts are scarcely, if at all, below full-grown horses in height; and that while still young they can touch their heads with the hind legs, though this is no longer possible when they are older.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 10

claims.label: Man has hands because he is intelligent, not intelligent because he has hands
claims.statement: Man does not owe his superior intelligence to his hands, as Anaxagoras held; he has hands because he is the most intelligent animal, nature giving each organ to the animal that can use it.
claims.quote: we must conclude that man does not owe his superior intelligence to his hands, but his hands to his superior intelligence.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 10

claims.label: Wolves, lions, dogs and leopards have five front toes and four hind
claims.statement: Some polydactylous quadrupeds, such as wolves, lions, dogs and leopards, have five digits on each forefoot but only four on each hind foot.
claims.quote: It is this hand-like office of the anterior limbs which explains why in some of the polydactylous quadrupeds, such as wolves, lions, dogs, and leopards, there are actually five digits on each forefoot, though there are only four on each hind one.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 10

claims.label: Mammae: two at the thighs in animals with few young, many on the belly in litter-bearers
claims.statement: Animals that bear few young at a time, whether horned or solid-hoofed, have two mammae in the region of the thighs, while litter-bearing or polydactylous animals have numerous teats along the belly or two in the middle of the abdomen.
claims.quote: Thus in such animals as produce but few at a birth, whether horned quadrupeds or those with solid hoofs, the mammae are placed in the region of the thighs, and are two in number, while in such as produce litters, or such as are polydactylous, the dugs are either numerous and placed laterally on the belly, as in swine and dogs
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 10

claims.label: All female quadrupeds urinate backwards; only a few males do
claims.statement: All female quadrupeds urinate backwards, while among males only a few do so, such as the lynx, lion, camel and hare; no solid-hoofed quadruped urinates backwards.
claims.quote: All female quadrupeds void their urine backwards, because the position of the parts which this implies is useful to them in the act of copulation. This is the case with only some few males, such as the lynx, the lion, the camel, and the hare.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 10

claims.label: Man alone lacks a tail and alone has buttocks
claims.statement: Man has no tail but has buttocks, which no quadruped has; the nourishment that would go to a tail goes to the buttocks and fleshy legs that upright posture requires.
claims.quote: But man is tail-less. He has, however, buttocks, which exist in none of the quadrupeds.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 10

claims.label: Huckle-bones occur mostly in cloven-hoofed animals, never in many-toed ones
claims.statement: No polydactylous quadruped has a huckle-bone (astragalus), solid-hoofed animals as a rule lack one, and most animals that have one are cloven-hoofed.
claims.quote: As to the polydactylous quadrupeds, none of them have huckle-bones. For if they had they would not be polydactylous, but the divisions of the foot would only extend to that amount of its breadth which was covered by the huckle-bone. Thus it is that most of the animals that have huckle-bones are cloven-hoofed.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 10

claims.label: The river crocodile alone among these animals has no tongue
claims.statement: All oviparous quadrupeds and serpents have a tongue in the mouth except the river crocodile, which has only a space where a tongue would be.
claims.quote: and in all, with the single exception of the river crocodile, there is a tongue inside the mouth.
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 11

claims.label: Oviparous quadrupeds have no upper eyelid and close the eye with the lower
claims.statement: Oviparous quadrupeds have no upper eyelid and close the eye with the lower lid, as birds do.
claims.quote: These animals have no upper eyelid, but close the eye with the lower lid In this they resemble birds
claims.chapter: On the Parts of Animals, Book IV, Part 11

claims.label: The crocodile moves its upper jaw rather than its lower
claims.statement: In all other animals it is the lower jaw that moves, but in the river crocodile it is the upper jaw.
