claims.statement: The spacing of a Turing pattern at onset is set by the reaction rates and diffusivities, not by the size of the tissue, so changing these parameters predictably changes the number of repeated elements.
claims.chapter: The chemical basis of morphogenesis (1952)

claims.label: Reaction-diffusion of morphogens accounts for biological pattern
claims.statement: Chemical substances that react and diffuse through tissue (morphogens) are sufficient to account for the main phenomena of morphogenesis.
claims.chapter: The chemical basis of morphogenesis (1952)

claims.label: Kimura fixation probability of a mutant allele
claims.statement: The probability that a mutant allele eventually fixes in a finite population depends on its initial frequency, its selective advantage and the effective population size, and equals its initial frequency when it is neutral.
claims.work: On the probability of fixation of mutant genes in a population
claims.chapter: On the probability of fixation of mutant genes in a population (1962)

claims.label: Neutral substitution rate equals the mutation rate
claims.statement: For neutral mutations the long-run rate of molecular substitution equals the mutation rate per generation, independent of population size, which yields a molecular clock.
claims.work: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level
claims.chapter: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level (1968)

claims.label: Mean time to fixation of a neutral mutant
claims.statement: A neutral mutant that does go to fixation takes on average about four times the effective population size, in generations, to do so.
claims.work: The average number of generations until fixation of a mutant gene in a finite population
claims.chapter: The average number of generations until fixation of a mutant gene in a finite population (1969)

claims.label: Neutral equilibrium heterozygosity (Kimura-Crow)
claims.statement: Under neutral mutation to new alleles and drift, expected heterozygosity reaches an equilibrium that rises with the product of effective population size and mutation rate.
claims.work: The number of alleles that can be maintained in a finite population
claims.chapter: The number of alleles that can be maintained in a finite population (1964)

claims.label: Neutral theory: most molecular substitutions are neutral
claims.statement: Most evolutionary changes at the molecular level are caused by random drift of selectively neutral or nearly neutral mutations, not by positive selection.
claims.work: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level
claims.chapter: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level (1968)

claims.label: Hamilton's rule
claims.statement: A gene for social behaviour increases in frequency when the benefit to the recipient, weighted by genetic relatedness, exceeds the cost to the actor.
claims.work: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. I
claims.chapter: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. I (1964)

claims.label: Haplodiploidy hypothesis for eusociality
claims.statement: Because full sisters in haplodiploid species share three quarters of their genes, more than a mother shares with her offspring, haplodiploid insects are predisposed to evolve sterile worker castes.
claims.work: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. II
claims.chapter: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. II (1964)

claims.label: Local mate competition sex ratio
claims.statement: When a few mothers lay eggs on a patch and their offspring mate there before the daughters disperse, the evolutionarily stable sex ratio is female-biased, and the bias weakens as the number of mothers grows.
claims.chapter: Extraordinary Sex Ratios (1967)

claims.label: Declining force of selection with age
claims.statement: The strength of selection on survival falls with age after reproduction begins, so senescence is an inevitable outcome of natural selection.
claims.work: The moulding of senescence by natural selection
claims.chapter: The moulding of senescence by natural selection (1966)

claims.label: Evolutionarily stable strategy conditions
claims.statement: A strategy is evolutionarily stable if, once common, it cannot be invaded by any rare alternative strategy.
claims.chapter: The Logic of Animal Conflict (1973)

claims.label: Hawk-Dove mixed ESS
claims.statement: When the cost of injury exceeds the value of the contested resource, the stable outcome is a mixture in which animals escalate with probability equal to the ratio of resource value to injury cost.
claims.work: Evolution and the Theory of Games
claims.chapter: Evolution and the Theory of Games (1982)

claims.label: War of attrition ESS
claims.statement: In contests settled by display, where the animal willing to persist longer wins and costs grow with time, the stable strategy is to choose a persistence time at random from an exponential distribution whose mean equals the resource value.
claims.work: The theory of games and the evolution of animal conflicts
claims.chapter: The theory of games and the evolution of animal conflicts (1974)

claims.label: Twofold cost of sex
claims.statement: An asexual mutant female in a sexual population with equal sex ratio produces twice as many grandchildren as a sexual female, so sex needs a compensating advantage of up to twofold to persist.
claims.chapter: The Evolution of Sex (1978)

claims.label: Genetic hitchhiking (selective sweep)
claims.statement: When a favourable mutation sweeps to fixation, it reduces genetic variation at closely linked neutral sites, and the reduction is larger the tighter the linkage relative to the strength of selection.
claims.work: The hitch-hiking effect of a favourable gene
claims.chapter: The hitch-hiking effect of a favourable gene (1974)

claims.label: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
claims.statement: In an infinitely large, randomly mating diploid population with no selection, mutation or migration, the genotype frequencies at a biallelic autosomal locus reach p^2, 2pq, q^2 after a single generation and stay there, with allele frequencies unchanged.
claims.thinker: G. H. Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg
claims.work: Mendelian Proportions in a Mixed Population
claims.chapter: Mendelian Proportions in a Mixed Population (1908)

claims.label: The Price equation (covariance form)
claims.statement: For any population partitioned into entities i with fitness w_i and character value z_i, the change in the population mean character between generations equals the covariance of fitness with character plus the fitness-weighted mean of within-entity transmission change, each divided by mean fitness.
claims.chapter: Selection and Covariance (1970)

claims.label: Bilayer curvature from differential swelling (Timoshenko)
claims.statement: A thin two-layer strip whose layers swell by different amounts bends with a uniform curvature proportional to the swelling-strain mismatch, with a geometric coefficient fixed by the thickness ratio and modulus ratio of the layers; the pine cone scale is such a bilayer, its outer (active) sclerenchyma layer swelling along the scale and its inner (passive) layer not.
claims.work: Hygromorphs: from pine cones to biomimetic bilayers
claims.chapter: Hygromorphs: from pine cones to biomimetic bilayers (2009)

claims.label: Hygromorph response time scales as thickness squared
claims.statement: The time a hygromorphic bilayer takes to respond to a change in ambient humidity is set by diffusion of water through its thickness, so it grows as the square of the thickness divided by the diffusion coefficient.
claims.work: Hygromorphs: from pine cones to biomimetic bilayers
claims.chapter: Hygromorphs: from pine cones to biomimetic bilayers (2009)

claims.label: Antisymmetric fibre angles turn differential swelling into twist
claims.statement: When the two layers of a swelling bilayer have their stiff fibres at equal and opposite angles to the strip axis, the in-plane shear strains of the layers are equal and opposite, so the through-thickness mismatch is a pure shear mismatch that drives helical twisting rather than bending; this is how chiral seed pods and wheat awns open.
claims.thinker: Shahaf Armon, Efi Efrati, Raz Kupferman & Eran Sharon
claims.work: Geometry and Mechanics in the Opening of Chiral Seed Pods
claims.chapter: Geometry and Mechanics in the Opening of Chiral Seed Pods (2011)

claims.label: Venus flytrap snaps when a geometric parameter exceeds a threshold
claims.statement: A doubly curved leaf with a slowly changing natural curvature snaps between two stable shapes only if the dimensionless parameter combining its size, thickness and curvature is large enough; below the threshold it deforms smoothly, and the snap time is set by the leaf's elastic and poroelastic time scales rather than by cellular motor speed.
claims.thinker: Yoël Forterre, Jan M. Skotheim, Jacques Dumais & L. Mahadevan
claims.chapter: How the Venus flytrap snaps (2005)

claims.label: Stimulus–response systems with simulation-preserving maps form a category
claims.statement: Stimulus–response dynamical systems (a state space, a stimulus space and an evolution law) together with pairs of smooth maps on states and stimuli that commute with time evolution form a category: identities satisfy the simulation condition and the condition is closed under composition, so a chain of locally valid scale transitions in a material hierarchy is globally valid.
claims.work: A category-theoretic framework from biological mechanics to engineered stimulus-response systems
claims.chapter: A category-theoretic framework from biological mechanics to engineered stimulus-response systems (2026)

tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right that domestic dogs descend from several distinct wild species (he had in mind wolves and jackals), then some domestic dog maternal lineages should trace to a wild canid species other than the grey wolf: a non-trivial fraction of dog mitochondrial genomes should be closer to Canis aureus, C. lupaster, C. latrans, C. simensis, Cuon alpinus or Lycaon pictus than to any wild Canis lupus.
tests.pass: Using complete mitochondrial genomes from GenBank (a systematic one-in-three sample of all 'Canis lupus familiaris' records, every wild 'Canis lupus' record, and every record of the other wild canid species), with CYTB and COX1 coding sequences extracted and compared by ungapped p-distance: at least 3 dog sequences AND at least 2 % of sampled dog sequences have their nearest non-dog sequence in a species other than Canis lupus. That outcome supports a multi-species origin.
tests.fail: Zero dog sequences are nearer to a non-wolf species than to wild wolves: refutes (every maternal lineage sampled is wolf-derived). One or two such sequences (consistent with mislabelled hybrids) or the per-cent threshold unmet: mixed. If fewer than 100 dog sequences or fewer than 20 wild wolf sequences can be retrieved and parsed: inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'several wild species' is read as more than one wild canid species contributing ancestry to domestic dogs. The species Darwin would have counted (wolf, jackals, coyote, dhole, African wild dog, Ethiopian wolf) are the wild canids with GenBank mitogenomes. Mitochondrial DNA tests maternal ancestry only; if even the maternal lineages are exclusively wolf-derived, the multi-species claim is refuted for the component that pre-genomic data can address, and nuclear genomic literature is cited in caveats but is not used as data. Dingoes and 'Canis lupus dingo' records are reported separately and excluded from the dog sample; records of 'Canis lupus' other than familiaris and dingo are treated as wild wolves (GenBank labels, which can include captive or admixed animals, are taken at face value). Modern taxonomy already files the dog inside Canis lupus, which the test does not assume.

measured.unit: sampled dog mitogenomes whose nearest non-dog sequence belongs to a species other than Canis lupus
measured.uncertainty: fraction 0.0000; p-distances over 2685 bp of CYTB+COX1

datasets.name: NCBI GenBank (nuccore) complete mitochondrial genomes of Canis lupus familiaris, wild Canis lupus, Canis latrans, Canis aureus, Canis lupaster, Canis simensis, Cuon alpinus and Lycaon pictus, retrieved through E-utilities

tests.hypothesis: If all domestic pigeon breeds descend from Columba livia (with its geographical sub-species) and not from several wild stocks, then every domestic-breed mitochondrial sequence should fall within the Columba livia cluster: nearer to C. livia sequences than to any other Columba species, and within intraspecific distance of C. livia.
tests.pass: Using GenBank mitochondrial records of Columba livia and of all other Columba species, aligned by best ungapped offset to the COI and CYTB genes of the C. livia reference mitogenome NC_013978: every domestic-labelled sequence (organism 'Columba livia domestica', a /breed qualifier, or a breed name in the record) has its nearest non-domestic sequence in C. livia (or in a wild C. livia subspecies), and the maximum p-distance from any domestic sequence to the nearest C. livia sequence is < 2 %. Requires >= 10 domestic-labelled sequences from >= 5 named breeds or 'domestica' records; otherwise inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.fail: At least 2 domestic sequences from at least 2 different breeds (or records) are nearer to another Columba species (C. rupestris, C. oenas, C. palumbus, C. guinea, C. leuconota, C. hodgsonii, etc.) than to any C. livia sequence, or exceed 2 % from all C. livia sequences while being within 2 % of another species: refutes (a second wild stock contributes maternal ancestry). Exactly one such sequence: mixed.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's claim concerns descent of all domestic breeds from one wild species; mitochondrial DNA tests the maternal component of that descent, which is what pre-genomic public data allow. 'Columba livia with its geographical sub-species' is taken as all records with organism Columba livia (any subspecies, including domestica for the domestic set). Columba rupestris, the hill pigeon, is a separate species in modern taxonomy and is treated as an alternative wild stock, although Darwin may have regarded it as a form of C. livia; a domestic sequence nearest to C. rupestris is therefore reported separately in the extra fields as well as counted. Alignment is by best ungapped offset because indels are rare in these coding genes; sequences overlapping the reference gene by < 400 bp are discarded.

measured.unit: domestic-labelled Columba livia records whose nearest non-domestic mitochondrial sequence (COI or CYTB) belongs to another Columba species
measured.uncertainty: max p-distance from a domestic record to the nearest C. livia record 0.013740458015267175; MIN_SHARED 300 bp

datasets.name: NCBI GenBank (nuccore) mitochondrial records of Columba livia (534) and of all other Columba species (645), including the C. livia reference mitogenome NC_013978.1, retrieved through E-utilities

tests.hypothesis: Among seed plant species, those that split most recently from their closest sampled relative (shortest terminal branch on a dated molecular phylogeny) have smaller native ranges than their congeners with longer terminal branches.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: tips of the GBMB tree of Smith & Brown 2018 (dated seed plant phylogeny built from GenBank sequences only) are matched exactly (binomial, underscores to spaces) to WCVP accepted non-hybrid species. Nearest-relative distance d = terminal branch length (Myr). Range size r = number of TDWG level-3 regions with a non-doubtful native, non-extinct WCVP record (species with r = 0 dropped). Genera qualify if >= 5 matched species and matched species >= 50% of the genus's WCVP accepted species. Within each qualifying genus, Spearman rho_g between d and r; the summary is the mean of Fisher-z(rho_g) weighted by (n_g - 3), back-transformed, with a two-sided combined z test. SUPPORTS if the weighted mean rho >= 0.10, combined p < 0.01 and rho_g > 0 in more than half of qualifying genera with at least one non-tied variable.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if the weighted mean rho <= 0. Any other outcome (0 < rho < 0.10, or not significant, or positive in at most half of genera) is MIXED. Fewer than 30 qualifying genera: inconclusive (underpowered). Tree or WCVP unobtainable: inconclusive (data-unavailable). Descriptive secondary statistics: the same weighted rho restricted to species native to Great Britain (GRB) genera with >= 3 matched species, and the pooled Spearman rho without genus stratification.
tests.interpretation: 'Very closely allied to other species, and in so far resemble varieties' is read as a short phylogenetic distance to the nearest relative, measured as the terminal branch length on a dated tree (half the patristic distance to the sister lineage). 'Much restricted ranges' is read as the number of botanical-country (TDWG level-3) units in which the species is native, a coarse range measure. Stratifying by genus controls clade differences in range size and rate; the sampling threshold limits inflation of terminal branches by unsampled relatives. Darwin's scope began with the British flora and extended to species generally; the global seed plant test is the general reading and the British subset is descriptive. Molecular divergence is a modern stand-in for Darwin's morphological closeness.

measured.unit: weighted mean within-genus Spearman rho between terminal branch length (Myr) and number of native TDWG level-3 regions
measured.uncertainty: combined two-sided p=0.00232; species in qualifying genera=16223

datasets.name: Smith & Brown 2018, Constructing a broadly inclusive seed plant phylogeny (GBMB: GenBank-only dated tree with Magallón et al. 2015 backbone), release v0.1
World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP), Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: wcvp_names.csv and wcvp_distribution.csv

tests.hypothesis: Among flowering plants, species that are trees have separate sexes (dioecy or monoecy, i.e. unisexual flowers) more often than non-woody (herbaceous) species, and this excess recurs across orders rather than being confined to one or two clades.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using the GIFT database public API, join the sexual-system trait (3.4.1: dioecious / monoecious / bisexual) to the growth-form trait (1.2.1: tree / shrub / herb / other) for angiosperm species (Angiospermae in the GIFT taxonomy), keeping species whose growth-form value is a single category. 'Separate sexes' = dioecious or monoecious. The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) the odds ratio of separate sexes in trees versus herbs is >= 1.5 with two-sided Fisher exact p < 0.01, and (ii) among orders with at least 10 trees and at least 10 herbs in the joined data, the proportion of species with separate sexes is higher in trees than in herbs in at least two-thirds of orders.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if the odds ratio is <= 1.0 or p >= 0.05, or if trees exceed herbs in fewer than half of the qualifying orders. Other outcomes are 'mixed'. Supplementary: the same odds ratio for trees vs shrubs, for dioecy alone, and the proportion of separate-sexed species in each growth form.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'trees' is read as GIFT growth form 'tree'; 'other plants' primarily as herbs (the claim's scope says 'comparing trees with non-woody plants'), with shrubs reported separately; 'sexes separated' as dioecious or monoecious (both have unisexual flowers, which is what Darwin's argument about cross-pollination needs); 'belonging to all Orders' as the across-order replication test. Darwin's observation was for Britain ('in this country') with Hooker's report of failure in Australia; the GIFT data are global, so the test is of the generalisation rather than the British observation. Modern caveat known in advance: GIFT sexual-system coverage (~3,000 species) is a small, non-random subset of angiosperms, so coverage bias is possible in either direction.

measured.unit: odds ratio of separate sexes (dioecious or monoecious) in trees versus herbs, angiosperms in GIFT
measured.uncertainty: Fisher exact p = 1.62e-43

datasets.name: GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits) public API: traits 3.4.1 (Reproduction sexual) and 1.2.1 (Growth form), species list
GIFT public API: taxonomy (nested set of genera, families, orders, Angiospermae)

tests.hypothesis: For a regional flora, the number of genera added by naturalised (introduced) plants, as a proportion of the native genera, exceeds the number of naturalised species as a proportion of native species.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For every TDWG level-3 botanical country in the World Checklist of Vascular Plants with at least 100 native accepted species and at least 20 introduced accepted species, compute r_sp = (introduced species not native to the area) / (native species) and r_gen = (genera represented only by introduced species) / (genera with at least one native species). The claim is SUPPORTED if r_gen > r_sp in at least 80% of qualifying areas AND the median of r_gen / r_sp across areas is at least 1.25.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if r_gen > r_sp in 50% or fewer of qualifying areas, or if the median r_gen / r_sp is 1.0 or less. Intermediate outcomes are 'mixed'. As a secondary, non-decisive analysis, the observed number of new genera per area is compared with the expectation when the same number of species is drawn at random from the global pool of species not native to that area (200 draws per area), to show whether the excess is more than a taxonomic-rank artefact.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'naturalisation' is read as the WCVP 'introduced' distribution status (established alien occurrence), his 'flora' as a TDWG level-3 area (the unit of the WCVP distribution table), and 'proportionally with the number of the native genera and species' as the two ratios above. Only accepted species (taxon_rank Species, taxon_status Accepted, no hybrids) are counted; records flagged location_doubtful are excluded. Darwin's own examples are the floras of the United States (Asa Gray's Manual) and Britain; the modern test covers all botanical countries that meet the sample-size rule. Modern reinterpretation: WCVP genus concepts are those of current taxonomy, not of 1859.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying level-3 areas with r_gen > r_sp

null_model.description: 200 random draws per area of the observed number of introduced species from all accepted species not native to the area; seed 20261031

datasets.name: World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP), Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

tests.hypothesis: In a phylogeny containing obligate cave (troglobitic/stygobitic) animals and surface animals from North America and Europe, each cave lineage is nested among, or sister to, taxa of its own continent; American and European cave taxa do not form clades with each other to the exclusion of surface taxa.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree induced on the taxa listed in derived/taxa.csv (continent assignment verified with GBIF occurrences), for every cave taxon compute the node-count distance to the nearest same-continent taxon (cave or surface, d_same) and to the nearest other-continent cave taxon (d_othercave). The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) d_same <= d_othercave for at least 70% of cave taxa, and (ii) the induced tree contains no clade that includes at least one North American and at least one European cave taxon while containing no surface taxon ('exclusive transcontinental cave clade').
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if fewer than 50% of cave taxa satisfy d_same <= d_othercave, or if two or more independent exclusive transcontinental cave clades occur (in different taxonomic groups). Results between the two thresholds, or a single such clade, are recorded as 'mixed'. If fewer than 10 cave taxa (across at least 3 groups) can be placed in the tree, the verdict is inconclusive/underpowered.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'cave-animals of America' and 'of Europe' are read as obligate subterranean species of North America and Europe; 'affinities to the other inhabitants of that continent' is read as phylogenetic relationship (sister-group or nesting) to surface lineages of the same continent, versus the alternative he rejects, that the two continents' cave faunas are specially allied to each other. Taxa were chosen before any tree was inspected and are listed in derived/taxa.csv; groups are Amphibia (Urodela), Amphipoda, Isopoda, Coleoptera (Trechini and Leiodidae) and Orthoptera (Rhaphidophoridae), the groups in which both continents have well-known troglobites. Continent assignment of each species is verified post hoc against GBIF: a species is kept only if at least 90% of its GBIF occurrences on the two continents fall on the pre-registered continent; names that the Open Tree TNRS cannot match are dropped. Phylogenetic 'affinity' is measured by node counts on the synthetic tree because it has no branch lengths; polytomies produce ties, which count in favour of whichever criterion they satisfy (a tie between a same-continent and an other-continent cave neighbour satisfies d_same <= d_othercave).

measured.unit: fraction of cave taxa with nearest same-continent taxon at least as close as nearest other-continent cave taxon

datasets.name: Open Tree of Life synthetic tree (current version via API v3)
GBIF occurrence search API (continent facet)

tests.hypothesis: Electric organs (Darwin's stated example) occur in fish lineages that are separated on an independently estimated phylogeny by lineages lacking electric organs, so that the organ must have arisen more than once rather than being inherited from one common ancestor; the same holds for light-producing organs in insects (his second example).
tests.pass: Pre-registered: on the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree induced on a fixed list of electric-organ-bearing fish families and a fixed list of non-electric fish families, count (i) the Dollo minimum number of independent origins = number of maximal clades whose tips are all electric, and (ii) the Fitch parsimony minimum number of state changes. SUPPORTS if, for the electric-fish case, (i) >= 3 and (ii) >= 3 (no reconstruction with a single origin and fewer than three changes exists). The insect light-organ case is scored the same way and reported; it does not decide the verdict because the claim is existential ('has sometimes').
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if the electric-organ-bearing families form a single clade in the synthetic tree (Dollo origins = 1, Fitch changes = 1). MIXED if Dollo origins = 2, or if the two statistics disagree about whether >= 3 changes are needed. If the Open Tree API is unreachable or fewer than 80% of the listed families map to the tree, the result is inconclusive (data-unavailable).
tests.interpretation: Darwin's claim has two parts: that similar organs sometimes arose independently in distantly related organisms (testable from a phylogeny) and that natural selection acting on analogous variations produced them (a mechanism not tested here). Only the first, pattern part is tested. 'Electric organs of fishes' = the families with electrogenic organs in the modern literature: Torpedinidae, Narcinidae, Narkidae, Hypnidae (Torpediniformes), Rajidae (skates), Mormyridae and Gymnarchidae (Mormyroidea), Gymnotidae, Apteronotidae, Sternopygidae, Hypopomidae, Rhamphichthyidae (Gymnotiformes), Malapteruridae (electric catfish) and Uranoscopidae (stargazers); Darwin knew Torpedo, Gymnotus and the electric catfish. 'Luminous organs of insects' = Lampyridae, Phengodidae, Rhagophthalmidae, Elateridae (Pyrophorini), Keroplatidae (Arachnocampa, Orfelia). 'Independently estimated phylogeny' = the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree, whose fish and insect backbones derive mostly from molecular studies. Independence is counted on a tree whose tips are families; origins within a family are not counted separately, which makes the count conservative.

measured.unit: minimum independent origins (Dollo) of electric organs among fish families on the Open Tree synthetic tree
measured.uncertainty: Fitch parsimony minimum changes = 6; 10 electric tips of 45

datasets.name: Open Tree of Life synthetic tree opentree16.1 (taxonomy 3.7draft3) via the v3 API: tnrs/match_names and tree_of_life/induced_subtree

tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right that the migratory instinct varies within species in extent and may be lost, then partial migration (some individuals or populations of a species migrate while others of the same species stay resident) is a common condition among birds rather than a rare anomaly, and species classified as partial migrants show measurably more winter presence inside their breeding latitudes than obligate migrants do.
tests.pass: Primary (AVONET, Tobias et al. 2022, BirdLife taxonomy sheet): P = share of bird species with a coded Migration score that are coded 2 (partially migratory) among all species, and Q = share coded 2 among non-sedentary species (score 2 or 3). Secondary (GBIF occurrence counts, Northern Hemisphere, years 2000 onward, non-fossil non-captive records, 5-degree latitude bands 0-80 N): for 12 pre-registered species, W = fraction of December-February records that fall in the latitude bands holding the central 80 % of June-July records (winter residency index). Partial-migrant set: Erithacus rubecula, Turdus merula, Sylvia atricapilla, Fringilla coelebs, Sturnus vulgaris, Turdus migratorius. Obligate-migrant set: Hirundo rustica, Apus apus, Phylloscopus trochilus, Setophaga striata, Tyrannus tyrannus, Cuculus canorus. Supports if P >= 0.20 and W is higher in the partial-migrant set than in the obligate set by a one-sided Mann-Whitney test at p < 0.05 with median W of the partial set >= 0.25.
tests.fail: Refutes if P < 0.05 (within-species variation in migratory extent is a rare anomaly) or if the obligate set has median W >= the partial set (the trait classification does not correspond to any measurable difference in winter residency). Otherwise mixed. The nest-construction clause is not tested (no public, geographically coded nest-architecture dataset at the within-species level was identified) and is recorded as untested in caveats.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's examples of instinct variation are migration (extent, direction, total loss) and nest form; this test addresses the migration example only. 'Varies within species in a state of nature' is operationalised as partial migration: a species whose populations or individuals differ in whether or how far they migrate. AVONET's Migration score (1 sedentary, 2 partially migratory, 3 migratory) is an expert synthesis from handbooks; it is used for the global prevalence P. The GBIF index W checks that this classification corresponds to an observable pattern: a species whose individuals all migrate should have few winter records at breeding latitudes, whereas a partial migrant retains many. Recent records (2000 onward) are used because eBird dominates GBIF bird data and gives dense year-round coverage; the Northern Hemisphere restriction avoids mixing austral seasons. Latitude bands are global in longitude, so for species occurring on more than one continent (Sturnus vulgaris, introduced in North America) the index pools populations. Thresholds: 20 % of all bird species being partial migrants is taken as 'common'; 5 % as 'rare'. Direction of migration and the evolutionary loss of migration are not measured separately, since occurrence data cannot attribute a wintering bird to its breeding population.

measured.unit: share of bird species coded as partially migratory (AVONET Migration = 2) among all species with a migration score
measured.uncertainty: AVONET expert coding; GBIF winter residency index from 5-degree band counts (eBird-dominated, effort-biased)

datasets.name: AVONET: morphological, ecological and geographical data for all birds (Tobias et al. 2022), Supplementary dataset 1, sheet AVONET1_BirdLife, column Migration
GBIF occurrence search API: record counts per 5-degree latitude band (0-80 N), years 2000-2030, months 6-7 and 12-2, non-fossil non-captive georeferenced records, for 12 species

tests.hypothesis: If close interbreeding lessens fertility and an occasional cross with a distinct stock increases it, then (i) in a pedigreed wild mammal population, litter size should decline with the mother's inbreeding coefficient, and (ii) in experimentally inbred Drosophila populations, fecundity should be lower than in the outbred control and should rise again when individuals from different inbred populations are crossed (heterosis).
tests.pass: Dataset 1 (Auclair et al. 2025, Pyrenean brown bear, Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.w9ghx3g1s, file litter_size_dt.csv): the slope of litter size on maternal inbreeding coefficient (ordinary least squares, one row per litter; if the file supplies repeated mothers, a mother-level mean is also reported) is negative with one-sided p < 0.05, or, if the coefficient is categorical, mean litter size of the most inbred category is below that of the least inbred with p < 0.05. Dataset 2 (Pekkala et al. 2014, Drosophila littoralis, Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.10154): (a) mean fecundity of inbred populations is below the outbred control in at least two of the three population-size treatments (N = 2, 10, 40), and (b) mean fecundity of inter-population crosses exceeds that of within-population matings (heterosis > 0) in a majority of population pairs or treatments for which both are reported. Verdict 'supports' if dataset 1 passes and both 2(a) and 2(b) pass; 'mixed' if dataset 1 passes but only one of 2(a)/2(b), or dataset 1 fails while both 2(a) and 2(b) pass; 'refutes' if litter size does not decline with inbreeding and inbred fecundity is not below control.
tests.fail: Refuted if the litter-size slope on inbreeding is >= 0 (or not significantly negative) and inbred Drosophila populations are not less fecund than the outbred control. Clause (ii)(b) failing alone (no heterosis) with the others passing gives 'mixed'. If either Dryad archive cannot be downloaded, that dataset is recorded as unavailable and the verdict rests on the other; if neither can be obtained, the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable'.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'close interbreeding lessens fertility' is read as inbreeding depression in a fertility component (litter size in a wild mammal; fecundity in a laboratory fly), and 'an occasional cross with a distinct individual or variety increases it' as heterosis on crossing distinct inbred populations. The inbreeding coefficient (Wright's F) is a post-Darwinian quantity. The clause attributing the decline of multi-generation hybrids to close interbreeding is not tested; only the general inbreeding-depression and heterosis pattern is. Exact column names and the form of the inbreeding variable were not inspected before pre-registration; the mapping used is stated in 'method'.

measured.unit: cubs per litter per unit maternal inbreeding coefficient (OLS slope)
measured.uncertainty: SE 0.716; one-sided p = 0.0443

datasets.name: Data from: Inbreeding depression across multiple life history traits in a long-lived mammal (Pyrenean brown bear), file litter_size_dt.csv
Data from: The effect of inbreeding rate on fitness, inbreeding depression and heterosis over a range of inbreeding coefficients (Drosophila littoralis)

tests.hypothesis: If first-generation hybrids are only slightly variable while later generations are extremely variable, then in an experimental cross the phenotypic variance of F2 hybrids should exceed that of F1 hybrids for most measured traits, and F1 variance should be no greater than that of the parental species.
tests.pass: Dataset: Dryad doi:10.25338/B8QS5T (Cakile edentula x C. maritima artificial crosses with F1, F2 and backcross generations; CC0). For every continuous trait recorded for both F1 and F2 individuals from the artificial crosses (identified from the data files after download; traits with < 8 individuals in either generation are excluded), compute the variance of log-transformed values (equivalent to a squared coefficient of variation for positive traits; for traits with zero or negative values use the variance of the trait divided by its squared mean) in F1 and in F2. Primary statistic: the median across traits of the variance ratio F2/F1. Pass ('supports') if the median ratio is >= 1.5 AND the F2 variance exceeds the F1 variance in a majority of traits with an exact binomial sign-test p < 0.05. 'Mixed' if F2 exceeds F1 in a majority of traits with p < 0.05 but the median ratio is between 1.0 and 1.5 (more variable, but not 'extremely' so relative to F1), or if the median ratio is >= 1.5 but the sign test is not significant. The comparison of F1 variance with parental variance is reported as an extra and does not enter the verdict.
tests.fail: Refuted if F2 hybrids are not more variable than F1 hybrids: the median F2/F1 variance ratio is <= 1.0, or F2 exceeds F1 in half or fewer of the traits. If the archive cannot be downloaded, the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable'.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'variable' is read as phenotypic variance among individuals of the same hybrid generation raised under common conditions, scaled by the trait mean so that traits of different magnitude are comparable. 'First generation' = F1 (cross between the two species), 'succeeding generations' = F2 (F1 x F1); backcrosses are not used because Darwin's statement concerns hybrids bred inter se. The claim's causal clause (disturbed reproductive system of the hybrids) is not tested; the quantitative-genetic explanation (segregation of parental alleles in F2) would produce the same pattern and is the modern reinterpretation. One plant cross is tested; the claim is stated for plant and animal hybrids generally.

measured.unit: median across traits of the F2/F1 ratio of mean-scaled phenotypic variance
measured.uncertainty: 11 of 21 traits with ratio > 1; exact sign-test p = 0.5000; ratio range 0.03-8.01

datasets.name: Asymmetry in fitness-related traits of later-generation hybrids between two invasive species (Cakile edentula x C. maritima), file Chengjun_Experiment.csv

tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, more than 300 million years have elapsed since the latter part of the Chalk formation (the close of the Secondary, i.e. Mesozoic, era), so the radiometric age of the top of the Cretaceous / Mesozoic must exceed 300 Ma, and the denudation of the Weald (removal of the Chalk and underlying beds over the Wealden dome) could have occupied about 300 million years.
tests.pass: The age of the Cretaceous-Paleogene (Mesozoic-Cenozoic) boundary in the current International Chronostratigraphic Chart, as served by Macrostrat and cross-checked against the Paleobiology Database timescale, is >= 300 Ma; equivalently the maximum possible duration of post-Chalk denudation (time since the youngest Chalk) is >= 300 Myr.
tests.fail: The age of the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary is < 300 Ma. The claim is refuted outright (not merely imprecise) if it is < 150 Ma, i.e. less than half of Darwin's figure, since the denudation of the Weald cannot have taken longer than the time elapsed since the youngest Chalk was deposited.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'latter part of the Secondary period' and 'latter part of the Chalk formation' are mapped to the top of the Cretaceous System (= top of the Mesozoic Erathem), whose numerical age is fixed by radiometric calibration in the International Chronostratigraphic Chart. The Chalk Group of south-east England is the youngest formation that was removed over the Weald, so the time since its deposition ended is an upper bound on the duration of the denudation. Darwin's own erosion-rate premise (one inch per century on a 500-foot cliff) is not tested; only his numerical conclusion is. No modern reinterpretation of the claim is needed: Darwin states a number of years, and radiometric dating measures the same quantity.

measured.unit: Ma (age of the top of the Cretaceous / Mesozoic = end of Chalk deposition)
measured.uncertainty: all 7 readings agree to within 0 Myr; ICS quotes no error bar on the K/Pg boundary age

extra.pbdb_timescale_reference: The ICS International Chronostratigraphic Chart v2024/12

tests.hypothesis: If Darwin's denudation argument holds, the time elapsed since the latter part of the Secondary (Mesozoic) period, i.e. since the youngest Chalk, is roughly 300 million years or more on the modern radiometrically calibrated timescale.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: the International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) chronostratigraphic boundary ages as served by the Macrostrat API (defs/intervals, timescale 'international ages'), which carries the ICS chart's numeric ages in Ma. Quantities: age of the top of the Maastrichtian (= Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, the end of Chalk deposition) and age of the base of the Campanian (start of the youngest Chalk stages). SUPPORTS if the top-of-Maastrichtian age is >= 225 Ma (within 25% of 300 Myr, or older). Reported alongside: the base-of-Campanian age and the ratio of Darwin's 306.7 Myr to the measured age.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the top-of-Maastrichtian age is < 225 Ma (Darwin's figure is off by more than 25%). MIXED is not possible for this one-number test. INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if the API cannot be reached; INCONCLUSIVE (not-operationalizable) if the API does not return a Maastrichtian interval.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'latter part of the Secondary period' is the Late Cretaceous, and 'since the late Chalk' is the time from the youngest Chalk Group strata (Campanian-Maastrichtian) to the present. The claim is a duration (about 300 million years, which he says is an underestimate of the time since the late Secondary) inferred from an assumed erosion rate; the test compares that duration with the radiometric timescale and does not test the erosion rate. Darwin himself withdrew the calculation in later editions. This follows the swarm thread's draft plan for this claim with the same 25% tolerance. READINGS CHECK (added after the result, at the hub's request; no number or threshold changed). Darwin's 306,662,400 years is the time he computed for the denudation of the Weald, which he takes to have begun after the Chalk was laid down; he then says more than that has elapsed 'since the latter part of the Secondary period'. Reading 1 (tested): 300 Myr is a lower bound on the time since the end of the Chalk; measured 66 Ma, refuted. Reading 2: 300 Myr is the duration of the Weald denudation itself; that denudation can have taken at most the time since the Chalk ended (66 Myr) and most of it is Neogene, so refuted by a wider margin. Reading 3: 'since the latter part of the Secondary' means since the start of the Late Cretaceous (base Cenomanian, 100.5 Ma); the ratio is then 3.05, still outside the 25% tolerance, refuted. Reading 4 (qualitative): Darwin's point was only that geological time is immense, far longer than Kelvin's physics allowed; that reading is supported by the modern timescale (the Mesozoic began 252 Ma; the Earth is 4.5 Gyr old), but it is not the claim as the claim graph states it, which carries the 300 Myr figure. The verdict is 'refutes' under every numeric reading and flips only under the non-numeric one.

measured.unit: Ma, age of the top of the Maastrichtian (end of the Chalk); Darwin's figure was 306.7 million years
measured.uncertainty: ICS boundary ages for these stages carry uncertainties of about 0.2 Ma, far below the threshold

datasets.name: International Chronostratigraphic Chart boundary ages (ICS), as served by the Macrostrat API (defs/intervals, timescale 'international ages')

tests.hypothesis: Clause 1 (absolute): wholly soft-bodied organisms leave no fossils, so animal phyla without mineralised or sclerotised hard parts should have zero fossil occurrences. Clause 2 (bias): the fossil record is strongly biased toward organisms with hard parts, so fossil occurrences per living species should be far higher for biomineralising phyla than for wholly soft-bodied phyla.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Wholly soft-bodied phyla: Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Nemertea, Chaetognatha, Priapulida, Onychophora, Nematoda, Nematomorpha, Xenacoelomorpha, Gastrotricha, Placozoa, Rotifera, Tardigrada. Biomineralising phyla: Mollusca, Brachiopoda, Echinodermata, Bryozoa, Porifera, Cnidaria. For each phylum, count fossil occurrences in the Paleobiology Database (occs/list, rowcount) and accepted living species in the GBIF backbone taxonomy. Clause 1 is REFUTED if the soft-bodied phyla together have >= 10 fossil occurrences spread over >= 3 phyla, and SUPPORTED if they have 0. Clause 2 is SUPPORTED if the median of (fossil occurrences / living accepted species) over biomineralising phyla is >= 100 times the median over soft-bodied phyla, and REFUTED if it is < 10 times. Overall verdict: 'supports' if clause 1 supported and clause 2 supported; 'mixed' if clause 1 refuted and clause 2 supported; 'refutes' if clause 2 refuted (whatever clause 1 shows).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. See pass_criterion: clause 1 fails on >= 10 occurrences in >= 3 soft-bodied phyla; clause 2 fails if the biomineralising/soft-bodied ratio of occurrences per living species is < 10. The third sentence of the claim (shells and bones decay where sediment is not accumulating) is not tested here; no public dataset pairs preservation with sedimentation rate at the needed scale, and the two assessors' operationalisations also concentrate on the first two clauses.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'organism wholly soft' is read as membership of an animal phylum whose members have neither biomineralised skeletons nor robust sclerotised cuticles, jaws or tubes (list fixed above; Annelida, Hemichordata, Arthropoda and Chordata are excluded as mixed). 'Preserved' is read as having at least one occurrence recorded in the Paleobiology Database, which records body and trace fossils by taxon; trace fossils are excluded by restricting to body fossils where the API allows (pres=regular). The bias clause is read as the ratio of fossil occurrences to living described species, a crude but standard measure of preservation potential. Modern reinterpretation: the phylum-level classification and the notion of exceptional (Lagerstätte) preservation post-date Darwin.

measured.unit: PBDB body-fossil occurrences in the 13 wholly soft-bodied phyla
measured.uncertainty: ratio of median occurrences-per-living-species, mineralised/soft = 960.9

datasets.name: Paleobiology Database, data service 1.2: occs/list record counts per phylum (body fossils)
GBIF Backbone Taxonomy, accepted species counts per phylum (species/search)

tests.hypothesis: If oceans have occupied their present areas and continents theirs since the earliest Silurian, then at every time from ~440 Ma to the present the geographic locations now occupied by land were occupied by continental land, and the locations now occupied by ocean were ocean.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using the GPlates Web Service with the Merdith et al. (2021) plate model, the model's coastline polygons are reconstructed to 440, 400, 350, 300, 250, 200, 150, 100 and 50 Ma. On a 2x2 degree global grid (area-weighted by cos latitude), classify each present-day grid cell as land or ocean from the time-0 coastlines. L_all = area fraction of present land cells that fall inside reconstructed coastline polygons at every one of the nine times; O_all = area fraction of present ocean cells that fall outside them at every time. The claim is SUPPORTED if L_all >= 0.75 and O_all >= 0.75.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if L_all < 0.50 or O_all < 0.50. Intermediate outcomes are 'mixed'. For comparison the per-time fractions (L_t, O_t) and the expected overlap for randomly placed continents (equal to the present land fraction) are reported. The PALEOMAP model is run as a robustness check and is not part of the verdict.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'where our oceans now extend, oceans have extended' and 'where continents now exist, large tracts of land have existed ... since the earliest silurian period' is read as spatial persistence of land and ocean in a fixed geographic (Earth) frame, which is how he and his contemporaries understood it (he explicitly allows 'great oscillations of level' but not lateral movement). Plate reconstructions place continental crust in a palaeomagnetic / mantle reference frame; the coastline polygons of the plate model are used as the outline of continental land at each time. Modern reinterpretation: the claim is tested against reconstructed continental positions, which did not exist as a concept in 1859; palaeolongitude in the Palaeozoic is uncertain, which could shift overlap either way.

measured.unit: area fraction of present-day land that lies within reconstructed continental coastlines at all nine times 440-50 Ma (MERDITH2021)
measured.uncertainty: O_all (present ocean that was ocean at all times) = 0.3377; PALEOMAP robustness: L_all = 0.0046, O_all = 0.3436

datasets.name: GPlates Web Service, reconstruct/coastlines with model MERDITH2021 (Merdith et al. 2021, Earth-Science Reviews 214:103477)
GPlates Web Service, reconstruct/coastlines with model PALEOMAP (Scotese PALEOMAP PaleoAtlas)

tests.hypothesis: If different classes and genera change at different rates, then taxonomic turnover measured as the stratigraphic duration of extinct genera in the Paleobiology Database should differ substantially among major animal classes, and, within classes, among orders.
tests.pass: Using PBDB genus-rank taxa with first- and last-appearance ages for 14 higher taxa (Trilobita, Brachiopoda, Bivalvia, Gastropoda, Cephalopoda, Anthozoa, Echinoidea, Crinoidea, Ostracoda, Bryozoa, Mammalia, Reptilia, Actinopterygii, Chondrichthyes), restricted to extinct genera with >= 5 occurrences, genus duration = midpoint of first-appearance range minus midpoint of last-appearance range. Clause A (between classes): a Kruskal-Wallis test of genus duration across the higher taxa has p < 0.001 AND epsilon-squared effect size >= 0.02 AND the ratio of the largest to the smallest group median duration is >= 2. Clause B (between genera grouped by order, within classes): within each higher taxon having >= 3 orders with >= 20 qualifying genera each, a Kruskal-Wallis test of genus duration across orders has p < 0.001 and epsilon-squared >= 0.02; clause B passes if this holds in a majority of eligible higher taxa. Verdict 'supports' if A and B pass; 'mixed' if exactly one passes; 'refutes' if neither.
tests.fail: Clause A fails if genus durations are statistically indistinguishable across classes (p >= 0.001), or the effect is trivial (epsilon-squared < 0.02), or every class median lies within a factor of 2 of every other. Clause B fails if orders within a class differ significantly and non-trivially in half or fewer of the eligible classes. Both failing refutes the claim. A sensitivity re-run with >= 20 occurrences per genus is reported; if the sign of either clause flips under that filter the result is downgraded to 'mixed' regardless.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'rate of change' of species is read, following the Grok assessor, as taxonomic turnover: shorter genus durations mean faster replacement of forms. 'Classes' are mapped to PBDB classes or, where PBDB class structure is unstable (brachiopods, bryozoans), phyla. 'Species of different genera' is approximated by genera grouped into orders, because species-level ranges in PBDB are too noisy and species durations are strongly tied to the genus concept. Durations are taxonomic, not morphological; the morphological reading (rates of character change) is not tested. Differences in preservation potential and taxonomic splitting between classes can mimic rate differences, which is why the pass criterion requires a non-trivial effect size and a two-fold spread of medians rather than mere significance.

measured.unit: ratio of largest to smallest median genus duration among the 14 higher taxa (Myr/Myr)
measured.uncertainty: Kruskal-Wallis H = 3080.0, p = 0.00e+00, epsilon2 = 0.203

datasets.name: Paleobiology Database taxa lists (genus rank, show=app,class) for 14 higher taxa

tests.hypothesis: For extinct marine-invertebrate families, the number of genera recorded per geological stage rises from a low value at the family's first appearance to an interior maximum and then declines to a low value at its last appearance, rather than appearing or disappearing at or near maximal diversity or showing several separate peaks.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: a family's trajectory is scored 'Darwinian' when, with R_i = range-through genus richness in stage bin i (from the family's first to last bin) and M = max R_i: (a) R_first <= 0.5 M, (b) R_last <= 0.5 M, and (c) the set of bins with R_i > 0.5 M is contiguous (a single peak). The claim is SUPPORTED if at least two thirds (>= 0.667) of qualifying families are Darwinian, where qualifying = extinct family within the sampled higher taxa with >= 10 genera having occurrences and a duration spanning >= 6 stage bins.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTED if fewer than half (< 0.5) of qualifying families are Darwinian. A fraction in [0.5, 0.667) is MIXED. If fewer than 50 families qualify the result is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'group' is read as a family and 'number of species' as number of genera per stage (the level with usable fossil coverage, as both assessors note). 'Gradual increase to a maximum, then gradual decrease' is operationalised as the three shape conditions (a)-(c): low start, low end, single peak. The sampled higher taxa are fixed in advance: Trilobita, Brachiopoda, Cephalopoda, Bivalvia, Gastropoda, Crinoidea, Anthozoa, Echinoidea, Bryozoa. Only extinct families are used because the decline-to-extinction half of the claim is only observable for them. Counts are raw range-through counts from the Paleobiology Database diversity endpoint at stage resolution; no sampling standardisation is applied, which is recorded as a caveat.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying extinct families with low start, low end and a single peak
measured.uncertainty: 95% Clopper-Pearson CI [0.528, 0.640]

datasets.name: Paleobiology Database data service 1.2: taxa/list (family sampling frame) and occs/diversity (range-through genus counts per stage)

tests.hypothesis: If Tertiary extinctions were gradual and place-by-place rather than catastrophic, the last occurrences of extinct genera should be spread across many Tertiary stages rather than concentrated in one or two, and genera recorded on several continents should usually disappear from those continents at demonstrably different times, more often than genera killed in the known K-Pg catastrophe.
tests.pass: Two groups are analysed separately with Paleobiology Database genus-level occurrences from the Campanian through the Pliocene: Mollusca and Mammalia. Clause A (no catastrophic concentration): among PBDB-extinct genera whose global last occurrence (midpoint of its age range) falls in the Tertiary (Danian to Piacenzian, 17 ICS stages), the single stage holding the most last occurrences holds < 1/3 of them, and at least 4 stages are needed to accumulate 50% of them when stages are ranked by count. Clause B (place by place): among those Tertiary-extinct genera that have >= 2 occurrences on each of >= 2 continents (PBDB continent codes), the fraction whose regional last occurrences are staggered (the earliest-vanishing continent's last-occurrence minimum age is older than the last-vanishing continent's last-occurrence maximum age, i.e. non-overlapping age ranges) is > 0.5 AND exceeds the same fraction computed for the K-Pg control set (PBDB-extinct genera whose global last occurrence midpoint falls in the Maastrichtian, using Campanian-Maastrichtian occurrences). A clause passes only if it passes in both groups. Verdict 'supports' if both clauses pass, 'mixed' if exactly one passes, 'refutes' if neither passes.
tests.fail: Clause A fails if, in either group, one Tertiary stage holds >= 1/3 of the genus last occurrences or <= 3 stages hold 50% of them. Clause B fails if, in either group, the staggered fraction is <= 0.5 or does not exceed the K-Pg control's staggered fraction (which would mean the apparent staggering is no greater than what incomplete sampling produces in a known simultaneous extinction). Both clauses failing refutes the claim; the K-Pg control itself is outside the claim's Tertiary scope and is used only as a sampling-artefact baseline.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'species and groups of species' are tested at the genus level because genus-level identifications are far more complete and less affected by taxonomic noise in PBDB. 'Disappearing from one spot, then another' is read as non-overlapping last-occurrence age ranges on different continents (modern continents, PBDB cc codes). 'Swept away together by catastrophes' is read as a strong concentration of last occurrences in one or two stages. The Signor-Lipps effect makes any extinction look gradual and staggered in an incomplete record; the Maastrichtian (K-Pg) control set provides an empirical baseline for how staggered a real catastrophe looks in the same database, so clause B requires Tertiary staggering to exceed that baseline. Scope is the Tertiary, as Darwin stated; the K-Pg event itself is not used to judge the claim.

measured.unit: mean over the two groups of the fraction of multi-continent Tertiary-extinct genera with staggered regional last occurrences
