tests.hypothesis: Extinct animal families in the fossil record are bottom-heavy: their genus diversity peaks early in their history and tapers over a longer decline, so the centre of gravity of the diversity trajectory lies in the first half of the family's duration.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: from the Paleobiology Database taxa API, all accepted animal (Metazoa) genera with first and last appearance ages and family assignment. A family is extinct if none of its genera is flagged extant and every genus has lastapp_min_ma > 0. Each genus ranges from firstapp_max_ma to lastapp_min_ma; the family's range is the union. Diversity D(t) = number of genera ranging through t on a 0.1 Myr grid. Centre of gravity CG = sum(D(t) * tau(t)) / sum(D(t)), tau = (family origin - t) / (family origin - family end), so CG < 0.5 means diversity is concentrated early and decline is slower than rise. Families qualify with >= 5 genera and duration >= 10 Myr. SUPPORTS if the median CG < 0.5, the one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of CG - 0.5 < 0 has p < 0.01, and at least 55% of families have CG < 0.5.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if the median CG >= 0.5. Any other outcome is MIXED. Fewer than 100 qualifying families: inconclusive (underpowered); PBDB API unreachable: inconclusive (data-unavailable). Descriptive secondary statistics: median CG and share below 0.5 for families ending at the five big mass extinctions (end-Ordovician 443.8, Late Devonian 372.2, end-Permian 251.9, end-Triassic 201.4, end-Cretaceous 66.0 Ma, within 2 Myr) versus all others, and for Paleozoic-, Mesozoic- and Cenozoic-originating families.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'complete extinction of the species of a group is generally a slower process than their production' is read through clade shape (Gould et al. 1977): if production is fast and extermination slow, the diversity trajectory rises steeply and tapers, giving a centre of gravity in the first half of the clade's duration. Groups are extinct animal families as classified in PBDB (Darwin's 'groups' of genera and families); diversity is counted in genera, because Darwin's species are rarely resolved in the fossil record. Range-through ranges from database first and last appearances are used without sampling correction; the Signor-Lipps effect pulls last appearances earlier and can shorten or lengthen the tail, so the test measures the record as compiled.

measured.unit: median centre of gravity of range-through genus diversity of extinct animal families (0 = origin, 1 = extinction; < 0.5 = slow decline)
measured.uncertainty: Wilcoxon one-sided p (CG < 0.5) = 1.06e-18; IQR 0.409-0.547

datasets.name: Paleobiology Database data service 1.2, taxa/list: accepted Metazoa genera with first and last appearance ages (show=app) and classification (show=class)

tests.hypothesis: Marine faunas on different continents change in step: the genus composition of a stage on one continent identifies the same (or an adjacent) stage on the other continents, and the magnitude of faunal change between consecutive stages is correlated across continents.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using Paleobiology Database marine Metazoa genus lists per ICS stage (stages >= 1 Myr) for each of six PBDB continents (North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia), (A) for every continent-stage with >= 100 genera, find the stage whose pooled genus list from the other five continents has the highest Jaccard similarity with it; and (B) for every continent, compute the series of proportional genus loss between consecutive stages (fraction of genera in stage i absent from stage i+1, both stages >= 100 genera) and the Spearman correlation of this series between every pair of continents. The claim is SUPPORTED if in (A) the best-matching stage is the same or an adjacent stage for >= 85% of continent-stages, AND in (B) the mean pairwise Spearman correlation is > 0 with permutation p < 0.01 (independent permutation of stage order within each continent, 2000 permutations).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if the same-or-adjacent matching rate in (A) is < 60%, or the mean pairwise correlation in (B) is <= 0. Other outcomes are 'mixed'. Exact-stage matching rate, matching rate within two stages, and per-continent-pair correlations are reported as supplementary numbers.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world' is operationalised by its own consequence, which he states: that formations in distant regions can be correlated by their fossils. Test (A) is that correlation exercise done with genera: a continent's fauna from one stage should pick out the same stage elsewhere in the world. Test (B) checks that the amount of change between consecutive stages co-varies across continents (synchronous turnover). 'Almost simultaneously, in a broad geological sense' is read as within one stage (typically 2-10 Myr). PBDB continents are the geographic units; marine environments only. Known limitation stated up front: PBDB stage assignments rest partly on biostratigraphic correlation, which makes some agreement across continents expected by construction; a failure of test (A) would nevertheless be possible if faunas were strongly provincial, and test (B) uses magnitudes of change that are not used in dating.

measured.unit: fraction of continent-stages (>= 100 genera) whose fauna best matches the same or an adjacent stage on the other continents

datasets.name: Paleobiology Database, data service 1.2: occs/taxa (marine Metazoa genera per stage and continent) and intervals/list (stage ages)

tests.hypothesis: The taxonomic similarity of marine fossil faunas from two geological stages decreases with the time separating them, consecutive stages being far more similar than widely separated ones, and the fauna of each stage is intermediate between the faunas of the stages before and after it.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using Paleobiology Database marine Metazoa genus lists per international stage (ICS 2020 scale as served by PBDB; stages shorter than 1 Myr excluded; stages with fewer than 200 genera excluded), compute Jaccard similarity between all stage pairs. The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) the Spearman correlation between pairwise Jaccard similarity and the separation of stage midpoints (Myr) is <= -0.5 with Mantel permutation p < 0.001, (ii) the mean Jaccard similarity of consecutive stage pairs is at least 2 times the mean similarity of pairs separated by 5 or more intervening stages, and (iii) for at least 80% of stages i with both neighbours, J(i-1, i+1) <= min(J(i-1, i), J(i, i+1)) (intermediacy).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if the Spearman correlation is > -0.2, or the consecutive/remote similarity ratio is < 1.2, or intermediacy holds for fewer than 50% of stages. Other outcomes are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'formations' are read as international chronostratigraphic stages (the finest global units with ages), 'fossils ... closely related' as sharing of genera (the finest rank that is comparable across regions in PBDB), and 'remote' as separation by five or more stages. 'Intermediate' is read as: two stages bracketing a third never share more genera with each other than either shares with the middle stage. Only marine environments are used because marine faunas have the most continuous record. Modern reinterpretation: PBDB stage assignments of collections rest partly on biostratigraphy, which could inflate within-stage faunal homogeneity; the pass criterion therefore requires a large, graded effect over multi-stage separations, not merely a within-stage one.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between pairwise Jaccard genus similarity of stages and their midpoint age separation (Myr)
measured.uncertainty: Mantel permutation p = 0.0005 (2000 permutations)

datasets.name: Paleobiology Database, data service 1.2: occs/taxa (genus lists of marine Metazoa per stage) and intervals/list (stage ages)

tests.hypothesis: If each area's later-Tertiary inhabitants left modified descendants in the same area, then the families of terrestrial mammals recorded as fossils on a continent in the Miocene-Pliocene should have living members on that same continent more often than they have living members on any other continent.
tests.pass: Fossil side: PBDB Miocene-Pliocene (23.03-2.58 Ma) occurrences of Mammalia on each of five continents (Africa, Eurasia = PBDB EUR+ASI, North America, South America, Australia), excluding marine orders/families (Cetacea, Sirenia, Desmostylia, Phocidae, Otariidae, Odobenidae), giving for each continent the set of fossil families with >= 2 occurrences there. Living side: GBIF non-fossil, non-captive occurrence facets by family for Mammalia on each GBIF continent (Europe+Asia merged), a family counting as living on a continent if it has >= 20 such records there (same marine exclusions). For each continent X, S(X) = fraction of X's fossil families that are living on X, and O(X) = mean over the other four continents Y of the fraction of X's fossil families living on Y. Pass if S(X) > O(X) for all five continents AND the pooled ratio mean S / mean O >= 1.2 AND, in a permutation test that randomly reassigns the five living-family sets to continents (all 120 permutations, i.e. exact), the observed sum of S(X) is the maximum or tied maximum (p <= 1/120 + ties). The same statistics at genus level (fossil genera that are extant and living on the same continent) are reported as an extra and do not enter the verdict.
tests.fail: Fails if fossil families are no more likely to survive on their own continent than elsewhere: S(X) <= O(X) for two or more continents, or the pooled ratio is < 1.2, or the observed sum of S(X) is not the maximum over the 120 continent-label permutations. One continent failing with the other conditions met gives 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'closely allied' is read as membership in the same family (his examples, marsupials and edentates, are order- or family-level alliances, so family is a conservative choice). 'Later Tertiary' is read as Miocene plus Pliocene. 'Same continent or area' uses modern continents, merging Europe and Asia. Birds and molluscs, also in the stated scope, are not tested because their later-Tertiary fossil record in PBDB is far sparser and their family-level taxonomy less stable; islands are not tested. The GBIF side measures where families live today, which includes recent introductions (e.g. Muridae everywhere), a bias toward sharing with other continents that works against the claim.

measured.unit: ratio of mean same-continent survival fraction to mean other-continent survival fraction, later-Tertiary mammal families
measured.uncertainty: exact permutation p = 0.0083 (1 of 120 label permutations >= observed)

datasets.name: Paleobiology Database Mammalia occurrences, Miocene-Pliocene, genus-resolved, per continent (AFR, EUR, ASI, NOA, SOA, AUS)
GBIF occurrence search API, Mammalia, family and genus facets per continent (non-fossil, non-captive records)
GBIF Backbone Taxonomy species API (names, ranks and orders for family and genus keys)

tests.hypothesis: Across regions of the world, the taxonomic similarity of their biotas is explained by which land mass they belong to (shared history and barriers) rather than by the similarity of their climates; in particular, climatically matched regions on different continents (e.g. the Mediterranean-climate belts of Australia, South Africa and Chile) share fewer taxa than climatically different regions on the same continent.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For the 23 regions in derived/regions.csv (5x5 degree boxes, pre-assigned to a continent and to one of six climate classes), genus lists of mammals, birds and vascular plants are taken from GBIF occurrences (genera with >= 3 georeferenced records in the box), and climate from the NASA POWER climatology (annual mean 2 m temperature, annual precipitation, seasonal temperature range at five points per box). For each taxon group, pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity between regions is regressed on standardised climate distance and a same-continent indicator (permutation test over region labels, 2000 permutations). The claim is SUPPORTED if, in at least 2 of the 3 taxon groups, (a) the same-continent effect is significant (p < 0.05) and its partial R-squared exceeds that of climate distance, and (b) the mean Jaccard similarity of climate-matched pairs on different continents is lower than the mean similarity of climate-mismatched pairs on the same continent.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if, in at least 2 of the 3 taxon groups, climate distance has the larger partial R-squared and the same-continent effect is not significant, or climate-matched cross-continental pairs are more similar than climate-mismatched same-continent pairs. Other outcomes are 'mixed'. If GBIF returns fewer than 20 genera for a region/group, that region is dropped for that group; if fewer than 15 regions remain for a group, the group is not evaluated.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'inhabitants of various regions' are read as the genus-level composition of three well-recorded groups (Mammalia, Aves, Tracheophyta); 'climatal and other physical conditions' as the NASA POWER temperature and precipitation climatology; 'similarity' as Jaccard similarity of genus lists. His 'accounted for' is read comparatively: climate distance should explain less of the variation in biotic similarity than does being on the same land mass, and his own example (Australia, South Africa, western South America at 25-35 degrees S) is tested directly as the climate-matched cross-continental pairs. The absolute wording ('neither ... nor ... can be accounted for') is not testable as stated because climate obviously limits distributions within a continent; the comparative reading is the one tested. Regions and climate classes were fixed before any data were retrieved. GBIF records include introduced species, which inflate cross-continental similarity and therefore work against the claim.

measured.unit: taxon groups (of 3) in which same-continent membership outweighs climate distance and climate-matched cross-continental pairs are less similar than climate-mismatched same-continent pairs
measured.uncertainty: permutation p-values per group in extra

datasets.name: GBIF occurrence search API (genus facets within bounding boxes)
NASA POWER climatology API (temporal/climatology/point)

tests.hypothesis: Across pairs of regions of similar size, the species-level dissimilarity of their terrestrial faunas increases with the impassability and age of the barrier separating them (none < large river < shallow recently-dry strait < mountain range or desert < deep never-bridged strait < ocean basin), and this ordering persists after controlling for the geographic distance between the regions.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: 26 fixed region pairs are assigned a barrier rank (0 none, 1 large river, 2 shallow strait dry at glacial low stands, 3 mountain range or desert, 4 deep strait never bridged, 5 ocean basin). For each pair and each of three groups (Rodentia, Squamata, Amphibia) the Sørensen dissimilarity (1 - 2|A∩B|/(|A|+|B|)) of species sets (GBIF occurrences, >= 3 records per species in the box) is computed and averaged over the three groups. SUPPORTS if Spearman's rho between mean dissimilarity and barrier rank is >= 0.5 with p < 0.01 (n = 26), AND the partial Spearman correlation controlling for log centroid distance is > 0 with p < 0.05, AND mean dissimilarity of the rank-0 (no barrier) pairs is lower than that of every barrier class with rank >= 2.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if Spearman's rho <= 0, or if the no-barrier pairs are on average at least as dissimilar as the deep-strait and ocean pairs (ranks 4-5). Any other outcome is MIXED. A pair in which any group has fewer than 10 species in either box is dropped for that group; if fewer than 20 pairs retain all three groups, groups are averaged over those available and this is reported; if fewer than 15 pairs remain the result is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'barriers of any kind' are represented by six classes with replicate pairs, ranked by a pre-registered judgement of how impassable and long-standing they are: contiguous land (0), the Amazon main stem (1), straits shallower than ~120 m that were land during Pleistocene low stands (English Channel, Palk Strait, Bass Strait, Malacca Strait, Torres Strait, Gulf of Paria, Sunda Strait) (2), high mountain ranges (Andes twice, Sierra Nevada) and wide deserts (Nullarbor, Sahara) (3), deep straits with no Pleistocene land bridge (Makassar Strait, Lombok Strait, Mozambique Channel, Yucatán Channel) (4), and ocean basins (Atlantic, Indian) (5). 'Difference between the inhabitants' is species-level Sørensen dissimilarity of three terrestrial, non-volant, non-marine vertebrate groups; bats and birds are excluded because they fly over barriers, and marine mammals because the barriers are their habitat. Distance is a confound Darwin himself names ('distance... is of less importance than barriers'), so the partial correlation controlling for distance is part of the criterion. Introduced species (notably Rattus, Mus, Hemidactylus, Rhinella marina) cannot be removed from GBIF data in general; Rattus and Mus species are removed explicitly, the rest remain and bias against the claim by making distant regions look similar.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between barrier rank and mean species-level Sørensen dissimilarity (Rodentia, Squamata, Amphibia)
measured.uncertainty: one-sided p=1.40e-05; partial Spearman controlling log distance rho=0.800, one-sided p=1.34e-06

datasets.name: GBIF occurrence search API (facet counts of speciesKey for Rodentia, Squamata, Amphibia within bounding boxes; GBIF Backbone Taxonomy for keys)

tests.hypothesis: Within one continent, the genus-level composition of the fauna/flora of two strongly contrasting habitats (hot desert vs. humid tropical forest) is more similar than the composition of the same habitat type on two different continents; i.e. geographic region, not habitat, is the primary predictor of taxonomic affinity.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: for each of five taxonomic groups (Mammalia, Aves, Squamata, Amphibia, Magnoliopsida), compute the Sørensen similarity of genus sets (2|A∩B|/(|A|+|B|), GBIF occurrence-derived genus lists, genera with >= 5 records per region) for (i) the 5 within-continent / different-habitat region pairs and (ii) the 20 between-continent / same-habitat region pairs. The claim is SUPPORTED if the mean of (i) exceeds the mean of (ii) in at least 4 of the 5 groups AND a one-sided Mann-Whitney U test pooling all groups' pairs (i) vs (ii) gives p < 0.01.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTED if the mean of (i) exceeds the mean of (ii) in 2 or fewer of the 5 groups, or if the pooled one-sided Mann-Whitney test in the opposite direction ((ii) > (i)) gives p < 0.05. Any other outcome is MIXED. If fewer than 4 groups have >= 20 genera in every region, the result is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'productions of the same continent' are taken as the native genera recorded in GBIF within fixed bounding boxes on five continents (South America, Africa, Australia, North America incl. Central America, mainland Asia). 'Different stations' is operationalized as two habitat types with the strongest possible contrast on each continent: a hot desert/semi-desert box and a humid tropical forest box. 'Affinity' is operationalized as sharing genera (and, secondarily, families), which is the pre-phylogenetic measure of relatedness Darwin himself used. The 'same sea' half of the claim is not tested here. Regions are fixed before any data are downloaded; genera of domestic and commensal species that humans have spread worldwide (Homo, Rattus, Mus, Canis, Felis, Bos, Ovis, Capra, Sus, Equus, Columba) are excluded, as are fossil and living (zoo/garden) specimen records, because the claim concerns natural distribution.

measured.unit: groups (of 5) where within-continent/different-habitat mean genus Sørensen > between-continent/same-habitat mean
measured.uncertainty: pooled one-sided Mann-Whitney (within > between-same-habitat), genus level: U=2086, p=1.22e-07

datasets.name: GBIF occurrence search API (facet counts of genusKey/familyKey within bounding boxes; GBIF Backbone Taxonomy for keys)

tests.hypothesis: Across well-recorded classes of animals and plants, most genera (and a larger share of genera than of families) have essentially all of their modern occurrence records within a single continental region; and among mammal genera, those whose species are most closely related (youngest crown age in a dated phylogeny) occupy fewer regions and are more often confined to a single region than genera whose species are more distantly related.
tests.pass: Clause 1 (regional confinement by rank): in each of the analysed classes (Mammalia, Aves, Amphibia, Reptilia, Magnoliopsida, Liliopsida, Pinopsida; GBIF backbone), the fraction of assessable genera that are confined to one region (>= 95% of their continent-assigned, non-fossil, non-captive occurrence records in one of six regions: Africa, Eurasia, North America, South America, Oceania, Antarctica) is > 0.50 in at least five of the seven classes, and in at least five of seven classes the confined fraction for genera exceeds the confined fraction for families. Clause 2 (natural genera are local, mammals): the Spearman partial correlation between genus crown age (MRCA age of the sampled congeneric species in the Upham et al. 2019 DNA-only MCC tree) and the number of regions holding >= 5% of the genus's records, controlling for log(number of sampled species in the genus), is positive with p < 0.05, AND the single-region fraction among genera in the youngest crown-age tercile exceeds that in the oldest tercile. The claim is 'supports' if both clauses pass; 'mixed' if exactly one passes; 'refutes' if both fail.
tests.fail: Clause 1 fails if the confined fraction of genera is <= 0.50 in three or more of the seven classes, or genera are not more confined than families in three or more classes. Clause 2 fails if the partial Spearman correlation between crown age and number of regions is <= 0 or not significant at p < 0.05, or the youngest-tercile single-region fraction does not exceed the oldest-tercile fraction. Both clauses failing refutes the claim.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'region' is read as a continental biogeographic region (six regions, with Europe and Asia merged into Eurasia following Sclater's Palaearctic). 'Confined to a single region' is read with a 5% tolerance for misidentified, vagrant, introduced or mislabelled records. Sub-families and sections of genera are not available in the GBIF backbone and are not tested; the rank gradient is tested only between family and genus, with species reported as an extra. 'Most natural genera (species most closely related)' is read, following the assessors, as genera with the youngest crown age in a dated molecular phylogeny; this is a modern phylogenetic reinterpretation of a pre-evolutionary taxonomic notion. Only genera with >= 20 qualifying occurrence records are assessed, so that poorly recorded taxa do not appear confined merely through lack of records.

measured.unit: mean across classes of the fraction of assessable genera with >= 95% of records in one region

datasets.name: GBIF occurrence search API, faceted counts by genus/family/species key per continent
GBIF Backbone Taxonomy species API (genus names for mammal genus keys)
Upham, Esselstyn & Jetz (2019) mammal phylogeny, DNA-only 4098-species node-dated MCC tree (NDexp, topoFree)

tests.hypothesis: If now-separate continents and the existing oceanic islands were not continuously or almost continuously joined by land during the period of existing species, then even at the lowest Quaternary sea level (about -130 m) the sea floor between them should remain submerged: oceanic islands should not connect to any continent, and the Atlantic, Indian and Southern Ocean gaps between continents should not close.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using the NOAA ETOPO 2022 global relief model exported from the NCEI image service onto a 0.1-degree grid, cells with elevation >= -130 m are treated as potentially emergent and labelled into connected components (with longitude wrap). The 45 pre-registered oceanic islands in derived/sites.csv are checked for membership of a continental component (continent seeds in the same file). Five continental gaps are tested for connection at -130 m: (T1) Eurasia-North America via the Atlantic, with the Bering region (lat > 55 N, lon 160 E to 160 W) masked as deep; (T2) Africa/Eurasia-South America; (T3) Australia/New Guinea-Asia; (T4) Antarctica-South America; (T5) Antarctica-Australia. The claim is SUPPORTED if none of T1-T5 is connected at -130 m and at least 90% of the oceanic islands are unconnected. A set of 20 continental (shelf or fragment) islands is run as a positive control and is not part of the verdict.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if two or more of T1-T5 are connected at -130 m, or if 25% or more of the oceanic islands connect to a continent at -130 m. Other outcomes are 'mixed'. The Bering connection between Eurasia and North America is reported separately with its sill depth (the shallowest threshold at which the two connect) because Darwin's wording concerns continents that are 'now quite separate' and he explicitly accepted a near-continuous circumpolar land connection during the glacial period (Chapter XI); it does not enter the verdict.
tests.interpretation: 'The recent period' / 'period of existing species' is read as the Quaternary, for which the maximum glacio-eustatic sea-level fall (about 120-130 m below present) is the most generous possible allowance for land exposure; a gap that remains submerged at -130 m cannot have been bridged by land at any time in that period without vertical crustal movement, which Darwin's opponents (Forbes) invoked and Darwin doubted. 'Oceanic islands' are the volcanic and coral islands listed in derived/sites.csv (one representative point each). 'Continuously or almost continuously united' is approximated by connectivity at the extreme lowstand; connections that exist only near -130 m were at most intermittent, which already satisfies Darwin's denial, so the test is conservative with respect to the claim. The 0.1-degree grid (about 11 km) cannot resolve straits narrower than a cell; bilinear resampling smooths sills, which is noted as a limitation.

measured.unit: fraction of pre-registered oceanic islands whose emergent component at -130 m contains no continent seed
measured.uncertainty: 36 of 45 islands resolved as present-day land on the 0.1-degree grid (the rest located by their -130 m bank); 0 of 5 continental gaps connected at -130 m; 43 of 45 oceanic islands not joined to any continent even at -1000 m

datasets.name: NOAA NCEI ETOPO 2022 Global Relief Model, 60 arc-second surface elevation (ETOPO_2022_v1_60s_N90W180_surface.nc), accessed through the NCEI THREDDS NetCDF Subset Service with horizStride=6 (0.1-degree nearest-sample grid)

tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right that the temperature of the whole world was simultaneously cooler during the Glacial period, then within one and the same dated interval of the last glaciation (the Last Glacial Maximum chronozone, 19-23 ka) surface temperature should have been below modern values everywhere: in both hemispheres, at all latitudes, and in every ocean basin, not only in the northern regions where glacial geology was first described.
tests.pass: In the MARGO gridded compilation of LGM (19-23 ka) sea-surface temperature anomalies (modern minus LGM, annual mean, 5x5 degree cells), (i) >= 90 % of cells with data show cooling (anomaly > 0), (ii) in every 30-degree latitude band of each hemisphere with >= 5 cells, and in each of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific basins, >= 80 % of cells show cooling and the area-weighted mean anomaly is > 0 with a one-sample t-test p < 0.01, and (iii) the area-weighted global mean anomaly is >= 1 degree C.
tests.fail: Refutes if any hemisphere, or any 30-degree band of a hemisphere with >= 5 cells, or any basin, has a majority of cells warmer than modern, or if the global fraction of cooling cells is < 60 %. Any other outcome is mixed.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'Glacial period' is read as the last glaciation and 'this period' as its culmination; the MARGO project's LGM chronozone (19-23 ka, defined on independent radiocarbon and stratigraphic age models) is the standard operationalisation of a single simultaneous interval, so testing whether cooling is found in every region within that window tests simultaneity directly. 'Temperature of the whole world' is tested with sea-surface temperature because the ocean compilation is global, gridded and has quantified errors; land temperatures are not tested here. Darwin's own hedge ('or at least along broad longitudinal belts') is covered by the per-band and per-basin criteria. A cell counts as 'cooler' if the central anomaly estimate is positive; a sensitivity count using only cells whose anomaly exceeds its total error is reported but is not part of the rule.

measured.unit: fraction of 5x5 degree ocean grid cells with LGM (19-23 ka) annual SST below modern
measured.uncertainty: area-weighted mean cooling 2.063 C; 0.433 of cells cooler by more than the stated total error

datasets.name: MARGO Project Members (2009) Constraints on the magnitude and patterns of ocean cooling at the Last Glacial Maximum, Nature Geoscience 2:127-132; supplementary Table S9 (MARGO_all_LGM_SST, 5x5 degree grid), archived at PANGAEA

tests.hypothesis: If the Glacial period lasted a very long time at each place and was at least in part simultaneous across the whole world, then (a) a globally mixed marine proxy of ice volume and deep-water temperature (benthic d18O) shows prolonged cold, ice-rich states lasting well over 10 thousand years and recurring through the Pleistocene, with the last glacial maximum in such a state, and (b) a southern-hemisphere high-latitude temperature record (Antarctic ice core) is cold at the same times as the global proxy is ice-rich, within age-model uncertainty.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: (1) LR04 benthic d18O stack of Lisiecki and Raymo (2005), the LR04stack.txt file served by the author (columns: age in ka, benthic d18O in per mil, error), and (2) EPICA Dome C deuterium-derived temperature anomaly on the EDC3 age scale (Jouzel et al. 2007), the NOAA paleoclimatology file edc3deuttemp2007.txt. Criterion A (long-lasting cold states): with d18O linearly interpolated to a 1-kyr grid over 0-2600 ka, d18O >= 4.0 per mil during at least 20% of the interval AND at least 5 separate contiguous intervals with d18O >= 4.0 per mil each lasting >= 10 kyr. Criterion B (last glacial maximum): mean d18O over 18-26 ka >= 4.5 per mil. Criterion C (simultaneity, north-dominated ice volume vs southern temperature): both series interpolated to a 1-kyr grid over 0-800 ka; the maximum Pearson correlation between EDC temperature anomaly and negative d18O across lags of -6 to +6 kyr (to allow for independent age models) is >= 0.6. SUPPORTS if A, B and C all hold.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if d18O >= 4.0 per mil covers < 10% of 0-2600 ka, OR fewer than 2 contiguous >= 4.0 per mil intervals last >= 10 kyr, OR the 18-26 ka mean d18O is < 4.2 per mil, OR the maximum lagged correlation in criterion C is < 0.3 (southern temperature not in step with global ice volume). MIXED otherwise (values between the support and refute thresholds, or A and B holding while C is between 0.3 and 0.6). INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if either file cannot be downloaded.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's Glacial period is mapped to the Pleistocene glacial stages. 'Lasted a very long time' is read as cold states of at least 10 kyr; 'simultaneous across the whole world' is read as the Antarctic (southern high-latitude) temperature record being in step with the benthic d18O stack, whose glacial signal is dominated by northern-hemisphere ice sheets; this is a two-hemisphere test of simultaneity at the resolution of orbital cycles, not of the sub-millennial bipolar seesaw. Darwin implied one long glacial episode; the data show many cycles, so the test asks whether long, globally cold intervals recur and co-occur. The 4.0 and 4.5 per mil thresholds and the 0.6 correlation threshold were fixed before any data were read. Criteria A and B follow the swarm thread's draft plan; criterion C was added to address the simultaneity clause the draft could not test.

measured.unit: fraction of the last 2.6 Myr with benthic d18O >= 4.0 per mil (pre-registered threshold 0.20)
measured.uncertainty: LR04 standard errors are 0.03-0.1 per mil per point, small relative to the 4.0 threshold

datasets.name: LR04: Pliocene-Pleistocene stack of 57 globally distributed benthic d18O records (Lisiecki and Raymo 2005), author's distribution file LR04stack.txt
EPICA Dome C ice core 800 kyr deuterium and temperature estimates on the EDC3 age scale (Jouzel et al. 2007), NOAA World Data Service for Paleoclimatology file edc3deuttemp2007.txt

tests.hypothesis: The vascular-plant floras of high tropical mountains share a few identical species and many more genera with the temperate lowland floras of both hemispheres, and they share more genera with those temperate floras than the tropical lowlands at the foot of the same mountains do; the temperate lowland floras of the two hemispheres are likewise related at the genus level beyond what tropical lowlands share with them.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Regions: 4 tropical high-mountain regions M (GBIF records with elevation >= 3500 m in the N Andes and Trans-Mexican volcanic belt, >= 3000 m in the East African mountains and New Guinea highlands), their 4 tropical-lowland controls C (same bounding box, elevation <= 800 m), 3 northern (N) and 3 southern (S) temperate lowland regions L (elevation <= 600 m). Species/genus present if >= 3 records. For a pair (X, L): f_sp = |species(X) ∩ species(L)| / |species(X)|, f_gen = |genera(X) ∩ genera(L)| / |genera(X)|. SUPPORTS requires all of: (A) in >= 20 of the 24 (M, L) pairs, 0 < f_sp < 0.5 f_gen (identical species exist but are the minority of allied relationships); (B) in >= 20 of 24 (M, L) pairs f_gen(M, L) > f_gen(C_M, L) (one-sided binomial sign test vs 0.5, p < 0.01); (C) in >= 7 of the 9 (N, S) pairs f_gen(N, S) exceeds the mean over k of f_gen(C_k, S).
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if (B) holds in <= 12 of 24 pairs or (C) holds in <= 4 of 9 pairs. Any other combination is MIXED. If any mountain region yields fewer than 50 species, that region is dropped; with fewer than 3 mountain regions remaining the result is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: 'Plants' = Tracheophyta (GBIF phylum key 7707728). 'Lofty mountains' including tropical ones = GBIF records above 3500 m (3000 m for Africa and New Guinea, whose summits are lower and more sparsely recorded) inside fixed tropical bounding boxes. 'Temperate lowlands of the northern and southern hemispheres' = fixed lowland boxes at 41-55 N and 34-55 S. 'Identically the same' = same GBIF backbone species; 'specifically distinct though related' = different species in the same genus (Darwin's own unit of alliance). Because 'remarkable' relatedness needs a reference, the tropical lowlands at the foot of each mountain range are the pre-registered control: Darwin's glacial-dispersal explanation implies the alpine flora, not the surrounding tropical lowland flora, is the one allied to temperate floras. Introduced species cannot be excluded from GBIF occurrence data; this inflates species identity (A) and is listed as a caveat.

measured.unit: of 24 (tropical mountain, temperate lowland) pairs in which the mountain flora shares a larger fraction of its genera with the temperate flora than the adjacent tropical lowland flora does
measured.uncertainty: one-sided binomial sign test vs 0.5: p=5.96e-08

datasets.name: GBIF occurrence search API (facet counts of speciesKey/genusKey for Tracheophyta within bounding boxes and elevation bands; GBIF Backbone Taxonomy for keys)

tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, many more European species have become naturalised in La Plata (and, to a lesser degree, in Australia) than species from those southern regions have become naturalised anywhere in Europe: the Europe-to-south naturalisation count should exceed the south-to-Europe count several-fold for each region.
tests.pass: Using World Checklist of Vascular Plants native and introduced distribution records by TDWG level-3 unit: A_LP = number of species native in Europe (TDWG level-1 region 1) and not native in La Plata that are recorded as introduced in La Plata (units AGE Argentina Northeast and URU Uruguay); B_LP = number of species native in La Plata and not native in Europe that are recorded as introduced in any European unit; likewise A_AU and B_AU for Australia (TDWG level-2 region 50: WAU, NTA, SOA, QLD, NSW, VIC, TAS). Supports if A_LP >= 5 * B_LP and A_AU >= 5 * B_AU.
tests.fail: Refutes if A_LP < 2 * B_LP or A_AU < 2 * B_AU (no strong asymmetry, or reversed). Otherwise mixed. The secondary clause 'in a lesser degree in Australia' is evaluated as A_LP > A_AU and reported, but is not part of the verdict rule because absolute counts now depend on two centuries of differing colonisation history.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'productions' is tested for vascular plants, the group for which native and introduced status is coded worldwide at consistent regional units; his La Plata examples (cardoon, thistles, fennel) are plants. 'Naturalised' is mapped to WCVP's 'introduced' flag, which records established alien occurrences in a unit (casual records and cultivated plants are excluded by WCVP's criteria). 'Europe' is TDWG level-1 region 1 (Iceland to the Urals, including the Mediterranean islands and European Russia; Macaronesia is in Africa in TDWG). 'La Plata' is the Rio de la Plata basin lowlands, mapped to Argentina Northeast (which includes Buenos Aires and Entre Rios provinces) plus Uruguay. Species native to both source and recipient regions are excluded. Counts are reported raw (Darwin's 'very many' versus 'extremely few') and as a fraction of each source flora. The claim is about the pattern, not its cause; propagule pressure is discussed in caveats only.

measured.unit: ratio of European plant species naturalised in La Plata to La Plata species naturalised in Europe (WCVP)
measured.uncertainty: exact counts from WCVP status flags; depends on completeness of introduced-status coding

datasets.name: World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP), Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: wcvp_names.csv and wcvp_distribution.csv in wcvp.zip

tests.hypothesis: Within each of three classes (insects, molluscs, flowering plants), species of fresh-water families occupy more continents than species of related terrestrial families, and fresh-water genera are more often spread over several continents than terrestrial genera.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: for every family in the fixed fresh-water and terrestrial lists, GBIF occurrence facets give the set of species and genera recorded (>= 3 records) on each of the six inhabited continents. Per class, compute P_sp = proportion of species recorded on >= 3 continents and P_gen = proportion of genera recorded on >= 3 continents, separately for the fresh-water and the terrestrial family set. SUPPORTS if in all three classes P_sp(fresh-water) > P_sp(terrestrial) AND P_gen(fresh-water) > P_gen(terrestrial), and the pooled species-level continent counts differ in the fresh-water direction (one-sided Mann-Whitney, p < 0.001).
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if, in at least two of the three classes, P_sp(fresh-water) <= P_sp(terrestrial) or P_gen(fresh-water) <= P_gen(terrestrial). Any other outcome is MIXED. A class with fewer than 200 species in either habitat set is dropped; with fewer than two classes remaining the result is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: 'Fresh-water species of quite different classes' is operationalised with three classes Darwin names in this section (insects, molluscs, plants), using families whose members live in fresh water, each paired with terrestrial families of the same class and, where possible, the same order (aquatic Adephaga beetles vs. Carabidae; aquatic Heteroptera vs. terrestrial Heteroptera; freshwater snails and mussels vs. land snails; aquatic angiosperm families vs. a fixed list of common terrestrial angiosperm families). 'Enormous range' is given a comparison group as both assessors demanded: a species recorded on three or more continents. 'Allied species prevail throughout the world' = the genus is recorded on three or more continents. Continents follow GBIF's continent field (derived from coordinates), excluding Antarctica. Human-mediated introductions are present in both habitat sets and cannot be separated in GBIF; this is a caveat, not a filter.

tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, an oceanic island supports far fewer native species than a continental area of the same size, after allowing for the physical conditions he thought could not explain the difference; for vascular plants (de Candolle's case) native species richness of oceanic island units should fall well below the continental species-area relationship.
tests.pass: Fit log10(native vascular plant species) = a + b*log10(area km2) + c*|centroid latitude| by ordinary least squares on continental (mainland-connected) TDWG level-3 botanical countries from the World Checklist of Vascular Plants, then predict richness for each pre-registered oceanic island unit at its own area and latitude. Supports if (i) the median ratio of observed to predicted richness across oceanic units is <= 0.5, (ii) >= 80 % of oceanic units lie below the continental prediction, and (iii) a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the oceanic log-residuals against zero gives p < 0.01.
tests.fail: Refutes if the median observed/predicted ratio is >= 1.0 or fewer than 60 % of oceanic units lie below the prediction. Any other outcome is mixed. Oceanic units whose area lies outside the range of continental areas used in the fit are excluded from the test and listed.
tests.interpretation: 'Species of all kinds' is tested for vascular plants, the group Darwin cites de Candolle for and the only group with a complete, native-status-coded global checklist at consistent regional units. 'Oceanic islands' are the TDWG level-3 units that are volcanic hot-spot islands, atolls or intra-oceanic arc islands never joined to a continent: AZO, MDR, SEL, CNY, CVI, STH, ASC, TDC, BER, GAL, HAW, MID, FIJ, SAM, TON, SCI, MRQ, TUA, TUB, COO, NUE, PIT, EAS, JNF, VAN, NFK, MAU, REU, ROD, COM, GGI, CRL, MRN, MRS, GIL, LIN, PHX, WAL, TOK, TVL, NRU, WAK, HBI, KER, CRZ, ASP, HMD, MPE, BOU, ICE, OGA, KZN, MCS, CGS, MDV, LDV, XMS, CKI, SGE, TRT, SOL (Solomon Is., oceanic arc), SCZ (Santa Cruz Is.), ALD (Aldabra). Units that are continental fragments or shelf islands (e.g. NWC New Caledonia, SEY Seychelles, FAL, NZN, NZS, MDG, GRB, JAP, SRL, CUB, FOR) are excluded from both groups; 'continental' means a level-3 unit whose polygons lie within 2 km of another unit's polygons (i.e. part of a connected mainland block), Antarctica excluded. Area is the spherical area of each unit's polygons; |latitude| of the area-weighted centroid is the only 'physical condition' covariate available at this resolution, so the physical-conditions clause is only crudely addressed. Native richness counts accepted species (rank Species) with a WCVP distribution record that is not introduced, extinct or doubtful. Small continental units (city-states, small countries) and the smallest oceanic islands may be undersampled in different ways; this is noted rather than corrected.

Oceanic islands are the 63 level-3 areas pre-registered as 'oceanic' in derived/island_classes.csv; the mainland comparison set is every level-3 area not listed in that file as any kind of island. Areas (km2) are computed from the TDWG WGSRPD level-3 polygons. The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) the median S of oceanic islands is below the median S of mainland areas ('scanty'), (ii) the median E/S of oceanic islands with at least 20 native species is at least twice the median E/S of mainland areas, and (iii) at least 70% of oceanic islands with at least 20 native species lie above the mainland regression line of logit(E/S) on log10(area) ('extremely large relative to their area'). Islands with fewer than 20 native species are excluded from (ii) and (iii) because a proportion is unstable for them.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if the median E/S of oceanic islands is not greater than the mainland median, or if fewer than 50% of oceanic islands lie above the mainland area regression line. 'Found nowhere else in the world' is read as native to exactly one level-3 area, so for mainland areas 'endemic' means endemic to that botanical country, which is the fairest available analogue. tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, bats are recorded on almost every remote oceanic island group that has been reasonably surveyed, and a substantial share of those groups have bat species found nowhere else, in sharp contrast with the near-absence of native non-volant land mammals on the same islands.
tests.pass: Using the 43 pre-registered island units lying > 300 statute miles from any landmass >= 100,000 km2 (the far units of darwin1859-ch12-09, same GBIF filters and representative points), a unit counts as 'surveyed' if GBIF holds >= 500 non-fossil, non-captive bird (class Aves) records for it. A surveyed unit 'has bats' if at least one Chiroptera species has >= 5 non-fossil, non-captive GBIF records inside the unit (single records are treated as possible vagrants). A bat species is 'endemic' to a unit if it has >= 10 records worldwide and >= 95 % of them inside the unit (same rule as ch12-09). Supports if >= 80 % of surveyed far units have bats AND >= 33 % of the surveyed far units with bats have >= 1 endemic bat species.
tests.fail: Refutes if < 50 % of surveyed far units have bats, or if < 10 % of the bat-occupied surveyed units have an endemic bat species. Otherwise mixed. The contrast with non-volant mammals is reported descriptively: the number of far units with an endemic bat species is compared with the number having an endemic non-volant terrestrial mammal from the same GBIF endemism rule (1 of 43 in darwin1859-ch12-09).
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'almost every island' is read as 'almost every remote oceanic island group that naturalists have actually searched', since he was generalising from the islands then known; the Aves-record threshold is a proxy for survey effort independent of bats. 'Their own species' is operationalised as GBIF endemism at the unit level; subspecies-level endemics (e.g. the Hawaiian hoary bat, treated by GBIF as Lasiurus cinereus or Aeorestes semotus depending on the backbone) are counted only if the backbone treats them as species. 'Remote' uses the ch12-09 distance rule (> 482.8 km from any landmass >= 100,000 km2), so the test is on the same 43 units for which the absence of terrestrial mammals was tested. Units are archipelago-level (country codes or bounding boxes), so a bat endemic to one island within a group counts as endemic to the unit. The threshold of >= 5 records per species is intended to exclude storm-blown vagrants (e.g. North American bats recorded in Iceland or Bermuda) while keeping genuinely resident but poorly recorded species; a sensitivity with >= 1 record is reported.

tests.hypothesis: Across continental and near-continental islands, the fraction of an island's terrestrial mammal species that also occur on the neighbouring mainland decreases with the maximum depth of the sea channel separating them, and this relationship holds after controlling for the width of the channel; islands whose channel is shallower than the Pleistocene low stand (about 120 m) share more species than islands whose channel is deeper.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: for each of 28 fixed islands, (i) the terrestrial mammal species set (GBIF Mammalia occurrences with >= 3 records inside the island box, minus bats, cetaceans, sirenians, pinnipeds and 12 domestic or commensal genera), (ii) the same for a fixed neighbouring-mainland box, (iii) channel depth = greatest water depth (GEBCO 2020 via the OpenTopoData API, 100 points) along a fixed straight transect between the nearest island and mainland shores, and (iv) channel width = transect length. f = |island ∩ mainland| / |island|. SUPPORTS if all of: Spearman rho(f, log depth) < 0 with one-sided p < 0.05; partial Spearman of f on log depth controlling log width < 0 with one-sided p < 0.05; mean f of islands with depth <= 120 m exceeds mean f of islands with depth > 120 m.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if Spearman rho(f, log depth) >= 0 or if mean f of shallow (<= 120 m) islands is <= mean f of deep (> 120 m) islands. Any other outcome is MIXED. Islands with fewer than 5 qualifying species are dropped; with fewer than 12 islands remaining the result is inconclusive (underpowered). If the bathymetry API is unreachable the result is inconclusive (data-unavailable).
tests.interpretation: 'Terrestrial mammals' excludes bats (Darwin treats them separately), marine mammals and species carried by humans (domestic stock, commensal rodents, Homo); other introductions remain in GBIF and bias against the claim by making deep-water islands look similar to the mainland. 'Depth of sea' is the present maximum depth along a straight line between the nearest shores; Darwin's reasoning is about former land connections, so the 120 m Pleistocene low-stand depth is the pre-registered dividing line, and present depth is an imperfect stand-in for past connection (caveat). 'Same or allied species' is measured at the species level only (shared species fraction); genus-level affinity is recorded as a secondary descriptive measure. For Wallacean islands (Sulawesi, Lombok) the Sunda-shelf islands Borneo and Bali serve as the 'mainland', and for Hokkaido and Ireland the larger neighbouring islands (Honshu, Great Britain) do, as Darwin himself discusses Britain and its islands; this is noted.

tests.hypothesis: For endemic vascular plants of oceanic islands, the nearest relatives outside the island group on an independent synthetic phylogeny are, in a large majority of cases, native to the nearest continent or to the island group's own neighbouring islands.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: endemics of island group A = WCVP accepted non-hybrid species whose non-doubtful native records (introduced = 0) all lie in A. For each genus containing such an endemic, all WCVP accepted species are matched exactly to Open Tree (TNRS, context 'Land plants') and the induced subtree of the synthetic tree is fetched. For a focal endemic, the outside relatives O are the non-A tips of the smallest clade containing the focal tip and >= 1 non-A tip. The focal endemic is 'near-related' if more than half of O have a native record in A's pre-registered near source S_A (the TDWG level-1 continent nearest to A, plus A's own TDWG level-2 region, i.e. other near islands). s_A = fraction near-related. Island groups with < 10 focal endemics are dropped. SUPPORTS ('almost universal rule') if pooled s >= 0.75 AND s_A >= 0.6 in at least 75% of remaining island groups.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if pooled s < 0.5 or if s_A < 0.5 in a majority of remaining island groups. Any other outcome is MIXED. Fewer than 5 island groups remaining: inconclusive (underpowered). WCVP or Open Tree unreachable: inconclusive (data-unavailable). As a descriptive control, the fraction of all non-A congeners native to S_A is reported for each island group.
tests.interpretation: 'Related to those of the nearest continent, or of other near islands' is read as: the closest non-island relatives (sister clade on the genus tree) are native to the nearest continent, with near islands meaning the TDWG level-2 region the island group belongs to. Nearest continents (TDWG level 1) are fixed in advance by great-circle proximity: Galápagos 8 (Southern America), Juan Fernández 8, Cape Verde 2 (Africa), Canaries 2, Madeira 2, Azores 1 (Europe), Hawaii 7 (Northern America), Bermuda 7, Mascarenes (MAU+REU+ROD) 2, Seychelles 2, Tristan da Cunha 2, Fiji 5 (Australasia). Darwin's own contrast with climatically similar distant regions (assessors' suggestion) is not modelled; the test asks only whether the nearest continent dominates. Plants only; genus-level trees, so endemics of island-endemic genera are not scored.

tests.hypothesis: For endemic vascular plants of oceanic archipelagos, the nearest relative on an independent synthetic phylogeny is, far more often than chance and in most cases, another species native to the same archipelago rather than a species from anywhere else.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: endemics of archipelago A = WCVP accepted non-hybrid species whose non-doubtful native records (introduced = 0) all lie in A. For every genus containing such an endemic, all WCVP accepted species of the genus are matched exactly to the Open Tree taxonomy (TNRS, context 'Land plants', no approximate matching) and the induced subtree of the Open Tree synthetic tree is fetched; tips are labelled A-native or non-A. A focal endemic qualifies if its genus tree has >= 1 other A-native tip and >= 1 non-A tip. Walking up from the focal tip to the first ancestor whose clade holds other tips, the outcome is 'inside' if those tips are all A-native, 'outside' if all non-A, 'tie' if mixed. f_in = inside / (inside + outside). Null per focal tip: the same clade size k drawn at random from the other tips of its genus tree (hypergeometric P_in, P_out); the null distribution of f_in is simulated (10,000 draws, seed 1). Archipelagos with < 10 resolved (inside + outside) endemics are dropped. SUPPORTS if pooled f_in >= 0.67 AND at least 75% of remaining archipelagos have f_in > 0.5 with simulated one-sided p < 0.05.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if pooled f_in <= 0.5, or if in a majority of remaining archipelagos f_in does not exceed its null expectation. Any other outcome is MIXED. Fewer than 5 remaining archipelagos: inconclusive (underpowered). WCVP or Open Tree API unreachable: inconclusive (data-unavailable). The tie fraction (unresolved polytomies, often taxonomy-only placements) is reported.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'inhabitants of each separate island ... related in an incomparably closer degree to each other than to the inhabitants of any other part of the world' is read for endemic vascular plants: the nearest relative of an endemic should lie in the same archipelago. WCVP level-3 units are whole archipelagos, so 'separate islands' cannot be resolved except for the Mascarenes, which WCVP splits into Mauritius, Réunion and Rodrigues and which are pooled here as one archipelago (MAU+REU+ROD); for the others the test asks whether archipelago endemics cluster with archipelago natives. Relatives are searched within the genus only (genus trees from Open Tree), so endemics whose whole genus is confined to the archipelago contribute nothing. Archipelagos (WCVP level-3 codes): HAW, GAL, CNY, MDR, AZO, CVI, JNF, SCI, MRQ, FIJ, SAM, TUB, VAN, SEY, Mascarenes (MAU+REU+ROD); codes absent from WCVP are dropped. Plants only; Darwin's examples include birds and insects.

tests.hypothesis: In well-documented regional floras, vascular plant species naturalised in a region belong to genera that have no native species there more often than do the species that have naturalised elsewhere in the world but not in that region (the pool of proven colonists that could have joined it).
tests.pass: Pre-registered: using WCVP (World Checklist of Vascular Plants, Kew) accepted non-hybrid species and their non-doubtful TDWG level-3 distribution records, for each of 24 fixed regions R: native genera G_R = genera with >= 1 species recorded native (introduced = 0, extinct = 0) in R; naturalised set N_R = species recorded introduced in R and not native in R; pool P_R = species recorded introduced in >= 1 other level-3 region and with no record (native or introduced) in R. 'Novel' = genus not in G_R. Odds ratio OR_R = odds(novel | N_R) / odds(novel | P_R), Fisher exact test one-sided in each direction. Regions with |N_R| < 50 are dropped. SUPPORTS if, among the remaining regions, at least two thirds have OR_R > 1 with one-sided p < 0.05 (naturalised species over-represented in genera absent from the native flora).
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if at least two thirds of the remaining regions have OR_R < 1 with one-sided p < 0.05 (naturalised species significantly more likely than the colonist pool to have native congeners). Any other outcome is MIXED. If fewer than 12 regions remain the result is inconclusive (underpowered); if WCVP cannot be downloaded, inconclusive (data-unavailable). The fraction of naturalised species in novel genera (Darwin's and de Candolle's 'large proportion ... distinct genera') is recorded per region as a descriptive statistic and does not enter the verdict.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'not closely allied to the aboriginal inhabitants ... belonging in a large proportion of cases ... to distinct genera' is read at the genus level (the level de Candolle used): a naturalised species is 'closely allied' to the natives if its genus has a native species in the region. The claim is comparative in substance (closely allied species 'tend to keep separate'), so the test compares naturalised species with a colonist pool rather than with zero; the pool is all species proven able to naturalise somewhere, which controls for the fact that only some plants become weeds at all. WCVP 'introduced' records are taken as naturalised occurrences. Restricted to vascular plants, the group de Candolle and Darwin discussed; animals are out of scope of this test. The 24 regions are TDWG level-3 units with well-documented floras on every continent and oceanic islands: NZN, NZS, HAW, GRB, IRE, FRA, GER, SPA, ITA, CAL, TEX, FLA, NSW, VIC, WAU, TAS, CPP, CLC, AGE, JAP, MAU, REU, CNY, AZO; codes absent from WCVP are dropped and reported.

measured.unit: fraction of regions where naturalised plants are significantly MORE likely than the colonist pool to belong to genera already native (OR < 1, one-sided p < 0.05)
measured.uncertainty: regions significant in Darwin's direction: 0/24; opposite direction: 23/24

datasets.name: World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP), Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: wcvp_names.csv and wcvp_distribution.csv

tests.hypothesis: If closer relatives are generally nearer in space and time, then (space, living forms) phylogenetic distance between bird species should correlate positively with the geographic distance between their range centroids, with congeneric pairs closer than confamilial pairs and those closer than pairs from different families of the same order; and (time, fossil forms) genera in the same family should have first appearances closer in geological time than genera in different families of the same order.
tests.pass: Space (all extant birds with a range centroid in AVONET and a tip in the BirdTree Hackett MCC tree supplied with AVONET): (S1) the Spearman correlation between patristic distance and great-circle centroid distance across a fixed random sample of 2,000,000 species pairs is positive, and exceeds all of 99 permutations in which centroids are shuffled among species (p <= 0.01); (S2) median centroid distance is strictly ordered congeneric pairs < confamilial non-congeneric pairs < same-order different-family pairs. Time (Paleobiology Database genera of Mammalia and of Mollusca with first-appearance ages and family/order assignments): (T1) in each of the two groups, the median absolute difference in first-appearance midpoint age between pairs of genera in the same family is smaller than between pairs of genera in different families of the same order, and this difference exceeds all of 99 permutations of family labels within orders (p <= 0.01). The space clause passes if S1 and S2 hold; the time clause passes if T1 holds in both groups. Verdict 'supports' if both clauses pass, 'mixed' if one passes, 'refutes' if neither.
tests.fail: The space clause fails if the Spearman correlation is <= 0 or does not exceed the permutation distribution at p <= 0.01, or if the median distances are not strictly ordered by relatedness. The time clause fails if in either group same-family genus pairs are not closer in first-appearance time than different-family same-order pairs, or the difference is not significant at p <= 0.01 against the within-order permutation null. Both failing refutes the claim.
tests.interpretation: 'Related by descent' is measured for living birds as patristic distance on a dated molecular supertree (Jetz et al. 2012 BirdTree, Hackett backbone MCC tree as distributed with AVONET), a modern reinterpretation of Darwin's classification-based relatedness, and for fossils by shared family versus shared order in PBDB taxonomy, which is closer to Darwin's own usage. 'Nearer in geographic space' is the great-circle distance between AVONET breeding-range centroids. 'Nearer in time' is the absolute difference between first-appearance ages (midpoints of PBDB first-appearance age ranges) of genera. Only two living/fossil systems are tested, not 'all organisms'; birds are chosen because tree, taxonomy and centroids come from a single curated source, and mammals and molluscs because they are the best-sampled terrestrial and marine fossil records. Sampling and taxonomic-practice confounds (geography informing species limits; fossils concentrated in a few basins) are noted as caveats rather than corrected.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between patristic distance and centroid great-circle distance, bird species pairs
measured.uncertainty: permutation p = 0.010; permuted rho range -0.0071 to 0.0068

tests.hypothesis: If distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form, then among bird species from different orders, pairs sharing an ecological niche should be closer in external morphology than pairs with different niches; external morphology should predict ecological niche better than it predicts order (deep ancestry), yet within an order it should still predict family membership well above chance.
tests.pass: Using AVONET (Tobias et al. 2022) species-level external measurements (beak length culmen, beak length nares, beak width, beak depth, tarsus length, wing length, Kipp's distance, secondary1, hand-wing index, tail length, body mass; log-transformed and z-scored) and AVONET ecological categories (trophic niche, primary lifestyle, habitat), three clauses are tested. (a) Convergence: among all between-order species pairs, the mean standardized Euclidean morphological distance of pairs with identical niche (same trophic niche AND same primary lifestyle) is at least 10% smaller than that of pairs with different trophic niche AND different primary lifestyle, with a permutation p < 0.01 (niche labels shuffled among species, 200 permutations). (b) Concealment between groups: leave-one-out k-nearest-neighbour (k = 5) prediction from morphology yields a Cohen's kappa for ecological niche (trophic niche x primary lifestyle combination) that is higher than the kappa for taxonomic order. (c) Affinity within groups: among orders with >= 3 families and >= 30 species, leave-one-out k-NN prediction of family from morphology (congeners excluded from the neighbour pool) gives kappa > 0.3 in a majority of such orders. Verdict 'supports' if all three clauses pass; 'mixed' if one or two pass; 'refutes' if none passes.
tests.fail: Clause (a) fails if same-niche between-order pairs are not at least 10% closer in morphology than different-niche pairs, or the permutation p >= 0.01. Clause (b) fails if morphology predicts order with kappa >= that for niche. Clause (c) fails if kappa for family within order is <= 0.3 in half or more of the eligible orders. No clause passing refutes the claim; (a) failing alone already refutes the central convergence statement and is reported as 'mixed' only if (b) or (c) pass.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'very distinct lines of descent' is read as different bird orders; 'similar conditions' as the same AVONET trophic niche and primary lifestyle; 'close external resemblance' as proximity in the space of AVONET external measurements (bill, wing, tail, tarsus, mass), which are exactly the adaptive external characters Darwin had in mind. 'Almost worthless for classification between groups' is read comparatively: external form carries more information about ecology than about ordinal membership. 'Can indicate true affinity within a group' is read as external form still predicting family within an order. Only birds are tested (the claim is stated for animals generally); taxonomy (BirdLife/AVONET orders and families) is used as the measure of relatedness, which is a modern phylogenetically informed classification but not a dated tree.

measured.unit: ratio of mean morphological distance, same-niche / different-niche between-order species pairs
measured.uncertainty: permutation p = 0.0050 (200 permutations); permutation ratios ranged 0.979-1.019

datasets.name: AVONET: morphological, ecological and geographical data for all birds (ELEData.zip, file TraitData/AVONET1_BirdLife.csv)

tests.hypothesis: On an independently estimated (largely molecular) tree of life, each class of animals and plants as recognised in 1859 forms a group of single origin: the most parsimonious reconstruction of class membership on the tree requires only one origin of the class (with any number of losses to nested groups), not several independent origins.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: for 22 classes as circumscribed in the Cuvier/Owen system current in 1859, each represented by 3-7 fixed modern taxa, an induced subtree of the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree is obtained. For each class, membership is coded on the tips and reconstructed by weighted parsimony (gain cost 2, loss cost 1; among equally cheap reconstructions the one with fewest gains); the number of origins = gains + 1 if the root is reconstructed as a member. A class is 'of single descent' if origins = 1. SUPPORTS if at least 80% of the classes (>= 18 of 22) are of single descent.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if 50% or fewer of the classes (<= 11 of 22) are of single descent. Between 12 and 17 is MIXED. If the Open Tree API is unreachable or fewer than 85% of the representative taxa can be placed as tips, the result is inconclusive (data-unavailable). The Dollo count (number of maximal all-member clades) is recorded as a secondary descriptive statistic.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'class' is read as the classes his contemporaries used (Cuvier's Règne animal as modified by Owen and Milne-Edwards; de Candolle's three plant classes), not modern monophyletic classes, because the claim says descent embraces 'all the members of the same class' as then delimited: Pisces include cyclostomes, Reptilia include turtles, crocodiles, lizards and snakes but not birds, Acephala include bivalves and tunicates, Insecta include myriapods, Echinodermata include sipunculans and priapulids, Entozoa unite parasitic worms, Acalephae unite jellyfish and comb jellies, Polypi unite corals, hydroids, bryozoans and sponges, Infusoria unite ciliates, flagellates, rotifers and diatoms, Dicotyledones include gymnosperms, and Acotyledones unite ferns, mosses, algae and fungi. 'Embraced by descent with modification' is read as single origin on the genealogy: a paraphyletic class (one origin, nested classes 'lost' from it, e.g. Reptilia relative to Aves) counts as embraced, a polyphyletic class (several origins) does not. Representatives are fixed in advance; the 'independently estimated' genealogy is the Open Tree synthetic tree whose backbone comes mostly from molecular studies.

measured.unit: of 22 classes as circumscribed in 1859 that have a single origin under weighted parsimony (gain 2, loss 1) on the Open Tree synthetic tree
measured.uncertainty: fraction 0.773; mapped fraction of representative taxa 0.883

datasets.name: Open Tree of Life synthetic tree opentree16.1 (taxonomy 3.7draft3) via the v3 API: tnrs/match_names and tree_of_life/induced_subtree

tests.hypothesis: On an independently estimated tree of life, the organisms Darwin called animals fall into at most four or five separate clades that contain no plants, and the organisms he called plants fall into no more such clades than the animals do.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: on the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree induced on a fixed set of major lineages (listed below with their 1859 kingdom assignment), count for each kingdom the Dollo number of progenitors = number of maximal clades whose tips all belong to that kingdom (tips of the other kingdom or of neither break a clade). Two readings are scored. Modern reading: animals = Metazoa, plants = Embryophyta + the other Archaeplastida. 1859 reading: animals = Metazoa plus the 'Protozoa' then placed among animals (Infusoria, Rhizopoda, Gregarinida), plants = land plants, green, red and brown algae, diatoms, fungi and blue-green algae. SUPPORTS if under BOTH readings animal progenitors <= 5 and plant progenitors <= animal progenitors.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if under the modern reading animal progenitors > 5 or plant progenitors > animal progenitors. MIXED if the modern reading satisfies both conditions but the 1859 reading violates either. If the Open Tree API is unreachable or fewer than 90% of the listed lineages map to the tree, the result is inconclusive (data-unavailable).
tests.interpretation: A 'progenitor' is read as an independent root of descent, i.e. a clade on the tree of life containing only members of the kingdom in question; the number of such clades needed to cover the kingdom is the number of progenitors the kingdom requires. Because the 1859 kingdoms differ from modern ones (Darwin's contemporaries placed ciliates, amoebae, foraminifera and gregarines among animals, and fungi, diatoms and blue-green 'algae' among plants), the count is made both for the modern kingdoms and for the kingdoms as understood in 1859; the pre-registered assignment follows the standard mid-19th-century arrangement (von Siebold 1845 for Protozoa; the botanical placement of fungi and algae). Diatoms were disputed (Ehrenberg: animals; most botanists: plants) and are assigned to plants; Euglenozoa were 'Infusoria' and are assigned to animals. The test uses the Open Tree synthetic tree as the independent genealogy; it does not test whether Darwin's own lower guess ('probably all organic beings from one primordial form') is right.

measured.unit: independent clades (Dollo progenitors) required for the animals of 1859 (Metazoa + Protozoa) on the Open Tree synthetic tree
measured.uncertainty: modern reading: animals 1, plants 3; 1859 reading: animals 6, plants 6
