tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, the primes below 10^8, generated by the sieve of Eratosthenes (the 'simple rule'), look random in most of a pre-declared list of statistical respects when compared with Cramer's random model (independent events with probability 1/ln n), while possibly showing structure in a minority of respects.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Generate all primes below N = 10^8 by sieve; validate against the OEIS A000040 b-file (first 10000 primes must match exactly) and the published value pi(10^8) = 5761455 (OEIS A006880). Simulate the Cramer model on the same range with numpy seed 20261031 and run every statistic on both. Seven respects, each with a threshold for 'random-like': R1 coarse gap distribution: for primes in [N/2, N], maximum over j of |F_emp(30 j) - (1 - exp(-30 j / mean gap))| < 0.03, where F_emp is the empirical CDF of gaps; R2 Pearson correlation of consecutive gaps in [N/2, N]: |rho| < 0.05; R3 equidistribution over the four residue classes coprime to 12: maximum deviation of a class share from 1/4 below 0.005 (the Cramer model is evaluated on its own coprime-to-12 events); R4 counts of primes in consecutive disjoint intervals of length H = round(ln N) in [N/2, N]: total variation distance between the empirical count distribution and Poisson with the same mean < 0.02; R5 discrete Fourier transform of the indicator of primes among the 2^22 odd numbers just below N: ratio of the largest non-zero-frequency power to the mean power < 30 (a Gumbel-scale maximum for random indicators is about ln(2^21) ~ 15); R6 sequential compressibility: lzma size of the sequence of half-gaps (clipped at 255) in [N/2, N] divided by the lzma size of a seeded random permutation of the same sequence >= 0.98; R7 maximum over x <= N of |pi(x) - Li(x)| / sqrt(x / ln x) < 3. A respect is calibrated only if the Cramer simulation satisfies its threshold; miscalibrated respects are dropped and reported. PASS (supports) if the primes are random-like in at least (K - 2) of the K calibrated respects (so 5 of 7 if all are calibrated).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if the primes are random-like in at most K - 4 of the K calibrated respects (3 of 7), or if the gap sequence is plainly regular (lzma ratio of the raw half-gap byte sequence below 0.1, or a single Fourier frequency carrying more than half the non-DC spectral power). MIXED for exactly K - 3 random-like respects (4 of 7). If the OEIS validation fails the generator is wrong and the result is 'inconclusive' (other). If the OEIS files cannot be fetched, validation falls back to the published pi(10^8) value only and this is reported.
tests.interpretation: The claim's testable core is 'their distribution seems in many respects random'; the historical remark about what mathematics neglected is not tested. 'Random' is given the book's own operational meaning (p. 1067 ff.: statistical indistinguishability from a random model in specified respects) with Cramer's model as the declared random model; 'many respects' is read as a majority of a list fixed in advance, which includes respects where structure is known to exist (Fourier peaks from small moduli, finite-size Poisson deviations) so that the test can fail. Trivial sieve structure (no even primes) is removed only in R3 by restricting to classes coprime to 12; all other statistics are applied to the raw sequences.

measured.unit: respects (of 7 calibrated) in which the primes below 10^8 are random-like at the pre-registered thresholds
measured.uncertainty: with 2.76 million primes in [5x10^7, 10^8] every reported deviation from the Cramer model is far outside sampling error (the Cramer simulation gives the sampling scale)

tests.hypothesis: When each of the 256 elementary cellular automata (Wolfram numbering, all 256 counted separately) is run from a single black cell on a white background, the pattern of cells that differ from the (possibly alternating) uniform background stays of bounded width for about two-thirds of the rules (~171) and grows without bound for about one-third (~85); and about 14% of all 256 rules (~36) produce growing patterns that are not space-time periodic, i.e. more complicated than repetition.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: run all 256 rules for T = 4096 steps on a ring of 2T + 64 cells (so the light cone never wraps). Width w(t) = extent of cells differing from the background value at time t, where the background follows b_{t+1} = f(b_t, b_t, b_t). A rule is 'fixed size' if max_{t in [T/2, T]} w(t) equals max_{t in [T/4, T/2]} w(t), otherwise 'growing'. A growing rule is 'repetitive' if some temporal period P <= 16 and spatial shift |s| <= 16 satisfy grid[t + P, x + s] == grid[t, x] for every t in [T/2, T - P] and every x in [-t + 16, t - 16]; otherwise it is 'more complicated than repetition'. The claim passes if the fixed-size fraction lies in [0.60, 0.73], the growing fraction in [0.27, 0.40] and the more-complicated fraction in [0.10, 0.18], and if the three-way classification of every rule is identical for T = 2048 and T = 4096 (no rule changes class with the cutoff).
tests.fail: Pre-registered: 'refutes' if the fixed-size fraction is below 0.55 or above 0.78, or the more-complicated fraction is outside [0.07, 0.21]; 'mixed' if the fractions fall between the pass and refute bands, or if more than 4 rules change class between T = 2048 and T = 4096 (indicating the cutoff, not the rules, decides the shares); 'inconclusive' if the periodicity search is not able to classify the growing patterns (e.g. because the width of the periodic window is inadequate for some rule) in a way that is stable across cutoffs.
tests.interpretation: The 256 rules are counted individually as Wolfram does ('all the cellular automata shown on the last few pages'), without quotienting by the left-right or black-white symmetries. 'Fixed size' includes patterns that die out (rules 0, 128), that flash with the background (7, 127) and that move at constant speed without changing width (2, 103). 'Grow forever' is operationalised as a width that keeps increasing between the third and fourth quarters of the run, which also captures the square-root growth of rule 225 noted in the text (width about 2*sqrt(t)). 'More complicated than repetition' is the complement of space-time periodicity with small period and drift inside the light cone, which is how a purely repetitive growing pattern (rules 50, 109) differs from a nested (22, 60, 90, 225) or random (30, 45) or complex (110) one. The shares are described as approximate ('about'), so a +-0.07 band around 2/3, 1/3 and a +-0.04 band around 14% are used; Wolfram's own count of 24 nested rules is recorded as an exploratory extra, not a criterion.

measured.unit: fraction of the 256 rules whose pattern stays of fixed size (170/256)
measured.uncertainty: exact for the given cutoffs and periodicity bounds

tests.hypothesis: When the 256 elementary cellular automata are run from a single black cell and classified by a fixed, calibrated compressibility criterion, about 10 produce random-looking patterns and these fall into three classes under left-right reflection and black-white complementation, while about 24 produce growing, non-periodic but highly compressible (nested) patterns.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Each rule is run for T = 4096 steps from a single black cell on a white background (zero boundary, width 2T+1). Statistics: (i) rho = 8 * lzma_bytes / cells of the central strip (columns -64..63 relative to the seed, rows 1024..4095, one byte per cell, preset 9); (ii) periodic: the strip rows are time-periodic with some period p <= 64 over rows 2048..4095; (iii) growing: the black-cell extent of row 4095 is at least 1.2 times that of row 2047, or the extent of row 4095 exceeds 64 cells while the strip is not periodic. Calibration (performed before the rules are run): random references are i.i.d. fair bits (numpy seed 20260303) in a 128 x 3072 strip; nested references are the same-size central strips of the Sierpinski gasket (Pascal's triangle mod 2), Pascal's triangle mod 3 thresholded to nonzero, and the outer products t_i XOR t_j of the Thue-Morse and of the period-doubling sequences; periodic references are random patterns of period 1..64 in time and 1..16 in space. tau_random = geometric mean of the smallest random-reference rho and the largest nested-reference rho. Classification: 'random-looking' iff rho >= tau_random; 'nested' iff not random-looking, not periodic, and growing; 'regular' otherwise. Symmetry classes: orbits under reflection (swap left and right inputs) and complementation (conjugation by colour swap). Secondary, reported but not decisive: for nested rules, the black-cell count exponent D = log2(N(4096)/N(2048)) with N(t) = black cells in rows 0..t-1, and the width exponent log2(width(4095)/width(2047)); the number of clusters when D is binned to 0.1 and the width exponent to {about 1, about 0.5} is compared with Wolfram's 'three fundamentally different forms'. 'supports' if the random-looking count is in [8, 12] and forms exactly 3 symmetry classes, and the nested count is in [20, 28].
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if the random-looking count is <= 5 or >= 16, or the nested count is <= 14 or >= 36, under the calibrated criterion. Otherwise 'mixed' (e.g. counts near but outside the pass windows, or random-looking rules forming a number of symmetry classes other than 3). 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the calibration fails to separate random from nested references.
tests.interpretation: 'Seem in many respects random' is read as 'the central region of the pattern is essentially incompressible, as judged against i.i.d. bits and classical nested patterns by a threshold fixed before the run'; 'nested' is read as 'grows, is not time-periodic, and is highly compressible'. Both are proxies for Wolfram's visual classification, so counts within a few of his 10 and 24 are treated as agreement. 'Basic forms' for the random rules is read as symmetry classes (the natural reading given that 10 = 4 + 4 + 2 under the 88-class symmetry reduction); for the nested rules Wolfram's three forms are visual (rule 22/60 type, rule 150 type, rule 225 type) and are only approximated by the dimension/width clustering. All patterns are generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.

measured.unit: rule counts (of 256)
measured.uncertainty: deterministic given the calibrated threshold tau = 0.190; the counts are sensitive to the classification proxies (see caveats)

tests.hypothesis: When all 2187 three-colour nearest-neighbour totalistic cellular automata are run from a single gray cell for a few thousand steps, about 85 % produce patterns whose late-time central region is time-periodic or compresses like classical nested patterns, and the remaining 15 % or so compress like random or class-4 (localised-structure) patterns.

Each code c in 0..2186 (Wolfram's convention: base-3 digit k of c is the new colour for neighbourhood sum k in 0..6; colours 0 = white, 1 = gray, 2 = black) is run for T = 3000 steps from a single gray cell on a white background with an array wide enough that boundary effects cannot reach the central 128 columns. Statistics on the central strip (columns -64..63): (i) periodic: rows 2250..2999 are time-periodic with some period p <= 256; (ii) rho = 8 * lzma_bytes / (cells * log2(3)) over rows 1500..2999. Calibration (performed before the codes are run): nested references are the same-size strips of Pascal's triangle mod 3 (3 symbols), Pascal's triangle mod 2, and the Thue-Morse and period-doubling outer-product patterns (normalised by log2 of their own alphabet size); irregular references are the strips of elementary rules 110, 124, 137, 193 (localised structures) and 30, 45 (random) run from a single black cell with the same geometry. tau = geometric mean of the largest nested-reference rho and the smallest irregular-reference rho. A code is 'regular' iff it is periodic or rho < tau. 'supports' if the regular fraction lies in [0.80, 0.90].
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if the regular fraction is below 0.70 or above 0.95. 'mixed' if it lies in [0.70, 0.80) or (0.90, 0.95]. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the calibration fails to separate the reference classes (largest nested rho >= smallest irregular rho). The number of irregular codes that are random-looking (rho above the smallest random reference) versus structured-irregular is reported but not decisive.
tests.interpretation: 'Ultimately quite regular' is read as 'repetitive or nested at late times', operationalised as late-time periodicity of the central strip or compressibility at the level of classical nested patterns; 'the remainder' as everything compressing like random or localised-structure patterns, with elementary class-3 and class-4 rules from a different family used to fix the threshold. 'About 85 %' is given a +/- 5 percentage-point band. Long transients (Wolfram mentions code 1599 resolving only after thousands of steps) may leave a few ultimately regular codes labelled irregular at T = 3000, which biases the regular fraction downward slightly. All patterns are generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.

measured.unit: fraction of the 2187 codes classified regular (late-time strip periodic with p <= 256, or rho < tau)
measured.uncertainty: deterministic given tau = 0.060; a few long-transient codes may be misclassified at T = 3000

tests.hypothesis: Every one of the 65,536 basic two-colour mobile automata (rule maps the colours of the active cell and its two neighbours to a new colour for the active cell and a move left or right), started from all-white cells, produces a step sequence that is eventually periodic or otherwise highly compressible (nested); no basic rule produces a step sequence whose compressibility is in the range of random or complex sequences. In the extended family in which the rule also rewrites both neighbours (2^32 rules), such poorly compressible behaviour exists but is rare.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Encoding: the behaviour of a mobile automaton is summarised by its step sequence s_t in {0,1,2,3} = 2 * (new colour of the active cell) + (1 if the active cell moves right else 0); for the extended family s_t additionally records the two neighbour colours written (16 symbols), and the sequence of active-cell positions is determined by it. Calibration (performed before the mobile automata are run, on reference sequences only): rho(L) = 8 * lzma_size(sequence of L symbols, one byte each, preset 9) / (L * log2(alphabet size)). References over a 4-symbol alphabet: periodic sequences with periods 1..500 (numpy seed 20260306), nested sequences (Thue-Morse, period-doubling, Fibonacci word, paper-folding, ruler sequence mod 4), and random sequences (numpy random symbols; rule 30 centre bits paired). The complexity threshold tau is the geometric mean of the largest rho(8000) over the periodic and nested references and the smallest rho(8000) over the random references. Stage 1: all 65,536 basic rules, 2000 steps (vectorised); a rule is 'periodic' if its last 1000 symbols have a period p <= 500. Stage 2: every non-periodic rule is run for 16000 steps and rho is computed on symbols 8000..16000 (tail); a rule is 'complex' if rho > tau. Stage 3: any rule flagged complex is re-run for 64000 steps and rho on symbols 32000..64000 is required to still exceed tau (guards against long transients). Extended family: 100,000 rules sampled uniformly (numpy seed 20260306), same three stages with the 16-symbol alphabet and a 16-symbol calibration run analogously. 'supports' if no basic rule is complex after stage 3 and the fraction of complex extended rules is <= 1 %. Secondary check reported but not decisive: the number of basic rules with non-periodic step sequences, which Wolfram gives as 218 (p. 72).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if at least one basic rule is complex after stage 3 (its tail step sequence compresses no better than the geometric midpoint between nested and random references at 32000 symbols). 'mixed' if no basic rule is complex but the extended family's complex fraction exceeds 1 %. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the calibration fails to separate the reference classes (largest nested/periodic rho >= smallest random rho).
tests.interpretation: 'Behaviour more complex than repetition or nesting' is operationalised by lossless compressibility of the step sequence, which is a complete description of the evolution from the fixed initial condition: periodic sequences compress to a constant, nested (substitution-generated) sequences compress to a slowly growing size, and sequences that are random-like or have irregular localised structures compress poorly. The threshold is fixed by calibration on classical reference sequences, not on the mobile automata themselves. Wolfram's own 'compressed form' (tape shown only when the active cell reaches a new extreme) is replaced by this generic measure. The rule convention is NKS p. 71: the rule reads (left, active, right) and writes the active cell's new colour and a direction; the extended rules (p. 73) also write both neighbours. The initial condition is all white with one active cell. Everything is generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.

measured.unit: rule counts; fraction of 100,000 sampled extended rules with tail rho above tau
measured.uncertainty: basic family exhaustive within the step horizons; extended fraction 0/100000 gives a 95 % upper bound of about 3e-5

tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, none of the 4096 two-state and none of the 2,985,984 three-state two-colour Turing machines (NKS conventions: no halt state, head starts in state 1 on an all-white tape) produces a step sequence whose subword complexity stays high after a long transient; every machine's sequence of (head state, colour read) letters becomes eventually periodic (repetitive) or stays of low, nested-type complexity.

The enumeration uses the book's numbering scheme (NKS p. 888) and its conventions (p. 78): s states, 2 colours, rule entries (new state, new colour, move +-1), blank tape, head in state 1.

tests.hypothesis: Every parallel substitution system in which each element is replaced according to its own colour alone (a context-free morphism iterated from a single element) produces a nested pattern: operationally, the sequence it generates has sub-exponential subword complexity (at most quadratic, as Pansiot's theorem gives for pure morphic words), never the near-maximal complexity of a random or 'complex' sequence; whereas substitution systems whose replacement depends on a neighbouring element can produce sequences of near-maximal subword complexity.

For every run that reaches 2^15 symbols ('growing'), compute the subword complexity p(n) (number of distinct length-n factors) of the first min(len, 2^17) symbols for n = 1..20. The claim passes if every growing neighbour-independent run has p(20) <= 10^4 and p(20)/p(10) <= 8 (a quadratic law gives 4, an exponential law about 2^10), and if the Thue-Morse system {0 -> 01, 1 -> 10} reproduces OEIS A010060 and the Fibonacci system {0 -> 01, 1 -> 0} reproduces OEIS A003849 term for term over the available b-file terms. tests.fail: Pre-registered: 'refutes' if any growing neighbour-independent run has p(20) > 10^4 or p(20)/p(10) > 8, or if the Thue-Morse or Fibonacci outputs disagree with the OEIS b-files; 'inconclusive' if the control family contains no system exceeding the thresholds (the complexity measure would then be too weak to distinguish nested from more complicated behaviour).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'nested pattern' is given a formal operational content as low (sub-exponential, at most polynomial) subword complexity, which is the standard combinatorial signature of self-similar/morphic sequences: the Thue-Morse, Fibonacci and Cantor examples he gives all have p(n) = O(n). Rules whose replacement for some colour is the empty string, or that keep every string bounded, are included in the enumeration but can only give finite or eventually periodic output, which is trivially nested; the complexity test is applied to growing runs only. The claim's second half ('more complicated behaviour requires neighbour dependence') is tested only in the direction that neighbour-dependent systems can exceed the complexity bound, as a check of discriminating power; the universal statement itself is tested by exhaustive enumeration of two finite families.

measured.unit: maximum subword complexity p(20) over all 5109 growing neighbour-independent runs (random reference 32319)
measured.uncertainty: exact

tests.interpretation: Tag systems follow NKS p. 93-94 and the implementation note (p. 894): at each step n elements are removed from the front and a block determined by the removed n elements is appended; a sequence shorter than n becomes empty. 'Neighbor-independent substitution system' is the map replacing each symbol by its block (NKS p. 83). 'Repetitive or nested' is operationalized as finite state space (eventual periodicity) or linear factor complexity (p(10) <= 60 for a two-letter sequence; the Thue-Morse sequence has p(10) = 28). 'Very complicated' is operationalized as non-terminating, non-recurring evolution with a length series that lzma cannot compress much better than its own shuffle. The test is computational; the program family is generated by analysis.py.

measured.unit: two-deletion rules meeting the pre-registered complexity criterion (of 400 fully tested)
measured.uncertainty: exact (deterministic computation)

tests.hypothesis: Among two-block cyclic tag systems started from a single black element, at least one produces a sequence whose length grows at a steady linear rate while the fluctuations about that growth behave like a random walk (unbounded, diffusive scaling) and the leading-element sequence that drives them is incompressible to a substantial degree.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all 225 cyclic tag systems with two blocks, each block a binary string of length 0-3 (15 choices per block), initial sequence {1}, Wolfram's update (remove first element; if it was 1 append the current block; blocks alternate every step). Stage 1: run each system 100,000 steps; a system is 'growing' if the sequence never empties and its final length is >= 1000. Stage 2: run each growing system 1,000,000 steps and compute (i) linear fit of length L(t) vs t: R^2 >= 0.999 and local growth rates over 10 equal windows all within 25% of the global slope ('steady growth'); (ii) Hurst exponent H of the detrended residual r(t) = L(t) - (a + b t), estimated as half the log-log slope of Var[r(t+tau) - r(t)] over tau = 2^0..2^13, in [0.35, 0.65] ('random-walk-like fluctuations'); (iii) lzma (preset 9 | EXTREME) compressed size of the packed leading-element bit sequence >= 0.25 bits per symbol ('incompressible driver'). The claim PASSES if at least one system satisfies (i), (ii) and (iii) simultaneously. Secondary, reported but not decisive: whether the book's own examples (d) {{1},{1,0,1}} and (e) {{1,1,1},{0}} pass.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if no system in the 225-member family satisfies all of (i)-(iii): i.e. every growing system has either unsteady growth, bounded or non-diffusive fluctuations (H outside [0.35, 0.65]), or a leading-element sequence that compresses below 0.25 bits per symbol (periodic or nested).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'fluctuations in this growth ... are in many respects random' (p. 95-96) is read as: fluctuations about the mean growth are unbounded and scale diffusively like a random walk (Hurst exponent near 1/2), and the binary sequence of leading elements, which fully determines the growth, cannot be compressed to a small fraction of its length (so it is neither periodic nor nested, in contrast to the book's example (c), whose leading column is a nested Sturmian sequence). 'Steady growth' is read as a linear fit with R^2 >= 0.999 and stable local rates. The family is the smallest natural family containing the book's examples (d) and (e). This is a computational test; no external data is needed.

measured.unit: systems passing all three pre-registered criteria

tests.hypothesis: Within the family of the simplest arithmetic iterations, repeated multiplication by a fixed small integer m viewed as a base-b digit array (Wolfram's opening example, pp. 116-120), some members produce digit arrays whose interior is incompressible with digit frequencies indistinguishable from uniform, while the trivial members (m a power of b) are detected as highly compressible.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all pairs (m, b) with multiplier m in 2..9 and base b in 2..9, iterating x_{t+1} = m x_t from x_0 = 1 for t = 1..T = 3000 (i.e. the digits of m^t). For each pair build the digit array of rows m^t written in base b; take the interior window of each row consisting of digit positions between 25% and 75% of that row's length (least significant digit = position 0), concatenate all interior digits in row order into one byte string (one digit per byte). Measure (i) bits per digit = 8 * lzma(preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size / number of digits; (ii) maximum absolute deviation of any digit-value frequency from 1/b. A pair is 'complex' if (i) >= 0.8 * log2(b) and (ii) <= 0.02; a pair is 'simple' if (i) < 0.1 * log2(b). The claim PASSES if at least one pair with m not a power of b is 'complex' AND every pair with m a power of b (m = b^j, j >= 1, e.g. (2,2), (4,2), (8,2), (9,3), (3,3), ...) is 'simple' (validity check that the measure separates trivially regular digit arrays). Reported, not decisive: how many of the 64 pairs are complex, and whether the pairs with m and b sharing all prime factors (e.g. (6,2), (4,8), (2,4)) behave differently.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if no pair with m not a power of b is 'complex' (every such digit array compresses below 0.8 log2(b) bits per digit or has digit frequencies deviating from uniform by more than 0.02). If any trivial pair (m a power of b) is not 'simple', the measure lacks discriminating power and the verdict is inconclusive (not-operationalizable).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'even rather simple systems based on numbers can lead to highly complex behavior' (p. 115) is illustrated by the digit sequences of successive powers (p. 116-120: 2^t in base 2 is trivial, 3^t in base 2 looks random). 'Highly complex behavior' is read as digit arrays that a general-purpose compressor cannot reduce below 80% of their entropy bound and whose digit frequencies are uniform to within 2%, in explicit contrast to the trivial members of the same family that compress to below 10%. The claim is existential; the family is the smallest natural one containing the book's opening examples. The window excludes the leading digits (biased by Benford-type effects) and trailing digits (eventually periodic in t at fixed position, and all zero when b divides m).

measured.unit: pairs (m,b) with m not a power of b whose interior digit array is 'complex' by the pre-registered criteria

tests.hypothesis: At least one of Wolfram's nested recurrences using only addition and subtraction, f[n] = f[p[n]] + f[q[n]] with variable look-back such as n - f[n-1], produces fluctuations about its trend that are incompressible (not periodic or nested) and sign-balanced, while his nested examples (c) and (d) are detected as highly compressible.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Rules (all with f[1]=f[2]=1, from NKS pp. 129-130): (c) f[n]=f[f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-1]] (OEIS A004001); (d) f[n]=f[n-f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-2]-1]; (e) f[n]=f[n-f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-2]] (OEIS A005185); (f) f[n]=f[n-f[n-1]-1]+f[n-f[n-2]-1]; (g) f[n]=f[f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-2]-1]; (h) f[n]=f[f[n-1]]+f[n-2f[n-1]+1]. Compute f[n] for n <= N = 2^20 (stop a rule if an index < 1 occurs). Residual r[n] = f[n] - n/2 for (c)-(g); for (h) r[n] = f[n] - a n^b with (a,b) a least-squares power-law fit in log-log. Statistics: (i) bits per symbol = 8 * lzma(preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size of the increment-sign sequence sign(r[n]-r[n-1]) in {-1,0,1} stored as one byte each, divided by N-1; (ii) sign balance |P(increment>0) - P(increment<0)|; (iii) dyadic self-similarity corr(r[n], r[2n]) for n in [N/4, N/2) (reported). A rule is 'complex/random-like' if it is well defined up to N, (i) >= 0.5 bits/symbol and (ii) <= 0.05. The claim PASSES if at least one of rules (e)-(h) is complex/random-like AND the nested controls (c) and (d) both have (i) < 0.15 bits/symbol (validity of the measure). Calibration from controls outside the family: binary digit sum s2(n) gives 0.002 bits/symbol, its partial sums 0.005, a symmetric random walk 1.10.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if none of rules (e)-(h) is complex/random-like (every one is undefined before N, or compresses below 0.5 bits/symbol, or is sign-unbalanced by more than 0.05). If the nested controls (c) or (d) do not compress below 0.15 bits/symbol the measure lacks discriminating power and the verdict is inconclusive (not-operationalizable). If computed terms disagree with the OEIS b-files for A005185 or A004001, the verdict is inconclusive (other) until the implementation is fixed.
tests.interpretation: 'Fluctuations ... complex and in many respects random' (p. 130-131) is read as: the increment-sign sequence of the detrended fluctuations is not compressible to a small fraction of its entropy bound by a general-purpose compressor (nested/digit-based fluctuations compress to < 0.01 bits/symbol), and positive and negative fluctuations are balanced (Wolfram's own stated 'respect' for case (f)). The claim is existential ('can produce'), so one qualifying rule suffices; the book's nested rules (c) and (d) serve as internal controls that must be detected as regular. The OEIS b-files provide independent public values of two of the sequences to verify the implementation. Trend n/2 for (c)-(g) follows the book's plots; the power-law trend for (h) follows the book's caption (0.42 n^0.916).

tests.hypothesis: The first 1,000,000 decimal and the first 1,000,000 hexadecimal digits of pi after the point show no statistically significant regularity under a fixed battery of frequency, block, poker, gap, serial-correlation, spectral and compression tests, i.e. they are indistinguishable from i.i.d. uniform digits by these tests.

For each base b in {10, 16}, on N = 1,000,000 digits after the point, compute 10 p-values: (1) digit frequency chi-square (b - 1 df); (2) non-overlapping pair chi-square (b^2 - 1 df); (3) non-overlapping triple chi-square (b^3 - 1 df); (4) poker test on non-overlapping 5-digit hands by number of distinct digits (probabilities b!/(b-r)! S(5, r) / b^5; categories with expected count < 5 merged into the next); (5) gap test for digit 0 (gap lengths 0..3b-1 and >= 3b against the geometric law with p = 1/b); (6-8) serial correlation at lags 1, 2, 3 (z = r sqrt(N - lag), two-sided normal); (9) maximum periodogram ordinate of the centred digits over the N/2 Fourier frequencies (p = 1 - (1 - exp(-max I / mean I))^(N/2)); (10) lzma (preset 9 extreme) size of the digit string (one byte per digit) compared with 20 strings of N uniform random digits from numpy PCG64 (seed 20261031): two-sided normal p of z = (size - mean) / sd. 20 p-values in total. 'supports' if no p-value is below 1e-4 and at most 2 are below 0.01 (under the null, P(>= 3 of 20 below 0.01) is about 0.1 %). Data validity: the published decimal digits must agree with digits computed independently by analysis.py (Chudnovsky series, exact integer arithmetic) at all 1,000,000 positions, and with the OEIS A000796 b-file; the computed hexadecimal digits must agree with the OEIS A062964 b-file. Any disagreement makes the verdict 'inconclusive' with reason 'other'.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any p-value is below 1e-6 or 4 or more p-values are below 0.01. Otherwise, if neither the pass nor the refute condition holds (exactly 3 below 0.01, or a minimum p in [1e-6, 1e-4)), 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: 'For practical purposes completely random' is read as: a standard battery of statistical tests of the kind used to vet random number generators finds no significant regularity. The claim's scope is 'any base'; bases 10 and 16 are tested (base 2 is tested separately in wolfram2002-ch10-15). Wolfram refers to 'all computed digits' (then about 2 x 10^11); this test examines only the first 10^6 digits in each base, so it can refute the claim (a regularity in a prefix would be a regularity) but supports it only for that prefix and that battery. Normality of pi is an open problem and is not what is tested. The published digit file is used for the decimal tests; the independent computation serves to validate it, and supplies the hexadecimal digits.

measured.unit: p-values of the pre-registered battery (minimum: maximum-periodogram test, base 16)
measured.uncertainty: deterministic digits; p-values are the tests' own (asymptotic chi-square / normal approximations); the lzma p-value depends on the 20-sample PRNG reference

tests.hypothesis: In any integer base, every rational p/q has an eventually periodic digit expansion with period at most q - 1 (and preperiod + period at most q), every eventually periodic digit sequence is the expansion of a rational number, and the published digit expansions of irrational constants show no eventual periodicity.

tests.fail: Pre-registered: any rational whose expansion has minimal period > q - 1 or does not become periodic within q digits; any disagreement with A007732; any eventually periodic pattern whose reconstructed rational re-expands differently; or an irrational constant's published digits exhibiting at least two full agreeing periods for some p <= N/3.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'repetitive digit sequences' are eventually periodic positional expansions in an integer base; the clause 'period at most q - 1' in the claim text is the standard long-division bound (there are only q - 1 non-zero remainders). Terminating expansions are treated as eventually periodic with repeating 0, as the assessors note; period blocks consisting only of the digit b - 1 are excluded from the random patterns because they denote the alternative expansion of a terminating rational and would re-expand in the terminating form. The converse ('rationals are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences') is tested constructively (every eventually periodic pattern reconstructs to a rational that reproduces it) and, as a sanity check only, on the published digits of three irrational constants; a finite digit string can never prove non-periodicity, so part (3) is a consistency check rather than a proof.

tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, the sequence of axis crossings of sin(x) + sin(a x) for a > 1, labelled by which of the two regularly spaced families each crossing belongs to, has exactly the same set of finite subwords as the word produced by the generalized substitution system whose n-th rule is tau_{c_n}: A -> A^{c_n} B, B -> A, where c_1, c_2, ... are the partial quotients of the continued fraction of theta = (a - 1)/(a + 1); and for quadratic-irrational a the partial quotients are eventually periodic, so the word is a fixed point of a fixed composite substitution (nested).
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Test set: a in {sqrt2, sqrt3, sqrt5, sqrt7, (1+sqrt5)/2, 1+sqrt2, 2+sqrt3} (quadratic irrationals), {pi, e, 2^(1/3), ln 10} and 20 pseudo-random a uniform in [1.05, 12] from numpy seed 20261031 (31 values). For each a: (1) take the first N = 20000 positive zeros of f(x) = sin x + sin(a x), each verified numerically (|f(x)| <= 1e-8), labelled A if it is a zero of sin((1+a)x/2) (spacing 2pi/(1+a)) and B if it is a zero of cos((1-a)x/2) (spacing 2pi/(a-1)); (2) build the substitution word s_1 = A^{c_1} B, s_n = s_{n-1}^{c_n} s_{n-2} (equivalently the composition tau_{c_1} ... tau_{c_n}(A)) to length >= 200000 from the continued fraction theta = [0; c_1, c_2, ...]. PASS (supports) if for every a and every n in 1..24 the set of length-n factors of the crossing word equals the set of length-n factors of the substitution word and has exactly n + 1 elements, and if for every quadratic-irrational a the continued fraction of theta is eventually periodic within 60 terms and the composite substitution over one period has the substitution word's tail as a fixed point (applying it to the first 2000 symbols of the tail reproduces a prefix of the tail).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if for any a there is some n <= 24 at which the factor sets differ, after excluding near-coincident zeros (two zeros closer than 1e-9 times the A spacing, which would make the ordering numerically undefined); or if any quadratic-irrational case has a non-eventually-periodic continued fraction or a tail that is not a fixed point of the period substitution. Partial agreement (factor sets equal only for some a, or only up to a smaller n without a numerical explanation) is 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram (p. 146) says the relative arrangement of the crossing points is 'related to' the output of a generalized substitution system whose rule at each step comes from a term of the continued fraction of (a-1)/(a+1), with repetitive (hence nested) structure when a is a square root. The two 'regularly spaced families' are the zeros of the two factors of sin x + sin ax = 2 sin((1+a)x/2) cos((1-a)x/2); their spacings are in ratio theta = (a-1)/(a+1), so the merged labelled sequence is a Sturmian (mechanical) word and the natural substitution system is the standard one driven by the partial quotients of theta (the word's own slope theta/(1+theta) has continued fraction [0; c_1+1, c_2, ...], so the directive sequence is exactly the partial quotients of theta). 'Related to' is operationalised as equality of factor languages, the strongest sense in which a finite segment of a mechanical word can match a substitution word whose intercept is not specified. The test uses exact arithmetic for the quadratic surds' continued fractions and double precision elsewhere, with partial quotients used only while the convergent denominators are below 10 N.

measured.unit: a-values (of 31) whose crossing word and substitution word have identical factor sets for all n <= 24
measured.uncertainty: exact combinatorial comparison; zero positions accurate to ~1e-11, minimum separation between distinct zeros >= 7e-6 spacings

tests.hypothesis: Under the shift map x -> 2x mod 1 the symbolic itinerary (1 if x_t >= 1/2 else 0) is exactly the seed's binary digit sequence read from the first digit onward, so the output is a suffix of the input: periodic seeds give periodic itineraries with the same period, nested seeds give nested itineraries, and the itinerary of a seed is never less compressible (more random) than the seed's own digits. By contrast a map that is not a digit shift in base 2 (control: x -> 3x mod 1) can produce incompressible itineraries from seeds with trivially simple binary digits.
tests.pass: Pre-registered, all of: (1) transcription identity: for 2000 random reduced fractions p/q with odd q in [3, 10^5], the itinerary of the exact rational orbit (Python Fractions) for 2000 steps agrees bit for bit with the binary digits d_1..d_2000 of p/q computed independently by long division (0 mismatches of 4,000,000), and for three seeds whose binary digits are taken from OEIS b-files truncated to N = 10000 digits (A004539 binary digits of sqrt(2), A010060 Thue-Morse, A030190 binary Champernowne) the exact itinerary agrees with the published digits for all t < N (0 mismatches), with A004539 additionally cross-checked against digits computed with integer isqrt (0 mismatches); (2) periodic seeds stay periodic: for every odd q in 3..2000 and p = 1, the itinerary of p/q, found by exact cycle detection, is purely periodic with minimal period equal to the multiplicative order of 2 modulo q (0 exceptions), and every seed p/2^k (k <= 60) reaches the fixed point 0 within k steps; (3) randomness is inherited, not created: for every seed class the lzma compression ratio of the 10000-bit itinerary differs from the ratio of the seed's own first 10000 digits by less than 0.01, the itinerary of a periodic seed (1/q, q <= 2000) has ratio below 0.10, the Thue-Morse itinerary has ratio below the 1st percentile of 200 random-bit references, and the itinerary of a random-bit seed has ratio within the central 98% of the random references; (4) control with discriminating power: the itinerary of x -> 3x mod 1 started at the seed 1/2^60 (whose binary digits are a single 1 followed by zeros, ratio below 0.05) for 10000 steps has compression ratio above 0.8 times the median random reference and passes an 8-bit block chi-square test at p > 0.001, i.e. it does produce randomness its seed did not have.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: any itinerary bit that differs from the corresponding seed digit in part (1); any odd-q seed whose itinerary period differs from the multiplicative order of 2, or any dyadic seed not reaching 0 within k steps; any seed class whose shift-map itinerary is more than 0.01 less compressible than the seed digits, or a periodic/Thue-Morse itinerary as incompressible as random bits (ratio within the central 98% of the random references). Failure of the control (4) alone does not refute the claim but would be reported as reducing the discriminating power of the test (verdict stays 'supports' with lower confidence if (1)-(3) pass). If (1) fails the verdict is 'refutes'; if (1) passes but (2) or (3) fails the verdict is 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'shift map' is x -> 2x mod 1 (NKS p. 149, 'doubling modulo 1'), and 'moving digits leftward' refers to the base-2 expansion; the output of the map is taken to be the coarse itinerary (which half of the interval x_t lies in), which is the standard symbolic coding and is what Wolfram's pictures show. 'Randomness' is operationalised as incompressibility by a general-purpose compressor (lzma) plus block-frequency uniformity, following the assessors' remark that the claim locates randomness in the digit sequence. Dyadic rationals have two binary expansions; the itinerary follows the terminating one (x_t = 1/2 gives bit 1 then zeros), so seeds are compared with that convention. All orbits are computed with exact rational arithmetic; a floating-point implementation would collapse to 0 after 53 steps, which is noted but not used.

measured.unit: itinerary bits differing from the seed's binary digits (out of 4,020,999 compared)
measured.uncertainty: exact

tests.hypothesis: The two-dimensional 8-neighbour outer totalistic cellular automaton with code 746 (the example Wolfram gives on p. 178), started from a row of 7 black cells, grows a pattern whose outer boundary stays close to a circle: the radial profile of the boundary has small relative spread and no appreciable fourfold (square-lattice) anisotropy, at the 400 steps shown in the book and at three times that many steps.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Run code 746 (a white cell becomes black iff exactly 3 of its 8 neighbours are black; a black cell stays black iff it has 0-4 black neighbours and becomes white with 5 or more; Wolfram's outer-totalistic numbering, bit index 2*s + c) from a horizontal row of 7 black cells for T = 400 and T = 1200 steps on a grid large enough that the pattern never touches the edge. Take the centroid of all black cells as centre, bin all black cells by polar angle into 360 one-degree bins and let r(theta) be the largest centre distance in each bin (outer boundary profile). Compute CV = std(r)/mean(r) and the anisotropy ratio A = mean of r within +/-5 degrees of the four axis directions divided by the mean of r within +/-5 degrees of the four diagonal directions (a square gives A = 0.707, a diamond 1.414, a circle 1). 'supports' if at T = 1200 both CV <= 0.03 and |A - 1| <= 0.03, and at T = 400 both CV <= 0.05 and |A - 1| <= 0.05. Measurement validation (not part of the verdict): the same statistics for the control rule 'a cell becomes black if any of its 8 neighbours is black' (which grows a square) must give A < 0.8 and CV > 0.06, otherwise the method is declared broken and the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'other'.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if at T = 1200 CV >= 0.06 or |A - 1| >= 0.06 (the outline is at least as far from a circle as a regular octagon is from its circumscribed circle in CV terms, or shows a clear square or diamond bias). Any intermediate outcome -> 'mixed'. Growth rate: the mean radius divided by T is reported and compared with Wolfram's 'about 0.37 t', but does not enter the verdict.
tests.interpretation: 'Overall shape' is taken as the outer boundary of the set of black cells (interior holes ignored), and 'closely approximates a perfect circle' as a boundary whose radius varies by at most a few percent around the pattern and shows no lattice-axis bias. The claim is existential ('it is even possible to find cellular automata that ...'), so one rule suffices; the rule tested is the one Wolfram himself exhibits (code 746, p. 178, with the stated initial condition and the 400-step figure). The 1200-step run checks that the circularity is not an artefact of the particular time shown. The pattern is generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.

measured.unit: CV = std/mean of the 360-bin outer radial profile; A = axis/diagonal mean radius (circle = 1, square = 0.707)
measured.uncertainty: deterministic computation; lattice discreteness contributes about 0.5/mean_r = 0.001 to CV at T = 1200

FAIL (refutes) if growth stops (population unchanged over steps 900-1000) or if the outline converges to a simple form: D(500,1000) < 0.02 and the minimum simple-shape distance at step 1000 is < 0.03. Any other combination is 'mixed' (e.g. shape still changing but growth slowing, or controls not behaving as expected, which would mean the descriptor is not discriminating).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's claim (pp. 176, 181) is existential: this one rule from this one seed produces an overall shape that 'seems continually to go on changing, with no simple overall form'. 'Overall shape' is mapped to the normalised angular outer-radius profile of the occupied set, so interior texture is ignored; 'no simple form' is mapped to distance from a small pre-declared family of simple convex shapes and to non-convergence of the outline between steps 500, 750 and 1000. 'Continually' can only be bounded by the run length; a finite run cannot exclude eventual regularity. Code 175850 (the '3 or 5 of 8' rule from p. 177, row of 7), which the book says is rough on small scales but smooth on large scales, is run as an additional comparison but is not part of the criterion.

measured.uncertainty: exact deterministic computation; descriptor resolution 1 degree

tests.hypothesis: Every two-dimensional substitution system in which each cell is replaced by a fixed block depending only on its own colour produces, from a single cell, a pattern that is exactly nested (decomposes at every scale into the patterns grown from single cells) and has at most quadratic block complexity, whereas rules in which the replacement depends on neighbours can violate both.

Neighbour-independent families: F1 = all 256 two-colour rules replacing each cell by a 2 x 2 block; F2 = 2000 random three-colour 2 x 2 rules; F3 = 2000 random two-colour 3 x 3 rules (numpy PCG64, seed 20261031). Each is iterated from a single cell of colour 1 for n steps (n = 9 for 2 x 2 rules, 512 x 512 cells; n = 6 for 3 x 3 rules, 729 x 729). Measures: (1) exact nesting: for every j = 1..n-1, P_n equals P_{n-j} with each cell of colour c replaced by P_j^(c), the j-step pattern grown from a single cell of colour c; (2) block complexity: the number N(k) of distinct k x k sub-blocks of P_n satisfies N(k) <= s^4 b^2 k^2 for k = 4 and 8 (s colours, b x b blocks; this bound follows from (1), since any k x k window lies in a 2 x 2 group of level-j supertiles with b^(j-1) < k <= b^j; a random s-colour image of this size has N(8) close to the number of positions, about 2.5 x 10^5). Control (validity): 2000 random two-colour neighbour-dependent 2 x 2 rules, where the block replacing a cell depends on its own colour and the colours of its right and lower neighbours (outside the pattern = colour 0), iterated and measured identically; at least 20 of them (1 %) must fail (1) or (2), and a Bernoulli(0.5) 512 x 512 image must fail (2), showing the measures can detect non-nested patterns. 'supports' if every rule in F1, F2 and F3 satisfies (1) and (2) and the control condition holds.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any neighbour-independent rule in F1-F3 fails (1) or (2). If the control condition fails (fewer than 20 neighbour-dependent rules flagged, or the random image not flagged), the measures are judged unable to discriminate and the verdict is 'inconclusive' (reason 'other').
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'completely regular nested structure' is formalized as exact hierarchical self-similarity: the pattern after n steps is the pattern after n - j steps with every cell replaced by the pattern grown in j steps from a cell of that colour, for every j. This holds for neighbour-independent rules by construction (the substitution acts cellwise and commutes with composition), so this test is a computational verification of a mathematical statement across an enumerated and a sampled rule space, plus a check that the formalization and the complexity bound genuinely discriminate (neighbour-dependent controls, as on NKS p. 191). Scope is limited to grid substitution systems with uniform b x b blocks (b = 2, 3; 2 or 3 colours); 'geometric replacement rules' of traditional fractal geometry with arbitrary affine maps, including overlapping ones, are covered by Hutchinson's theorem on self-similar sets in the literature but are not computed here.

measured.unit: count of rules failing the nesting identity or the block-complexity bound
measured.uncertainty: exact except that three-colour 8 x 8 window counts use a 64-bit hash (collision probability ~1e-8 per pattern, which could only lower a count)

tests.hypothesis: Directed networks in which every node is of one type and has exactly two outgoing connections can realize, through the connection pattern alone, structures equivalent to d-dimensional arrays for every d, as well as trees and nested (fractal) structures. 'Equivalent to a d-dimensional array' is taken in Wolfram's two senses: (i) grouping nodes into identical blocks yields exactly the d-dimensional grid (each block connected to its 2d neighbouring blocks), and (ii) the number of nodes reachable within r connection steps grows like r^d (the network dimension criterion of NKS chapter 9).
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (1) Arrays: for d = 1..6 construct the network by one uniform rule: each lattice point x of Z^d is a block of d nodes (x, i), i = 0..d-1, and node (x, i) has exactly two outgoing connections, to (x + e_i, (i+1) mod d) and (x - e_i, (i+1) mod d). Verify (a) every node has out-degree exactly 2 and the rule is identical for every node; (b) exact structural equivalence: on the torus (Z_L)^d with L = 5, contracting each block to a point gives a multigraph whose edge set equals the d-dimensional grid's edge set {x <-> x +- e_i} with every block connected to exactly 2d distinct neighbouring blocks (exact set comparison); (c) dimension criterion: breadth-first search along connections from one node of the infinite network, counting N(r) = nodes within r steps; the growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) at R = 20 d must lie within 0.5 of d for d = 1, 2, 3, 4 (so that it rounds to d), and is reported (not scored) for d = 5, 6. (2) Trees: the infinite binary tree (node k connects to 2k+1 and 2k+2) has N(r) = 2^(r+1) - 1 for r <= 15 (exact). (3) Nested: the level-7 Sierpinski gasket graph (3 corner nodes of degree 2, all others of degree 4) is given an Eulerian orientation along an Euler circuit plus a directed 3-cycle through the corners, which must give every node out-degree exactly 2; its undirected growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) at R = 64 from a corner must lie within 0.3 of log2(3) = 1.585, the gasket's dimension. 'Supports' if (1a), (1b), (1c), (2) and (3) all hold.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if the uniform construction fails structurally for some d <= 6 (out-degree not 2, or the block quotient is not the d-dimensional grid), or if the measured growth exponent for some d <= 4 rounds to an integer other than d, or if no out-degree-2 orientation of the gasket exists. 'Mixed' if arrays pass but the tree or nested construction fails its criterion. 'Inconclusive' is not expected: the test is a self-contained computation.
tests.interpretation: The claim is constructive and existential: one explicit family of networks suffices for each d, plus one tree and one nested example. The block-quotient check is the exact sense of 'equivalent to an array'; the growth exponent is Wolfram's own operational notion of network dimension (NKS p. 479 and notes) and adds a check that the effective geometry is d-dimensional without reference to the blocks. Blocks of d nodes connected to 2d neighbouring blocks follow the description on NKS p. 195 ('every block of nodes is connected to four rather than two neighboring blocks'). Growth exponents at finite radius are biased low (the lattice ball itself has local exponent below d at radius ~20), hence the +-0.5 window; the exact quotient check is the decisive part.

measured.uncertainty: exact counts; the exponent is biased below d at finite radius exactly as the plain lattice ball is (reference values given)

tests.hypothesis: For every one-dimensional local constraint system (a set of allowed length-w colour words over k colours) that admits any bi-infinite satisfying arrangement, there is a purely periodic satisfying arrangement, and its period can be taken at most V = k^(w-1).
tests.pass: Pre-registered: across all enumerated or sampled constraint systems, every system that admits a valid word of length 4V + w (the operational test of satisfiability, independent of any cycle argument) also admits a periodic arrangement u^infinity with |u| <= V whose every cyclic window of length w is allowed; and every system with no such long valid word has no periodic arrangement either. Zero violations in both directions.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: at least one constraint system admits a valid word of length 4V + w but no periodic arrangement with period <= V (this would refute the claim as stated, since the shortest possible periodic solution is bounded by V); or the two satisfiability indicators disagree in the other direction, which would indicate a broken test.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'local set of constraints' on a one-dimensional array of coloured cells (p. 210-211: each cell's neighbourhood must be one of a given set of allowed configurations) is a one-dimensional subshift of finite type: a set of allowed words of a fixed window length w over k colours. 'Can be satisfied at all' is read as the existence of a bi-infinite arrangement all of whose windows are allowed; by compactness this is equivalent to the existence of arbitrarily long valid finite words, and operationally it is tested by the existence of a valid word of length 4V + w (any valid word longer than V must revisit a de Bruijn vertex, so this length is far beyond the threshold, and the check is done by a reachability iteration, not a cycle search). 'Simple and purely repetitive arrangement' is read as a periodic configuration, found by brute-force enumeration of all period words u with |u| <= V = k^(w-1) and checking all cyclic windows. All constraint systems are enumerated exhaustively for (k, w) in {(2,2), (2,3), (2,4), (3,2), (4,2)} and sampled with a fixed seed for (2,5) and (3,3).

measured.unit: fraction of satisfiable constraint systems that have a periodic solution with period <= k^(w-1)
measured.uncertainty: exact for the exhaustive families; the two sampled families are 2000 and 5000 seeded draws

tests.hypothesis: The set of 56 allowed 3x3 templates shown on NKS p. 221 is satisfied by a shifted rule-30 space-time pattern (with the boundary structures shown in the figure), uses all 56 templates, encodes rule 30 in its interior templates, and admits no spatially periodic pattern containing the first template, consistent with the pattern being forced.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (T) Templates: the 56 templates are read automatically from the figure image fig-c.png of p. 221 (14 x 4 grid, 3 x 3 cells each, dark fraction of a 9 x 9 pixel patch at each cell centre > 0.5 = black); the extraction must yield 56 distinct templates listed in strictly decreasing order of their 9-bit binary value (Wolfram's usual ordering), which is the check that the transcription is sound. (A) Realisability and exhaustiveness: the candidate pattern is defined as follows, with rows indexed downward and columns rightward. Rows 0 and 1 are black for all columns <= C+1 and white for columns > C+1; columns C and C+1 are black in every row >= 0; every other cell with row < 2 or column > C+1 is white, and all cells above row 0 are white; interior cells (row t >= 2, column x <= C-1) are a(t, x) = rule30(a(t-1, x), a(t-1, x+1), a(t-1, x+2)), i.e. rule 30 shifted one cell to the left per step, using the black columns C, C+1 as fixed neighbours. On a window of 300 rows and 300 columns to the left of and below the corner (plus a white margin of 3 cells above and to the right), every 3 x 3 block must be one of the 56 templates, and every one of the 56 templates must occur. (R) Rule identification: a template is 'interior' if neither of its 3-cell rows is a boundary row (rows 0-1 or the two black columns); the test reports how many templates satisfy the relation middle-left = rule30(top row) and bottom-left = rule30(middle row), and lists the remaining templates. (U) No periodic alternative: for every horizontal period w = 1..9, build the transfer graph whose nodes are pairs of consecutive rows (r0, r1) on a cylinder of circumference w and whose edges (r0, r1) -> (r1, r2) exist when all w cyclic 3 x 3 blocks of (r0, r1, r2) are allowed; a valid pattern periodic horizontally with period w exists iff this graph has a cycle, and such a pattern contains template 1 iff some edge inside a non-trivial strongly connected component (or a self-loop) has template 1 among its w blocks. The claim PASSES if (T) holds, (A) holds in both directions, and (U) finds no cycle edge containing template 1 for any w <= 9. (R) is reported, not decisive.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. If (U) finds a cyclic (doubly periodic) pattern containing template 1 the uniqueness part of the claim is REFUTED (a second pattern satisfies the constraint). If (T) fails the result is 'inconclusive' (reason: transcription). If (A) fails in the subset direction (the candidate pattern contains a disallowed block) the result is 'inconclusive' (the pattern definition inferred from the templates is wrong, not the claim), unless the failing blocks are interior rule-30 blocks, in which case the templates do not encode rule 30 and the claim is refuted. If (A) holds as a subset but not all 56 templates occur, the verdict is 'mixed' (the figure's template set is larger than needed).
tests.interpretation: The caption on p. 221 states that only the 56 templates may occur anywhere, that the first template must appear at least once, and that the pattern required is a shifted version of the rule-30 evolution. Uniqueness on the infinite plane cannot be verified by finite computation; this test checks (i) that the published template set is actually satisfied by, and derived from, a shifted rule-30 pattern and (ii) the strongest finite consequence of uniqueness that is cheap to check: no spatially periodic competitor exists for periods up to 9 (a doubly periodic pattern containing template 1 would be a counterexample). Disclosed calibration before this pre-registration: the templates were extracted once to design the extraction check (56 distinct, strictly decreasing); a tally found 46 of the 56 templates satisfy the left-target shifted rule-30 relation; and constraint propagation from two black rows over a 45-column window determined rows 2-4 of the pattern (the double black column with white to its right and the rule-30 growth to its left), which is how the candidate pattern above was inferred. No pattern beyond row 4, no exhaustiveness count and no periodic search was computed before pre-registration.

measured.unit: number of cycle edges (doubly periodic valid patterns, periods 1-9) containing template 1; 0 = no periodic competitor
measured.uncertainty: exhaustive for periods 1-9 (pre-registered) and 10-11 (supplementary)

tests.hypothesis: For every finite deterministic discrete system we enumerate, every orbit (from every possible state) becomes eventually periodic, and its eventual period is at most N, the total number of possible states of the system (and the transient plus period is also at most N).
tests.pass: Pre-registered: across all enumerated systems and all initial states, 100% of orbits satisfy period <= N and transient + period <= N (zero violations), where N is the exact number of distinct global states of the system.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: at least one orbit of at least one enumerated system has eventual period > N, or never repeats within N + 1 steps (impossible to observe without a period > N, so equivalently a measured period exceeding N).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'system of limited size that involves discrete elements and follows definite rules' is read as a deterministic map f on a finite set of N global states, so 'definite rules' means the next state depends only on the current state. 'Eventually exhibit repetitive behavior' is read as: the orbit s, f(s), f(f(s)), ... is eventually periodic, with the eventual period (cycle length) at most N; the text's surrounding argument (p. 255) gives exactly this bound. Three concrete families of finite systems from the book's own repertoire are enumerated: the 256 elementary cellular automata on cyclic rings of n cells (N = 2^n), the 4096 two-state two-color Turing machines on cyclic tapes of n cells (N = 2 * n * 2^n: head state x head position x tape contents), and the modular multiplication maps x -> m x mod n (N = n). For every system every state is used as an initial condition, so the test is exhaustive within the enumerated sizes. The claim is a theorem (pigeonhole principle); the computation checks that the stated bound is never exceeded in these families and records how close observed periods come to it.

measured.unit: fraction of orbits with eventual period <= N and transient + period <= N
measured.uncertainty: exact (exhaustive enumeration, no sampling)

tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, the centre column of rule 30 started from a single black cell (an initial condition with no randomness) passes a standard battery of statistical randomness tests as well as the centre column of rule 30 started from a random initial condition and as well as a pseudo-random reference stream, whereas a nested deterministic sequence (Thue-Morse) fails the same battery.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Sequences of N = 2^20 bits: (S1) rule 30 centre column from a single black cell; (S2) rule 30 centre column from a random initial row (numpy seed 20261031, width 2N+1, so that the column is exactly the random-initial-condition case); (S3) numpy PCG64 bits, seed 20261031; (S4) the Thue-Morse sequence. Battery of 10 tests, each giving a p-value with pass meaning p >= 0.01: monobit frequency; block frequency (M = 128); runs; longest run of ones (M = 10000, K = 6); serial (m = 16, minimum of the two p-values); approximate entropy (m = 10); cumulative sums (minimum of forward and backward); discrete Fourier transform spectral test; autocorrelation (lags 1..64, Bonferroni-corrected normal p-value of the largest |r|); and a 16-bit non-overlapping block chi-square uniformity test. Also record the lzma compression ratio of the packed bits. PASS (supports) if S1 passes at least 9 of 10 tests and has lzma ratio >= 0.99, S2 and S3 each pass at least 9 of 10, S4 fails at least 4 tests, and the first terms of S1 agree exactly with the OEIS A051023 b-file over the whole length of the b-file.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if S1 passes 7 or fewer of the 10 tests or has lzma ratio < 0.98 (an exploitable regularity), or if S1 disagrees with OEIS A051023 (then the generator is wrong and the test is aborted as inconclusive/other). If S1 passes exactly 8, or S4 fails fewer than 4 tests (battery not discriminating), the verdict is 'mixed'. If the OEIS file cannot be fetched the OEIS cross-check is dropped and reported, and the verdict rests on the generated sequences.
tests.interpretation: 'Random behaviour' is read as the book itself reads it (practical randomness, pp. 261 and 1085 ff.): the sequence passes standard statistical tests and is incompressible, not algorithmic randomness, which no finite test can establish. 'No randomness in initial conditions' is realised by the single-black-cell seed; the book's own comparison (p. 261) is with random initial conditions, so S2 is the matched control and S4 is a control for a deterministic but nested (non-random) sequence that the battery must reject for the test to be discriminating. Rule 22 is also mentioned in the claim's context but its single-cell pattern is nested; only rule 30, the book's example on this page, is tested.

measured.uncertainty: at alpha = 0.01 per test a truly random sequence fails at least one of 10 tests with probability about 0.10

tests.hypothesis: Rule 90 is additive (linear over GF(2)): its local rule is l XOR r, so every evolution is the XOR superposition of shifted copies of the single-cell nested (Pascal mod 2) pattern. Consequently a biased random initial condition leaves a permanent trace: at every time t = 2^k each cell is the XOR of exactly two initial cells, so the density returns to 2p(1-p) forever for initial density p, and the single-cell pattern itself is nested, not random. Rule 22 (non-additive, class 3) instead forgets the initial density: from any initial density the density converges to one common value.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (A) Additivity: the rule-90 local map phi satisfies phi(a XOR b) = phi(a) XOR phi(b) for all 64 pairs of 3-cell neighbourhoods, and the rule-22 map does not; (B) superposition: for 50 random initial conditions on a cyclic lattice of width 513 run for 256 steps, the rule-90 evolution equals the cellwise XOR of the shifted single-cell evolutions exactly (100% of 50*256 rows); (C) single-cell pattern: for rule 90 from one black cell the row at t = 2^k (k = 0..10) has exactly 2 black cells and the row at t = 2^k - 1 has 2^k black cells (nested, Pascal mod 2); (D) persistence in rule 90: with initial densities p in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} on a measured window of 100000 cells (array padded by 1024 cells on each side so boundaries never reach the window), the measured density at t = 2^k for k = 0..10 is within 0.01 of 2p(1-p) in all 33 cases, and at t = 1024 the three densities differ from the p = 0.5 density by more than 0.1; (E) loss of memory in rule 22: with p in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5} on the same windows, the time-averaged densities over t = 512..1024 differ from one another by less than 0.01 (max minus min). 'Supports' requires A-E.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if A or B fails in any case (rule 90 is not additive / not a superposition), or if in D the rule-90 density at t = 1024 for p = 0.1 lies within 0.05 of the p = 0.5 density (the low-density effect has been forgotten), or if in E the rule-22 late-time densities spread by more than 0.05 (rule 22 remembers the initial density). Other combinations are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: The claim has an algebraic clause (additivity, superposition) and an empirical clause (density persistence in rule 90 versus rule 22, the quoted sentence on p. 265). Additivity is checked exhaustively on the local rule and by exact superposition on random configurations. 'Cannot generate randomness intrinsically' is operationalized by the exact nested structure of the single-cell pattern plus the superposition identity: everything in a rule-90 pattern is a XOR of shifted copies of that nested pattern. 'Low initial density persists forever' is operationalized by the density at times 2^k, where rule 90 reduces to x_t(i) = x_0(i-2^k) XOR x_0(i+2^k) and the density must equal 2p(1-p) at arbitrarily late times; 'no long-term effect' in rule 22 is operationalized as late-time density independent of the initial density. Random initial conditions are Bernoulli(p) with fixed seeds; the lattice is a finite array measured only in a window unaffected by the boundaries within the run length. Rule numbering is Wolfram's standard code (rule 90 = l XOR r; rule 22 = exactly one of l, c, r black).

tests.hypothesis: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata, every rule that is additive (linear over GF(2)) can emulate itself with blocks of cells and yields an exactly self-similar (nested) pattern from a single black cell; after removing trivial rules and identifying rules related by reflection or by the sublattice (shear) relation between rules 60 and 90, exactly two additive classes remain, represented by rules 90 and 150; self-emulation among the remaining 248 rules is uncommon, but rule 184 has it with blocks of three cells.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Definitions: a rule f is additive iff f(x XOR y) = f(x) XOR f(y) for all pairs of 3-cell neighbourhoods x, y (which forces f(000) = 0). Rule f self-emulates with block size b >= 2 and t >= 1 steps iff there are two distinct b-cell blocks B0, B1 such that for every arrangement of 2k+1 blocks (k = ceil(t/b)) drawn from {B0, B1}, running f for t steps leaves the centre block equal to B_{f(c-1, c0, c1)}, where c-1, c0, c1 are the bits represented by the three central blocks; this is the block-emulation notion of NKS pp. 269-271 and note p. 1118, which allows t != b. The search covers b in {2, 3, 4}, t in {1, 2, 3, 4} and all block pairs. Trivial rules: 0, 204 (identity), 170 and 240 (shifts). Equivalences for 'fundamentally different': reflection (rule 60 <-> 102) and the sublattice relation p90[t, 2j - t] = p60[t, j], verified computationally on the first 256 steps from a single black cell. Nested: the single-cell pattern p satisfies p[2t, 2i] = p[t, i] for all 0 <= t < 256 and |i| <= t. Clause A passes if every additive rule self-emulates with b = t = 2 and every non-trivial additive rule is nested in this sense. Clause B passes if the non-trivial additive rules fall into exactly two equivalence classes, one containing 90 and one containing 150. Clause C passes if rule 184 self-emulates with b = 3 for some t <= 4 and the fraction of the 248 non-additive rules with at least one self-emulation in the searched range is <= 0.25. 'supports' if A, B and C all pass.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if clause A or clause B fails (an additive rule that does not self-emulate with b = t = 2, a non-trivial additive rule that is not nested, or a third inequivalent non-trivial additive class). 'mixed' if A and B pass but C fails (rule 184 does not self-emulate with 3-cell blocks within the search, or self-emulation is found in more than 25 % of non-additive rules, so 'rather rare' would be an overstatement).
tests.interpretation: 'Additive' is read as linear over GF(2) (Wolfram's own definition on p. 264: patterns from two initial conditions can be superimposed by XOR). 'Emulate itself' is read as block emulation with 2 to 4 cells per block and 1 to 4 steps per emulated step. 'Fundamentally different' is read as 'not related by left-right reflection and not related by the sublattice/shear relation that maps the rule 60 pattern onto the even sublattice of the rule 90 pattern'; without the second identification rule 60 (and its mirror 102) would be a third additive rule, which the test records explicitly. 'Rather rare' is given the threshold 25 % of the non-additive rules. All patterns are generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.

measured.unit: rule numbers; fraction of the 248 non-additive rules with at least one block self-emulation (b <= 4, t <= 4)
measured.uncertainty: exhaustive finite check; exact within the searched block sizes and step counts

tests.hypothesis: Widely deployed linear congruential generators x_{n+1} = (a x_n + c) mod m that were chosen to have maximal period nevertheless produce consecutive d-tuples lying on a small number of parallel hyperplanes (Marsaglia 1968: at most (d! m)^(1/d)), a gross deviation from uniform randomness that is visible at sample sizes far below the period and that standard empirical tests detect.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Generators (all full period for their class): RANDU (a=65539, c=0, m=2^31; period 2^29, maximal for a multiplicative generator mod 2^31), ANSI C example rand (1103515245, 12345, 2^31), Numerical Recipes ranqd1 (1664525, 1013904223, 2^32), Borland C (22695477, 1, 2^32), VAX MTH$RANDOM (69069, 1, 2^32), Park-Miller minimal standard (16807, 0, 2^31-1), C++11 minstd_rand (48271, 0, 2^31-1), POSIX drand48 / java.util.Random (25214903917, 11, 2^48); for comparison Knuth's MMIX generator (6364136223846793005, 1442695040888963407, 2^64) and a cryptographic source (os.urandom). (1) Lattice: the exact spectral test on the dual lattice gives, for every generator with m <= 2^32 (7 generators), a family of at most 3000 parallel planes containing all consecutive triples of the whole period (minimal L1 norm of a nonzero dual vector in d = 3 at most 3000; Marsaglia's bound (6 m)^(1/3) is 2953 for m = 2^32), and at most 93000 parallel lines containing all consecutive pairs in d = 2 ((2 m)^(1/2) = 92682). (2) Visible deviation: projecting 2^20 consecutive triples (coordinates x/m) onto the minimal dual vector u and reducing mod 1, each of those 7 generators yields at most 3000 distinct values (<= 0.3% of 2^20) while os.urandom yields at least 99% distinct values under the same projection and rounding (1e-9). (3) Standard empirical test: the two-dimensional birthday-spacings test (L'Ecuyer and Simard 2001 setting: n = 2^15 points (x_i, x_{i+1}) in 2^21 x 2^21 cells, expected collisions lambda = 2, 32 independent replications from different seeds; total collisions compared with Poisson(64)) rejects (two-sided p < 1e-6) at least 6 of the 8 historical generators, while os.urandom and MMIX are not rejected (p > 1e-3). 'Supports' requires (1), (2) and (3).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if any of the 7 generators with m <= 2^32 has triples on more than 3000 planes (the lattice theorem would be wrong), or if the projection of the LCG triples gives more than 50% distinct values (the structure is not visible at 2^20 samples), or if fewer than 3 of the 8 historical generators fail the birthday-spacings test. Other combinations are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: 'Constructed to have maximal repetition period' is operationalized as the set of full-period historical generators listed, with RANDU included as maximal for its multiplicative class (it is Wolfram's own example in the NKS note). 'Very substantial deviations from perfect randomness' is operationalized as (i) the exact lattice structure (number of covering hyperplanes, Marsaglia/Knuth spectral test), (ii) its visibility at a sample size (2^20) far below the period, with a cryptographic source as the randomness baseline under the identical statistic, and (iii) rejection by a standard test from the TestU01 family that random sources pass. The lattice is analysed on the full state recurrence; generators that output only high-order bits (ANSI C, drand48) are analysed on the state, which is the sequence whose stripes Wolfram's pictures show. The MMIX 64-bit generator is outside 'over the years' up to 2002 as a deployed generator and is reported for contrast only.

measured.unit: largest number of parallel planes containing all consecutive triples, over the 7 historical generators with m <= 2^32 (threshold 3000; each has 2^29 to 2^32 triples)
measured.uncertainty: exact (lattice computation)

tests.hypothesis: Across exhaustively enumerated families of simple programs, measures of the complexity of a rule's definition are at most weakly rank-correlated with measures of the complexity of the behaviour it produces; some rules of minimal definitional complexity produce behaviour in the top quartile of behavioural complexity, some rules of maximal definitional complexity produce behaviour in the bottom quartile, and a non-negligible fraction of rules that differ in a single table entry differ greatly in behavioural complexity.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Families: (F1) the 256 elementary cellular automata; (F2) the 2187 three-colour nearest-neighbour totalistic cellular automata (Wolfram codes 0..2186). Rule-complexity measures: F1: (a) number of monomials in the algebraic normal form over GF(2), (b) minimal number of two-input gates (AND, OR, XOR, with negation free) computing the rule, found by breadth-first search over truth tables; F2: (c) Shannon entropy in bits of the 7-entry code table, (d) number of table entries that differ from the table's most frequent value. Behaviour-complexity measures: (e) lzma-compressed size (preset 9) of the space-time diagram, one byte per cell, from a random initial condition (width 300, periodic boundary, numpy seed 20260720, steps 200..600 after a 200-step transient); (f) the same for the single-seed pattern (one black / one gray cell, 400 steps, width 801, zero boundary). Statistics: Spearman rank correlation rho for each (rule measure, behaviour measure) pair within each family (8 pairs). 'supports' if max over the 8 pairs of rho <= 0.30, and in each family at least one rule at the minimum value of each rule measure has behaviour measure (e) in the top quartile of its family while at least one rule at the maximum value has (e) in the bottom quartile, and at least 5 % of F1 Hamming-distance-1 rule pairs (1024 pairs) differ in (e) by more than half of the family's range of (e).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any of the 8 Spearman correlations is >= 0.60 (a direct, monotone correspondence between rule complexity and behaviour complexity) or if in either family no rule at minimal rule complexity reaches the top quartile of behaviour complexity. Otherwise (e.g. 0.30 < max rho < 0.60, or the Hamming-neighbour fraction below 5 %) -> 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: 'Complexity of underlying rules' is operationalised by syntactic measures of the rule table (ANF size and minimal circuit size for Boolean rules; entropy and non-default entries for totalistic codes), and 'complexity of behaviour' by lossless compressibility of the space-time diagram, which treats both random-looking and structured-but-irregular behaviour as complex (Wolfram's usage also counts class 3 randomness as complex). 'No direct correspondence' is read as the absence of a strong monotone association (rho < 0.3 weak, rho >= 0.6 strong) plus the existence of the counterexamples Wolfram describes. The extension 'and by extension natural systems' is not tested. All patterns are generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between rule complexity and lzma size of the space-time diagram; fraction of 1024 Hamming-1 ECA pairs whose random-IC lzma sizes differ by more than half the family range
measured.uncertainty: one random initial condition per rule; lzma sizes in bytes (ECA random-IC range 152..17028)
