tests.hypothesis: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata run from random initial conditions, (almost) every rule in which a single-cell perturbation spreads to an ever-growing set of cells produces a black-minus-white count series that is non-periodic and incompressible relative to its own increment distribution.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all 256 elementary CA rules (Wolfram numbering), two colours, nearest neighbours. Propagation test (per rule): 20 trials; lattice of 1601 cells (non-wrapping: cells outside are fixed to the random background and the lattice is wide enough that the perturbation cannot reach the edge in 400 steps), random initial condition with density 1/2 from a fixed seed, second copy with the centre cell flipped; after 400 steps the damage width w = (rightmost differing cell - leftmost differing cell + 1) is recorded (0 if no cell differs); a rule is 'propagating' if w >= 100 (= 0.25 x 400, i.e. the damaged region grows linearly rather than staying bounded or merely moving) in at least 10 of 20 trials. Price-series test (per rule): ring of N = 400 cells, random initial condition density 1/2 from a fixed seed, discard 1000 transient steps, record d(t) = (#black - #white) for W = 4096 further steps; d(t) is 'significantly random' if (R1) it is not exactly periodic with any period p <= W/2 within the window and (R2) the first differences D(t) = d(t+1) - d(t), stored as int16, have plug-in marginal entropy H >= 1 bit and lzma (preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size >= 0.5 x H bits per sample. Calibration on controls: i.i.d. binomial counts give ratio 1.35, an AR(1) series 1.40, a period-97 series 0.09, a noiseless sinusoid 0.47. The claim PASSES if at least 90% of propagating rules are significantly random. Reported, not decisive: the fraction of non-propagating rules that are significantly random, and the list of propagating-but-not-random rules.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if fewer than 75% of propagating rules are significantly random (several counterexamples to 'essentially inevitable' inside the stated family). Between 75% and 90% the verdict is 'mixed'. If fewer than 5 rules are propagating under the definition the test is underpowered (inconclusive).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's market model (p. 431-432) is a one-dimensional CA of buy/sell agents, with 'price' the running difference of black and white counts; his figure uses rule 90. 'Information will eventually propagate from one entity to all others' is read as damage spreading in the sense he uses in Chapter 6: the set of cells affected by a one-cell change grows without bound (linear growth of the damage width), which excludes pure shifts and travelling defects whose influence merely moves. 'Significant randomness' of the running totals is read as non-periodicity plus incompressibility of the increments of the black-minus-white count. 'Essentially inevitable' is read as at least 90% of the propagating rules. The claim is a universal statement over the family, so the test looks for counterexamples.

measured.unit: fraction of propagating rules whose black-minus-white series is significantly random
measured.uncertainty: 40 propagating rules; 33 random, 7 not

tests.hypothesis: Among one-dimensional nearest-neighbour cellular automata, exactly 6 of the 256 two-colour rules and exactly 1800 of the 3^27 = 7,625,597,484,987 three-colour rules are reversible, where reversible means the global map on bi-infinite configurations is injective (equivalently bijective; equivalently, by Wolfram's note, all periodic configurations have distinct successors).
tests.pass: Pre-registered. An exhaustive enumeration with an exact injectivity test (pair graph of the de Bruijn graph: a rule is injective iff the pair graph has no cycle through an off-diagonal node and no diagonal-to-diagonal path through off-diagonal nodes; used both as a sound pruning condition during depth-first assignment of the rule table and as the exact test at the leaves) yields exactly 6 reversible rules for k = 2, r = 1 and exactly 1800 for k = 3, r = 1. As a check of the method, the same program must give 62 for k = 2, r = 2 (NKS note 'Numbers of reversible rules'), and the 6 elementary rules must be {15, 51, 85, 170, 204, 240}. Also, every rule found must pass Wolfram's finite test (distinct successors for all periodic configurations of period <= 9, as his note says suffices for k = 3) and every rule not found that is sampled (10000 random balanced k = 3 rules) must fail it. 'Supports' requires the counts 6 and 1800 and the consistency checks.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if the exhaustive enumeration completes and gives a count other than 6 for k = 2, r = 1 or other than 1800 for k = 3, r = 1 (with the k = 2, r = 2 check giving 62, so the method is validated). If the k = 3 enumeration cannot be completed within the compute budget (about 1 hour), the verdict is 'mixed' or 'inconclusive' (reason: other) with the k = 2 result and a lower bound on the k = 3 count reported.
tests.interpretation: 'Reversible' is taken as injectivity of the global map on the full shift (bi-infinite configurations), the standard notion and the one Wolfram's note tests through periodic configurations. Rule numbering is Wolfram's (table entry for neighbourhood (l,c,r) at digit position l*k^2 + c*k + r of the base-k rule number). The count is of raw rule tables, not of symmetry classes (the note gives 172 families for k = 3). The enumeration is exact, so there is no sampling uncertainty; the only risks are implementation errors, which the k = 2 (r = 1 and r = 2) checks and the independent periodic-configuration test guard against. Note: the pruning search is written in C (compiled with gcc from analysis.py) because a Python search over the pruned tree would be too slow; this is a deviation from 'python3 only' tooling and is recorded.

measured.unit: reversible rules among the 3^27 three-colour nearest-neighbour cellular automata (claimed 1800)
measured.uncertainty: exact (exhaustive enumeration)

tests.hypothesis: For graphs that are discretisations of ordinary d-dimensional space (hypercubic lattices Z^d) the number of nodes within graph distance r grows like r^d, while for tree-like and randomly connected graphs the growth is exponential, so no finite exponent d exists; the biconditional ('precisely') additionally requires that polynomial growth of degree d occur only for networks corresponding to ordinary d-dimensional space.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Primary (necessity and the tree/random clause): for the hypercubic lattices Z^1, Z^2, Z^3, Z^4 the growth exponent, estimated as the ordinary-least-squares slope of log N(r) against log r over r in [R/2, R] (R = 32 for d <= 3, R = 20 for d = 4), lies within 0.15 of d; for the infinite 3-regular tree (R = 13) and for a random 4-regular graph on n = 300000 nodes (R = largest radius with N(R) <= n/10) the same slope estimated over r in [R/2, R] exceeds 5, and log N(r) is better fit (higher R^2) by a straight line in r than in log r. If every one of these six conditions holds the primary test passes. Secondary (sufficiency / 'precisely'): the Cayley graph of the discrete Heisenberg group with generators x, y and inverses is known not to be quasi-isometric to any Z^d (Pansu 1983), yet has polynomial growth of degree 4 (Bass 1972 / Guivarc'h 1973). If its measured slope over r in [12, 24] lies in [3.5, 4.5], then a network with r^d growth exists that does not correspond to ordinary d-dimensional space in the strict sense. Verdict rule: primary passes and secondary slope in [3.5, 4.5] -> 'mixed' (the necessity direction and the tree/random clause hold; the sufficiency direction holds only if 'corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space' is read as 'has growth dimension d'); primary passes and secondary slope outside [3.5, 4.5] -> 'supports'.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any lattice exponent differs from d by more than 0.5, or if either the tree or the random 4-regular graph has a slope below 3 over the stated range (i.e. appears to have a small finite dimension), or if log N(r) for the tree or random graph is better fit by a straight line in log r than in r. Any other outcome (e.g. a lattice exponent off by between 0.15 and 0.5) -> 'inconclusive' with reason 'other'.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'number of nodes that appear out to distance r' is the size N(r) of the closed ball of graph-distance radius r around a node. 'Grows in some limiting sense like r^d' is operationalised as the local log-log slope of N(r) at the largest radii computed, which for an exact polynomial of degree d tends to d from below. 'Corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space' is taken, for the primary test, as 'is the nearest-neighbour graph of Z^d'; for the secondary test we use the standard geometric-group-theory meaning (quasi-isometric to R^d) and rely on published theorems for the Heisenberg group's status. 'Tree-like or randomly connected' is operationalised as the infinite 3-regular tree (BFS-generated) and a configuration-model random 4-regular graph. All graphs are generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.

measured.unit: log-log slope of N(r) over r in [R/2, R] (growth-exponent estimate)
measured.uncertainty: exact counts; slopes are OLS fits with R^2 >= 0.988 (log-log) for every graph

datasets.name: Graph families generated by analysis.py: hypercubic lattices Z^1..Z^4 (nearest-neighbour, L1 adjacency), infinite 3-regular tree, random 4-regular configuration-model graph (n = 300000, numpy seed 20261031), discrete Heisenberg group Cayley graph (generators x, y and inverses)

tests.hypothesis: For every string substitution system whose left-hand-side blocks can never overlap themselves or each other, every possible order of performing replacements from a given initial string yields the same causal network (up to isomorphism), whereas systems with overlapping blocks can yield different causal networks for different orders.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: among all enumerated (rule set, initial string) pairs whose rule set is syntactically non-overlapping and which admit at least two distinct complete evolutions, 100% have exactly one causal-network isomorphism class (and one final string) over all complete evolutions; and at least 10% of the overlapping rule sets exhibit at least two non-isomorphic causal networks for some initial string (otherwise the test has no discriminating power and the verdict is 'inconclusive', reason 'not-operationalizable').
tests.fail: Pre-registered: at least one non-overlapping (rule set, initial string) pair whose complete evolutions produce two or more non-isomorphic causal networks.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's generalized substitution systems (NKS pp. 497-503) replace one occurrence of a left-hand block at a time; which occurrence, and when, is the free choice of 'order'. A causal network has one node per replacement event and an edge from event P to event E whenever E's matched block contains an element that P produced; the initial condition is represented by a node 0 that 'produces' the initial elements. Two orders give 'the same causal network' if the networks are isomorphic as node-labelled directed graphs (labels = rule applied, node 0 fixed). Non-overlap is the syntactic condition of p. 503: no non-empty proper suffix of any block equals a prefix of any block (including the block itself), and no block is a substring of another. To compare complete histories across orders, the enumeration is restricted to systems whose every rule strictly shortens the string (|rhs| < |lhs|), so every evolution terminates after finitely many events; all complete evolutions (all choices at every step) from every initial string of length <= 5 over {A, B} are generated exhaustively. Wolfram's weaker condition (no overlap among strings actually generated) is not tested.

measured.unit: fraction of non-overlapping (rule set, initial string) pairs with >= 2 complete evolutions whose causal networks all coincide
measured.uncertainty: exact (exhaustive within the family)

tests.hypothesis: In a network that approximates a d-dimensional Riemannian space, the number of nodes at graph distance r grows like r^(d-1), and the leading curvature correction to it is proportional to the Ricci scalar R times r^(d+1): in the continuum the geodesic sphere of radius s has area d*omega_d*s^(d-1)*(1 - R s^2/(6d) + O(s^4)), so for a random geometric graph of fixed local density and connection radius the shell count on a curved space divided by the flat shell count equals 1 - R s(r)^2/(6d) to leading order, where s(r) is the geodesic radius reached in r hops; the correction is negative for positive curvature and positive for negative curvature.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Random geometric graphs with identical node density (3183 per unit area in d = 2, 7600 per unit volume in d = 3) and connection radius (geodesic epsilon = 0.045 in d = 2, 0.086 in d = 3, mean degree about 20) on: flat torus (R = 0), unit 2-sphere (R = 2), 2-sphere of radius 1.5 (R = 8/9), hyperbolic plane of curvature -1 (R = -2; sampled within hyperbolic radius 1.8, sources within 0.2 of the centre), flat 3-torus (R = 0) and unit 3-sphere (R = 6); 3 independent graphs per geometry, 500 BFS sources per graph. Let S_g(r) be the mean number of nodes at hop distance r, s(r) the mean geodesic distance of hop-r nodes measured in the flat graph of the same dimension, and Q_g(r) = S_g(r)/S_flat(r) - 1. Fit range: hops r with 0.25 <= s(r) <= 0.7. (a) Sign: Q_g(r) < 0 for every r in the fit range for the three positively curved geometries and > 0 for the hyperbolic plane. (b) Exponent: the least-squares slope of log|S_g(r) - S_flat(r)| against log r over the fit range lies within d+1 +/- 0.6 for every curved geometry. (c) Proportionality to R: the coefficient k_g of the through-origin fit Q_g(r) = k_g s(r)^2 over the fit range satisfies 0.7 <= k_g / (-R_g/(6d)) <= 1.3 for every curved geometry, and k(unit sphere)/k(sphere 1.5) is within 30% of 2.25. 'Supports' requires (a), (b) and (c).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if the sign in (a) is wrong for any geometry over the fit range, or if any exponent in (b) lies outside [d, d+2], or if any ratio in (c) lies outside [0.4, 2.5] (the correction is not proportional to the Ricci scalar with the continuum coefficient). Other combinations (e.g. correct sign and exponent but coefficient off by 30-60%) are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's count is of nodes reached by going r connections, i.e. the shell at graph distance r (claims.json paraphrases it as 'within distance r'; the test follows the book's wording and the r^(d+1) exponent, which is the shell exponent). 'Large network approximating d-dimensional space' is realised as random geometric graphs on constant-curvature model spaces, whose hop distance approximates geodesic distance up to a stretch factor that is measured on the flat graph of the same density and applied to the curved ones. Proportionality to the Ricci scalar is tested against the continuum coefficient -R/(6d) of the geodesic-sphere area expansion (Gray 2004, Tubes, ch. 3) across R = 8/9, 2, -2 (d = 2) and R = 6 (d = 3); only constant-curvature spaces are used, so the claim that no other curvature invariant enters at leading order is tested only through the coefficient, not through anisotropic examples.

measured.unit: fitted curvature coefficient k divided by the continuum prediction -R/(6d) (hyperbolic plane); other geometries in extra
measured.uncertainty: shell-count SD across 3 graphs is 0.2-1% of S in the fit range (derived/measured.json S_sd)

tests.hypothesis: Six structurally different lossless compression methods (run-length, block Huffman, LZ77/Deflate, LZMA, Burrows-Wheeler/bzip2 and a two-dimensional quadtree code) all strongly compress uniform and repetitive cellular automaton patterns, compress nested patterns at least partly, and achieve little compression of complex patterns from rules 30 and 45, relative to random patterns of the same density.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Patterns: elementary CAs from a single black cell, T = 2048 steps; window rows 1024-2047, columns -512..511 (1024 x 1024 cells, inside the light cone). Classes: uniform = rule 254; repetitive = rules 50 and 250; nested = rules 90 and 150; complex = rules 30 and 45; exploratory (not in the verdict) = rule 110. Methods: (1) run-length coding of the row-major bit stream with Elias-gamma run lengths; (2) static Huffman code on non-overlapping 8-bit blocks (size = code bits + 256-byte table); (3) zlib level 9; (4) lzma preset 9 extreme; (5) bz2 level 9; (6) quadtree code of the 1024 x 1024 bitmap (1 bit 'split' or 2 bits 'uniform leaf + colour'; 1 bit per single cell). Statistic: r = size(pattern) / size(Bernoulli(d) pattern of the same shape), d = pattern's black fraction clipped to [0.01, 0.99], Bernoulli control from numpy PCG64 seed 20261031. 'supports' if all of: (a) uniform: r <= 0.10 for all 6 methods; (b) each repetitive rule: r <= 0.20 for at least 4 of 6 methods; (c) each nested rule: r <= 0.80 for at least 3 of 6 methods; (d) each complex rule: r >= 0.85 for all 6 methods.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any method achieves r < 0.60 on rule 30 or rule 45 (substantial compression of complex behavior by a generic method), or if (b) and (c) both fail (the methods do not share the ability to compress repetition and nesting). 'mixed' otherwise when any of (a)-(d) fails.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram (p. 560-570) compares run-length, block (Huffman), pointer-based (LZ) and two-dimensional schemes on CA patterns and concludes they share the same capabilities. The four families are represented by our own run-length and block-Huffman coders, three standard library compressors (zlib/Deflate and lzma are pointer-based; bzip2 adds a block-sorting family Wolfram does not discuss) and a quadtree code as the two-dimensional scheme. 'Substantial compression' is measured relative to a random pattern of the same density, so that compression explained by an unequal black/white ratio alone does not count; thresholds of 0.85 (little compression) and 0.60 (substantial) are our choice. The universal 'all methods' wording cannot be tested; a purpose-built compressor for a specific rule is outside the claim's scope (generic methods), as the assessors note.

measured.unit: compressed size relative to a density-matched Bernoulli pattern (r)
measured.uncertainty: deterministic patterns; Bernoulli control sizes vary by well under 1 % between seeds (rules 50 and 250 controls: 0.00-0.03 %)

tests.hypothesis: Wolfram's two example sequences, a maximal-length linear feedback shift register output and the concatenated binary digits of successive integers, have block frequencies that are uniform (the LFSR exactly so over its period, the concatenation increasingly so with length) yet are detectably non-random by other tests, in particular an abnormally small spread of block counts for the LFSR, so uniform block frequencies cannot be a universal randomness test.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: (1) LFSR (taps {2,11} as in NKS p. 594, period 2047, and a 20-bit register with period 2^20 - 1): over one full period every block of length L <= r - 1 (r = register length) occurs a number of times within 1 of the uniform expectation (N - L + 1)/2^L; Berlekamp-Massey linear complexity equals r (a random sequence of the same length has about N/2); and the chi-square statistic of its block counts for each L in 4..8 lies below the 1st percentile of 200 random sequences of the same length (the 'abnormally small spread'). (2) Binary Champernowne sequence, N = 2^20 bits: for every L <= 8 the maximum relative deviation of any block frequency from 2^-L decreases from the first N/4 bits to the first N/2 bits to all N bits and is <= 0.5 at N (coarse accuracy: every block within a factor 1.5 of uniform); its lzma compression ratio is <= 0.5 while that of the random reference is >= 0.95 (detectable regularity); and its bits agree with OEIS A030190 for every term in the b-file. Verdict 'supports' if (1) and (2) both hold; 'mixed' if (1) holds but (2) fails; 'refutes' if (1) fails.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: the LFSR block counts deviate by more than 1 from uniform for some L <= r - 1, or its chi-square spread is not below the 1st percentile of random sequences for some L in 4..8, or its linear complexity is not r; for Champernowne, a block frequency deviation that does not decrease with N or exceeds 0.5 at L <= 8, or a compression ratio above 0.9 (no regularity detected by compression).
tests.interpretation: The claim is the negation of 'uniform block frequencies for all lengths is a universal test for randomness', argued by two explicit counterexamples on NKS p. 594: sequence (e), 'generated by a linear feedback shift register (essentially an additive cellular automaton) with tap positions {2, 11}', and sequence (f), 'formed by concatenating base 2 digits of successive integers'. The LFSR is implemented as a[n] = a[n-2] XOR a[n-11] from a register containing a single 1 (polynomial x^11 + x^2 + 1), and a longer one with a[n] = a[n-3] XOR a[n-20]; maximal period is verified by computation rather than assumed. 'Accurate block frequencies' is given two operational readings: exact (counts within 1 of uniform, which an m-sequence achieves by construction for L <= r - 1) and coarse (every block frequency within a factor 1.5 of uniform and converging with N). 'Non-random' is operationalised by linear complexity (LFSR), by lzma compressibility (Champernowne) and by the block-count spread that Wolfram names on p. 595, measured as the chi-square statistic of block counts compared with the empirical distribution over random sequences of the same length (block counts of overlapping windows are dependent, so no analytic chi-square p-value is used).

tests.hypothesis: The first 2^20 bits of the rule 30 centre column and the first 2^20 bits of the binary expansion of pi show no detectable deviation from randomness under (A) overlapping block-frequency statistics for block lengths 1-12 and (B) analysis by all 88 inequivalent elementary cellular automata run on the sequence, while the same CA analysis does detect known non-random sequences.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Sequences: S1 = rule 30 centre column from a single black cell, steps 0 .. 2^20 - 1 (computed; must agree with the OEIS A051023 b-file); S2 = binary digits of pi after the binary point, first 2^20 (computed by Chudnovsky series; must agree with the OEIS A004601 b-file). (A) Block frequencies: for each L = 1..12 the NIST SP 800-22 serial increment del-psi^2_L = psi^2_L - psi^2_{L-1} (cyclic overlapping L-blocks), p-value from chi-square with 2^(L-1) df; 12 p-values per sequence, 24 in total. (B) CA analysis: for each of the 88 elementary rules that are minimal under left-right reflection and black-white complement, take the first 16384 bits as a cyclic initial condition, run 64 steps and record two statistics of steps 1-64: mean black density and zlib (level 9) size of the bit-packed 64 x 16384 pattern. Compare each with the same statistic for 100 random initial conditions (numpy PCG64, seed 20261031): z = (x - mean) / sd (if sd = 0, z = 0 when x equals the reference value and infinite otherwise). 176 z-scores per sequence. Validity controls: (i) a fresh PCG64 sequence of 2^20 bits must give max |z| < 5 and pass (A) under the same rule as below (negative control); (ii) the binary Champernowne sequence (concatenated binary integers 1, 2, 3, ...) and the Thue-Morse sequence must each give max |z| > 5 (positive controls, showing the CA analysis can detect non-randomness). 'supports' if, for both S1 and S2, no (A) p-value is below 1e-4, at most 2 of the 24 (A) p-values are below 0.01 (P(>= 3 of 24) ~ 0.2 % under the null), every (B) |z| <= 5, and the controls hold.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any (A) p-value is below 1e-6, or 4 or more of the 24 are below 0.01, or any (B) |z| > 6 for S1 or S2. 'mixed' if neither the pass nor the refute condition holds. If the negative control fails, the verdict is 'inconclusive' (reason 'other'). If a positive control is not detected, the CA analysis is underpowered and the verdict can be at most 'mixed'. If a computed sequence disagrees with its OEIS b-file, the verdict is 'inconclusive' (reason 'other').
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's sequences (g) and (h) on p. 594-596 are the rule 30 centre column and the base-2 digits of pi; 'statistical analysis, even with some generalization' refers on those pages to block-frequency analysis and to running simple cellular automata on the sequence and examining the result. (A) is the standard overlapping-block frequency test (NIST serial increments), which covers block frequencies of all lengths up to 12 without double-counting. (B) generalizes by feeding each sequence as initial condition to every elementary CA (the 'simple cellular automata' class is fixed to the 88 inequivalent elementary rules, a pre-declared class as the assessors required) and checking two summary statistics of the output against random inputs. 'No detectable deviation' is bounded by these tests, these lengths, and this CA class; it is not a proof of randomness. A rule 30 centre-column NIST battery already exists (wolfram2002-ch02-05); this test is complementary and adds pi.

measured.uncertainty: deterministic sequences; z-scores use a 100-sample reference (sd estimated to about 7 %)

tests.hypothesis: For any fixed, mechanical method of perception and analysis there exist data with a very short generating description that the method fails to recognize as regular (assigns no significant compression), while a different, more specialized method does recognize some of these. In the limit this is the uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity (no total computable function lower-bounds description length usefully); here the testable content is checked on concrete methods: three general-purpose compressors (zlib, bz2, lzma) and two specialized recognizers (Berlekamp-Massey linear complexity over GF(2); affine-recurrence detection modulo 2^32), applied to sequences generated by programs of under 400 bytes.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Generate six byte strings of 4096 bytes (32768 bits) each: (1) rule 30 centre column from a single black cell; (2) a linear congruential generator modulo 2^32 (a = 1664525, c = 1013904223, seed 1), 32-bit words little-endian; (3) xorshift32 (shifts 13, 17, 5, seed 2463534242), 32-bit words; (4) binary digits of pi after the binary point (Machin formula, exact integer arithmetic); (5) Thue-Morse sequence bits (positive control, obviously regular); (6) os.urandom bytes (baseline, no short description assumed). Generating source for (1)-(5) must be under 400 bytes each (recorded). A method 'recognizes' a string if: for a compressor, its output is at most 0.97 times the compressed size of the urandom baseline of the same length (3% gain); for Berlekamp-Massey, the linear complexity of the bit sequence is below one quarter of its length; for the affine recognizer, the recurrence x_{i+1} = a x_i + c mod 2^32 solved from the first three words holds for every remaining word. 'Supports' if ALL of the following hold: (a) each of the three compressors fails to recognize at least two of the four simple-description strings (1)-(4); (b) at least one of (1)-(4) is recognized by a specialized method but by none of the three compressors; (c) at least one of (1)-(4) is recognized by none of the five methods; (d) controls: all three compressors recognize (5) with output below 0.2 of the urandom size, and no method recognizes (6).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is a theorem (uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity) and cannot be refuted by a finite computation; this test checks whether its concrete content is exhibited by actual methods. 'Mixed' if any compressor recognizes all four simple-description strings (the chosen simple descriptions are all perceptible to a standard method) or if any method recognizes the urandom baseline (false alarm, so 'recognition' is not meaningful at this length). 'Inconclusive' with reason 'construction-failed' if (b) or (c) fails, i.e. the chosen generators do not exhibit a regularity that some method misses while another catches, or none that every method misses.
tests.interpretation: Operationalizes 'recognize a regularity' as achieving a non-trivial compression or an exact fit by a specialized recognizer, and 'simple description' as a generating program of under 400 bytes. Criteria (a) and (c) exhibit the first half of the claim (current methods miss regularities with short descriptions); criterion (b) exhibits the second half (higher or different methods recognize some of what others miss). The expected witnesses are the rule 30 centre column and the digits of pi (missed by everything tested) and the xorshift/LCG outputs (missed by compressors, caught by linear-complexity or affine fitting). This is finite evidence for the empirical content of a mathematical theorem, not a proof; the theorem itself (Kolmogorov 1965, Chaitin 1966; see Li & Vitanyi) is not re-derived.

measured.unit: number of the four simple-description strings (description <= 207 bytes) recognized by none of the five methods (criterion c; pre-registered requirement >= 1)
measured.uncertainty: compression sizes are deterministic except the os.urandom baseline, which varies by a few bytes between runs

tests.hypothesis: A single fixed universal rule (Wolfram's 19-colour universal cellular automaton, verified as an emulator in claim-test wolfram2002-ch11-06), run from initial conditions that differ only in the encoded target rule, produces behaviour whose complexity under a fixed measure (lzma compressibility) ranges from that of the simplest target (uniform/periodic) to that of the most complex target tried (random-looking), both in the decoded emulated cells and in the universal automaton's own raw space-time pattern.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. analysis.py re-uses the published rule list (derived/uca_rule.txt copied from the ch11-06 test, or fetched live) and runs the universal automaton on a cyclic array of N = 128 encoded blocks for S = 128 emulated steps (128 x 53 = 6784 universal steps) from a single black cell, for targets: elementary rules 250 (uniform growth), 90 (nested), 110 (localised structures), 30 (random), and one random two-colour range-1 rule drawn with seed 20261104 from rules with f(000) = 0. For each target: rho_dec = 8 * lzma bytes / cells of the decoded S x N binary pattern; rho_ref = the same measure for the directly computed target pattern; rho_raw = 8 * lzma bytes / (cells * log2 19) of the universal automaton's raw S x 20N checkpoint array (rows at multiples of 53 steps). 'supports' if (i) rho_dec equals rho_ref for every target (the universal system's decoded behaviour is exactly as complex as the emulated system's) and (ii) rho_raw(250) < rho_raw(90) < rho_raw(30) with rho_raw(30) >= 2 * rho_raw(250), i.e. the universal system's own pattern spans a wide range of complexity set only by the initial condition. Thresholds fixed before running.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if some decoded pattern differs from the target pattern (then the universal system does not reproduce the emulated behaviour and (i) fails). 'mixed' if (i) holds but (ii) fails, meaning the emulated complexity is visible only after decoding and the universal system's own pattern is dominated by its fixed scaffolding. 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable' if the rule text is unavailable.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's statement is an implication: universality (ability to emulate any system) entails the ability to produce behaviour as complex as that of any system. Taken literally it is a consequence of the definition of emulation plus the existence of universal systems, and the 'arbitrarily' part (no upper bound) cannot be tested by a finite run. We test the concrete content for one universal system and one complexity measure: that the same fixed rule, changing only the initial condition, realises behaviour matching the complexity of targets across the four Wolfram classes, measured both after decoding and on the universal system's raw pattern. 'Complex' is operationalised as lzma incompressibility of the space-time pattern, which Wolfram uses himself (NKS ch. 10) as a proxy for apparent complexity. The 'in a sense' qualification is honoured by reporting both the decoded and raw measures. The claim's second reading noted by one assessor (complex behaviour from simple initial conditions) is not tested: the initial conditions here encode the target rule and are not simple.

measured.unit: ratio of raw universal-automaton compressibility rho_raw when emulating rule 30 to that when emulating rule 250 (same rule, different initial condition)
measured.uncertainty: deterministic for the fixed initial conditions

tests.hypothesis: Wolfram's fixed 19-colour range-2 rule, started from the published block encoding of a target rule table and cell colours, reproduces the target cellular automaton's evolution exactly: after the published number of steps per emulated step, every block again has the published form with its colour cell updated to the target rule's new value, for every elementary rule (range 1) and for random two-colour range-2 rules, which have more complicated rule tables than any elementary rule.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. analysis.py fetches the NKS online note 'Universal cellular automaton' (https://www.wolframscience.com/nks/notes-11-4--universal-cellular-automaton/), records byte size and SHA-256 of the page, and parses the published rule list (Mathematica replacement rules on 5-cell neighbourhoods, first matching rule applies; the arrow glyphs are lost in the HTML text, so each rule is read as 'pattern in braces' followed by 'output expression') and the published block encoding Flatten[{Transpose[{Join[{4, 18(1-a), 6}, Table[9, {2^(2r+1)-3}]], 10 - 3 rtab}], Table[{9, 1}, {r}], 9, 13}] with rtab in Wolfram's standard order (outcome for all-ones neighbourhood first). The universal automaton is run on a cyclic array of N blocks (N cells of the target automaton with cyclic boundaries) for S * P steps, where P = (3r+2) 2^(2r+1) + 3r^2 + 7r + 3 is the published period (53 for r = 1, 285 for r = 2). After each P steps, each block must equal the encoding of the directly computed target configuration (strict block-level check, which also verifies the decoded colours). Tests: (a) all 256 elementary rules, N = 16, S = 8, two random initial conditions each (seed 20261106); (b) 30 random two-colour range-2 rules (32-entry tables), N = 10, S = 4, one random initial condition each. 'supports' if the total number of mismatching universal-automaton cells over all checks is 0.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if, with the rule list and encoding exactly as published, some target rule's evolution is not reproduced (one or more mismatching cells at a checkpoint). If mismatches occur, the first action is to re-check the transcription of the published text (lost arrows, exponent formatting); a correction that makes the parse agree with the published text is a harness fix and is disclosed in caveats; any remaining mismatch is a refutation. 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable' if the note cannot be retrieved and no verifiable copy is at hand; 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the cyclic-boundary set-up turns out to be incompatible with the construction in a way that cannot be resolved from the published description (for example if the construction requires a special terminator block that the note does not specify).
tests.interpretation: The claim has two parts: the fixed 19-colour rule emulates any two-colour cellular automaton of any range (the note gives the encoding with range r as a parameter), and, via the reduction of multi-colour rules to two-colour rules with larger range (NKS p. 656), any cellular automaton whatsoever. This test checks the first part directly for r = 1 (all 256 rules) and r = 2 (random rules); the colour reduction is a separate construction and is not tested here, so 'any number of colours' is covered only through the general-range mechanism, not through a run of a multi-colour target. 'Rules more complicated than its own' is read as rule tables with more entries than the universal rule's own 19^5-neighbourhood description can be said to have: range-2 two-colour rules have 32 independent entries, already outside what elementary rules can express. The cyclic arrangement of blocks is our choice for a finite run; the note does not specify boundaries.

tests.hypothesis: The explicit cellular-automaton constructions Wolfram publishes for emulating mobile automata, Turing machines, neighbour-independent substitution systems, register machines and logic circuits (NKS notes pp. 1111-1112) reproduce the evolution of every instance of those systems exactly, under the decoding implied by each construction.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Five system types are tested with the rule lists given in the NKS notes, transcribed into analysis.py (first matching rule wins, as in Mathematica). (1) Mobile automata (MAToCA, 4 colours, range 2): all 65536 two-colour mobile automata in Wolfram's {colours, displacements} numbering, from the all-white initial condition and from one seeded random initial condition each; 60 steps; exact if at every step the CA colours mod 2 equal the mobile automaton's cells and the unique dark cell sits at the active position. (2) Turing machines (TMToCA, k(s+1) colours, range 1): all 4096 machines with s = 2, k = 2 and 4096 seeded random machines for each of (s,k) = (3,2), (2,3), (4,2), (3,3), each from a blank tape and from a seeded random tape; 60 steps; exact if tape, head position and head state agree at every step. (3) Substitution systems (SSToCA, 12 colours): all 36 neighbour-independent systems on {0,1} whose two blocks have length 1 or 2, from initial strings {0} and {1}; the CA is run until it has produced 8 'sweep-start' configurations (exactly one r cell, no p or m[0|1] cells), whose decoded strings must equal the substitution system's strings at steps 0..7; a run exceeding 3000 CA steps or reaching the array edge counts as not exact. (4) Register machines (RMToCA, m+7 colours): 300 seeded random programs with m = 2..6 instructions over two registers (i[r], d[r,q]) and initial registers a, b in 0..3, keeping only programs that run at least 20 steps without halting (the construction has no colour for a program counter past the end); the sequence of distinct decoded CA states (program-counter colour, r1 = #(m+2) + 2#(m+3), r2 = #(m+5) + 2#(m+6)) must equal the register machine's trajectory for up to 40 steps. Both the published construction and a one-rule repair described below are run. (5) Logic circuits (the 5-colour rule of p. 1112): 400 seeded random And/Or/Not expressions of depth <= 4 over constants, encoded with the published initial-condition rule and run for the published number of steps; exact if the final configuration has a single non-zero cell equal to 2 for false and 4 for true. The measured value is the number of system types (out of 5) for which 100% of tested instances are emulated exactly, using for register machines the repaired construction. The claim PASSES if the value is 5 and additionally at least 4 of the 5 published constructions are exact as printed.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. If some system type has fewer than 95% exact instances even with the repaired construction the verdict is 'inconclusive' (a failing construction does not show that no construction exists, so an existence claim cannot be refuted this way; reason: construction-failure). If every type is >= 95% but not all are 100%, or if two or more of the published constructions are not exact as printed, the verdict is 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: The claim is existential ('cellular automata can be set up to emulate ...'). The strongest finite test is to take the constructions the book itself supplies, run them against independent direct simulations of each emulated system, and look for counterexamples. Sequential substitution systems, tag systems, the multiplication CA, the RAM emulation and 'a practical computer' are not tested (the first two constructions use symbolic cell states whose decoding is not specified; the last is schematic), so a pass covers five of the eight named system types. Calibration before this pre-registration, disclosed here: the book's own examples (mobile automaton {35,57}, the 3-state Turing machine of p. 78, the substitution system {1 -> 10, 0 -> 01}, the register machine program of p. 99 and eight hand-written logic expressions) were used to fix the decodings. In that calibration the published register-machine construction failed on 14 of 60 and then 26 of 150 random programs. Tracing showed the cause: when an increment instruction fires while the register's only remaining cell is a pending-decrement signal (colour m+1 with background to its left, i.e. register value 0 whose deletion is still in flight), the published rule {_, _, p} -> m+3 converts the signal into an increment signal (worth two cells) instead of one cell. The repair adds one rule per increment instruction, {0, m+1, p} -> m+2 for i[1] and {p, m+4, 0} -> m+5 for i[2], placed before the published rules; 150/150 calibration programs were then exact. The main run uses a fresh seed.

measured.uncertainty: exact-emulation counts per family: MA 131072/131072, TM 40960/40960, SS 72/72 (44/72 under the pre-registered decoder), RM 300/300 repaired (255/300 published), logic 400/400

tests.hypothesis: A one-dimensional cellular automaton of radius r can enlarge the region of non-background cells by at most 2r cells per step (light-cone bound), whereas a neighbour-independent substitution system can multiply its number of elements by a constant factor lambda > 1 per step. Hence for every substitution system with lambda > 1, any emulation in which each element occupies at least one cell needs a number of cellular-automaton steps per substitution step that grows without bound (at least (L_t - L_{t-1})/2r for step t), while Turing machines can be emulated one step per cellular-automaton step.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (A) Light-cone bound: for all 128 elementary rules with quiescent background (000 -> 0), 10 random finite seeds of 20 cells each, 300 steps on a lattice wide enough never to reach the edge, the width of the non-zero region (rightmost minus leftmost black cell plus one) never increases by more than 2 in one step; likewise never by more than 4 for 50 random radius-2 two-colour rules with quiescent background (seeds 0-49), 5 seeds each, 200 steps. (B) Multiplicative growth: among all 225 two-colour neighbour-independent substitution systems with blocks of length 0-3, at least 50% have Perron root lambda > 1 of their 2x2 growth matrix, and for every system the lengths L_t for t <= 12 from a single black cell equal the matrix prediction exactly. (C) Growing cost: for every system with lambda > 1, the number of radius-1 cellular-automaton steps needed to contain L_12 cells starting from L_0 = 1, ceil((L_12 - L_0)/2), exceeds 12 (more than one CA step per substitution step on average), and the per-step requirement c_t = ceil((L_t - L_{t-1})/2) at t = 12 is at least 4 times c_t at t = 4 (progressively more steps). (D) Contrast with Turing machines: a radius-1 cellular automaton with k(s+1) colours (cell = tape colour x {no head, head state}) built mechanically from the Turing-machine rule reproduces the tape and head of 20 random 2-colour, 2-4-state Turing machines exactly at every one of 200 steps. 'Supports' requires A-D.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if A is violated for any rule, seed and step (the fixed-growth premise is false), or if any system with lambda > 1 has ceil((L_12 - L_0)/2) <= 12 (one CA step per substitution step is not excluded by the bound), or if D fails for any machine (Turing machines cannot be emulated step for step either, so the contrast is false). Other combinations are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: The claim is a counting argument. Its premise (fixed growth per CA step) is checked exhaustively over the elementary rules and on random larger-radius rules; the second premise (multiplicative growth of substitution systems) is checked over the complete family of two-colour systems with blocks of length 0-3 (NKS p. 82-83 convention: every element is replaced by the block for its colour; an empty block deletes the element); the conclusion is quantified as the minimal number of CA steps per substitution step under the only assumption that each element occupies at least one cell of the pattern (the encoding Wolfram's figures use; a compressed encoding would fall outside the claim's 'size of a pattern' reasoning). The clause 'unlike ... Turing machines' is checked by an explicit one-step-per-step construction (NKS p. 657). Computational; all programs generated by analysis.py.

measured.unit: minimum over growing substitution systems of radius-1 CA steps needed to hold 12 substitution steps of growth (threshold 12)
measured.uncertainty: exact (deterministic)

tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, every neighbour-independent substitution system in a complete enumerated family (2 colours with replacement blocks of length 1-3; 3 colours with blocks of length 1-2) produces, from a single cell, a sequence whose subword complexity stays bounded (repetitive) or grows at most polynomially slowly (nested), far below the near-exponential subword complexity of rule 30's rows and centre column, so none of them can reproduce rule 30; while a neighbour-dependent substitution system (one output cell per cell, chosen from the cell and its two neighbours) reproduces rules 90 and 30 exactly.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For each of the 196 two-colour rules {0 -> w0, 1 -> w1} with |w0|, |w1| in {1,2,3} and each of the 1728 three-colour rules with block lengths in {1,2}, start from a single cell of colour 1 and iterate until the word has >= L = 131072 symbols (or 60 steps if it never does), truncate to L, and compute the number p(n) of distinct length-n factors for n = 1..14. For rule 30 from a single black cell compute p(14) of (i) the central 40001 cells of the row at step 20000 and (ii) the first 65536 cells of the centre column. Build the neighbour-dependent substitution system whose rule maps each cell to one new cell given by the elementary-CA table of its (left, self, right) neighbourhood, and run it for 1000 steps from a single black cell. PASS (supports) if (a) every neighbour-independent rule has p(14) <= 225 = (14+1)^2 (eventually periodic words are those with p(14) = p(13); the rest are counted as nested), (b) both rule 30 sequences have p(14) >= 2000, and (c) the neighbour-dependent systems for rules 90 and 30 reproduce the cellular-automaton rows exactly at every one of the 1000 steps.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if any neighbour-independent rule in the family has p(14) >= 2000 (rule-30-like complexity), or if the neighbour-dependent construction does not reproduce rule 90 or rule 30. If some neighbour-independent rule has 225 < p(14) < 2000 the result is 'mixed' and the rule is reported with its complexity profile.
tests.interpretation: 'Repetitive' is operationalised as eventually periodic (bounded subword complexity, Morse-Hedlund), 'nested' as a self-similar word, which for fixed points of morphisms has subword complexity O(n^2) at most (Pansiot); the threshold (n+1)^2 at n = 14 is therefore a generous upper bound for repetitive-or-nested and about a tenth of what a random-like binary sequence of this length shows. 'Cannot emulate rule 30' is tested within the enumerated family by the complexity gap (a word with p(14) <= 225 cannot contain the rule 30 row, whose own p(14) is measured); it is not a proof over all encodings. The neighbour-dependent half is tested exactly as the book describes it (rules 'always yielding just one cell and corresponding quite directly to cellular automata', p. 666).

tests.hypothesis: For at least one of the system types named in the claim (Turing machines), a single uniform construction turns any one-dimensional cellular automaton rule (any number of colours k, any radius r) into a Turing machine that emulates it exactly; applied to rule 110 the construction yields an explicit Turing machine, which is then universal by the universality of rule 110 (Cook, Complex Systems 15 (2004) 1-40), so the system type contains a universal member as the claim asserts.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. analysis.py builds, for a given (k, r, rule table), a Turing machine whose tape holds the cellular-automaton configuration on W cells between two end-marker symbols, and whose head performs one left-to-right sweep (reading each old cell value once, carrying the last 2r old values in its state, stepping back r cells to write the new value) followed by a return to the left end, so that one round trip equals one cellular-automaton step with fixed white (0) boundaries. The machine must be a genuine finite table: every (state, symbol) pair reachable in the runs has exactly one transition writing one symbol and moving one cell. Tests: (a) all 256 elementary rules (k = 2, r = 1), W = 48, 40 steps, two random initial conditions each (seed 20261110); (b) 100 random 3-colour radius-1 rules (k = 3, r = 1), same W and steps; (c) 50 random 2-colour radius-2 rules (k = 2, r = 2); (d) 20 random 4-colour radius-1 rules and 10 random 3-colour radius-2 rules. After every round trip the tape between the markers is compared cell-for-cell with the directly computed cellular-automaton configuration (fixed-0 boundary). 'supports' if the total number of mismatching cells over all runs is 0 and the rule-110 machine is produced with a finite, fully specified state table (its state count and transition count reported).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any run produces a mismatch (one or more cells differing from the direct evolution) that cannot be traced to a bug in the harness rather than the construction; since the construction is uniform in (k, r, rule), a single irreparable mismatch shows the uniform construction does not emulate every cellular automaton. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the harness cannot complete the runs within the time budget.
tests.interpretation: The claim is a logical implication (if a system type can emulate every cellular automaton and a universal cellular automaton exists, the type has universal members). The implication itself is not empirical; what can be checked computationally is its first premise for a concrete system type. We check it for Turing machines, the second family named in the claim, by implementing a uniform emulation construction (the sweeping-head scheme NKS describes for Turing machines emulating cellular automata, p. 665-666, written here from scratch rather than copied) and testing it exhaustively on the elementary rules and on random rules with more colours and larger neighbourhoods. The second premise (existence of a universal cellular automaton) is taken from the published proof that rule 110 is universal; it is not re-derived. The other families in the claim (mobile automata, substitution systems, tag and cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems, register machines) are not tested here, so a 'supports' verdict confirms the claim's structure for one family only.

measured.unit: mismatching cells between Turing-machine tape and direct cellular-automaton evolution, summed over all runs
measured.uncertainty: exact (deterministic comparison)

tests.hypothesis: For any two-register machine in Wolfram's sense (program of L instructions, each 'increment register r and go to the next instruction' or 'if register r is nonzero decrement it and jump to instruction j, else go to the next instruction', cyclic program), there is an arithmetic system n -> (p*n + q)/s whose branch is chosen by n mod 6L such that, with the state (i, a, b) encoded as n = i + L * 2^a * 3^b (Wolfram's encoding on p. 673 with L = 5 and modulus 30), the integer trajectory decodes step for step to the register machine's trajectory.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. analysis.py compiles each register machine into the remainder-selected arithmetic map, then runs machine and map side by side. Test set: (a) all 200 register machines drawn with numpy seed 20261111 from the family with L = 5 and two registers (instruction type, register and jump target uniform), each from the state (1, 0, 0) and from one random state with registers in [0, 20], for 10000 steps; (b) three hand-written programs with L in {3, 5, 7} that move or copy register contents so that the registers grow without bound, 20000 steps each. 'supports' if at every step of every run the decoded (i, a, b) equals the directly simulated register-machine state (0 mismatches out of all compared steps) and, as a check that the comparison can fail, a deliberately perturbed map (one branch's additive constant changed by 1) produces a mismatch within 10000 steps on at least one of the hand-written programs. Universality of the arithmetic systems then follows from the universality of two-register machines (Minsky 1967), which is cited, not tested.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any run of the correctly compiled map disagrees with the register machine at any step. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the perturbation check fails to produce a mismatch (the comparison would then be too weak to count).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'system that takes a whole number, computes Mod[n, 30], and applies one of several arithmetic operations chosen by that remainder' is the family of generalised Collatz maps n -> (p*n + q)/s with the branch chosen by n mod M. The specific register machine of Wolfram's figure is not transcribed in the online text, so instead of checking his single example the test checks the general construction he describes (encoding n = i + L * 2^a * 3^b, modulus 6L; for L = 5 this is his modulus 30) on a random sample of register machines plus growth programs. Register-machine conventions follow NKS Chapter 3 (pp. 97-102): decrement of a zero register is a no-op that moves to the next instruction, and the program wraps around cyclically. The 'therefore universal' clause is a theorem of Minsky's and is outside what this computation establishes.

measured.unit: steps at which the arithmetic-system value differs from the encoding of the register-machine state
measured.uncertainty: exact integer arithmetic; none

tests.hypothesis: Rule 110 is computationally universal (Cook 2004, Complex Systems 15(1):1-40, doi:10.25088/ComplexSystems.15.1.1). Universality itself is a theorem that no finite simulation can establish, so this test checks the empirical premise the claim rests on: that rule 110 'naturally' produces, from random initial conditions, a background ether with the (time, space) periodicity lattice spanned by (3, 2) and (4, -2) (spatial period 14, temporal period 7), and persistent localized structures (gliders) whose space-time periods are exactly those tabulated by Cook (Figure 5): A (3, 2), B (4, -2), B-bar/B-hat (12, -6), C1-C3 (7, 0), D1-D2 (10, 2), E^n (15, -4), E-bar (30, -8), F (36, -4), G^n (42, -14), H (92, -18); in particular the classes used as components in Cook's construction (C2 tape data, E-bar table data, A moving data, E leaders) must occur.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: simulate rule 110 on rings of 1200 cells from 60 uniformly random initial rows (numpy default_rng seed 20261031) for 4000 steps. Ether cells are those whose 7 x 14 neighbourhood is invariant under the lattice translation (t, x) -> (t + 1, x - 4). In rows t = 3000..3900 (every 100 steps), maximal runs of non-ether cells of width <= 60 are 'structures'. For each structure, search for the smallest temporal period P <= 100 and shift |s| <= 50 such that the window (structure plus 14 cells of ether on each side) reappears exactly at (t + P, x + s). Component premise confirmed if: (1) the ether, i.e. the (3,2)/(4,-2) lattice, covers more than 50% of the cells at t >= 3000 in every run; (2) at least 90% of structures resolve to a period, and every resolved period (P, s) is a positive integer combination of Cook's A and B periods that coincides with one of Cook's tabulated glider periods (allowing the period to be a positive integer multiple of a tabulated one, for packets such as A^n); (3) the classes A, B, C, D, E and E-bar are each observed at least once. Because the test replays only the glider inventory and not the cyclic-tag-system emulation, the verdict when all three conditions hold is pre-declared as 'inconclusive' with reason 'not-operationalizable' (universality is settled by proof, not by this computation), with the component results reported as supporting evidence.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: 'refutes' if the standard ether does not form (condition 1 fails in a majority of runs), or if the A, C or E-bar classes (the data carriers of Cook's construction) are never observed in 60 random runs, or if resolved structures have space-time periods incompatible with Cook's table (a period that is not an integer combination of (3, 2) and (4, -2) would contradict his lattice argument). Such results would undermine the published construction that the claim cites and would be reported as 'refutes' of the component premise with confidence <= 0.6, since a construction could in principle use rarer gliders.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's claim is a theorem (Cook's proof, presented in NKS pp. 678-689 and published in 2004). The test does not re-derive the proof or replay the cyclic tag system emulation, which requires Cook's specific glider packets and spacings; it checks the computational premise that rule 110 has a stable ether and naturally occurring gliders with the stated periods, which is the part of the claim that is accessible to a few minutes of simulation. The glider table is taken from Figure 5 of Cook's paper (retrieved PDF; checksum recorded); 'period' is Cook's (time, horizontal displacement) pair for one repetition of the glider.

measured.unit: resolved isolated structures (out of 2674) whose minimal space-time period is not one of Cook's tabulated glider periods
measured.uncertainty: exact

tests.hypothesis: Every elementary cellular automaton that settles into a uniform or short-period state from random initial conditions (operational class 1 or 2) transmits a single-cell perturbation of that settled state only over a bounded distance, whereas rules that do not settle spread perturbations without bound.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all 256 elementary CA rules. For each rule, 10 trials: ring of N = 800 cells, random initial condition with density 1/2 (numpy default_rng seed 20261033), evolve 1000 steps to configuration C; the trial is 'settled' if C recurs within the next 64 steps (temporal period <= 64, which includes uniform and shifted-periodic states). A rule is 'operational class 1/2' if >= 9 of 10 trials settle. In every settled trial, flip one cell of C (the cell at index 400) and evolve both copies 400 further steps on the ring (N = 800 > 2 x 400, so the damage cannot wrap); record the damage width w = rightmost - leftmost differing cell + 1 (0 if none). A rule is 'bounded' if w <= 20 in all of its settled trials, 'spreading' if the median w over settled trials >= 100 (linear growth), otherwise 'intermediate'. The claim PASSES if 100% of operational class 1/2 rules are 'bounded'. Validation (reported, not decisive): the rules Wikipedia cites as Wolfram's class 1 and 2 examples (0, 32, 160, 232; 4, 108, 218, 250) must be operational class 1/2 and the class 3 and 4 examples (22, 30, 126, 150, 182; 110, 54) must not be; and the fraction of non-settled rules that are 'spreading' is reported.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if any operational class 1/2 rule is 'spreading' (a settled rule that nevertheless transmits a perturbation over a linearly growing region). If some class 1/2 rules are 'intermediate' but none 'spreading', the verdict is 'mixed'. If the Wikipedia example rules are misclassified by the operational definition, that is reported as a caveat on the mapping to Wolfram's phenomenological classes but does not change the verdict.
tests.interpretation: The claim has a conclusion (class 1 and 2 automata cannot be universal) and a stated mechanism ('never allow any transmission of information except over limited distances'). Non-universality is a statement about all possible encodings and is not testable by finite computation; the test addresses the mechanism, which is the premise of Wolfram's argument: perturbations of class 1/2 states stay localized. Wolfram's classes are phenomenological, so they are operationalised here as 'settles into a temporal cycle of period <= 64 on an 800-cell ring within 1000 steps from random initial conditions'; the damage width (not displacement) is used so that shifting class-2 rules, whose perturbation moves but does not grow, count as bounded, as the assessors noted. Perturbations are applied to the settled state because the claim concerns the asymptotic behaviour, not transients.

measured.unit: fraction of operational class 1/2 rules whose settled-state perturbation stays bounded (width <= 20 after 400 steps)
measured.uncertainty: 96 operational class 1/2 rules; 94 bounded, 2 intermediate, 0 spreading

tests.hypothesis: If the claim's premise holds, every additive elementary cellular automaton (the eight rules linear over GF(2): 0, 60, 90, 102, 150, 170, 204, 240) satisfies, for every initial condition and every k, that the configuration after 2^k steps is exactly the XOR superposition of copies of the initial condition shifted by 2^k times the offsets in the rule's support (rule 90: offsets -1 and +1; rule 150: -1, 0, +1); the empirical additivity screen picks out exactly these rules; the class-3/4 rules the book contrasts them with (18, 22, 30, 45, 54, 73, 110, 122) never return to such a superposition form at any power-of-two step; and the nested single-cell patterns of rules 90 and 150 have row populations matching the independently tabulated OEIS sequences A001316 and A071053.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (a) For each of the eight linear rules, each cyclic lattice size N in {1023, 2048}, 20 seeded random initial conditions of density 1/2 plus the single-cell initial condition, and each k = 0..10, the configuration after 2^k steps equals bit-for-bit the XOR of the initial condition shifted by d*2^k over the offsets d in the rule's support (the support is read off the rule table as the cells on which the one-step response to a single 1 is nonzero). (b) An additivity screen T(x xor y) = T(x) xor T(y) on 200 seeded random pairs at N = 256 identifies exactly the eight linear rules, and the affine screen T(x xor y) = T(x) xor T(y) xor T(0) exactly the eight linear plus the eight complementary rules (255, 195, 165, 153, 105, 85, 51, 15). (c) For each of the eight control rules 18, 22, 30, 45, 54, 73, 110, 122 and each k = 0..8, the 2^k-step map fails additivity on at least one of 50 seeded random pairs at N = 256 (so the state after 2^k steps is not a superposition of shifted copies of the initial condition for generic initial conditions). (d) The number of nonzero cells in row t of the single-cell pattern of rule 90 (t = 0..T) equals term t of OEIS A001316 and that of rule 150 equals term t of A071053, for every term available in the OEIS b-files up to t = 4095 (the b-files are fetched and their sha256 recorded). PASS (supports the claim's checkable premise) if (a), (b), (c) and (d) all hold. The non-universality conclusion itself is a proof-type statement (a map that is linear over GF(2) at every power-of-two step cannot emulate the non-linear behaviour an arbitrary computation requires under the encodings the book considers) and is not decided by this test; its evidential weight is recorded in the confidence.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes the premise) if (a) fails for any linear rule, k, lattice size or initial condition (the stated superposition property is false), or if (d) fails for rule 90 or rule 150 (the single-cell patterns are not the nested patterns the claim describes). MIXED if (a) and (d) hold but (b) or (c) fails (the superposition property is true of rules 90 and 150 but does not cleanly separate additive from complex rules as the book's argument requires). INCONCLUSIVE with reason data-unavailable only for part (d) if the OEIS b-files cannot be retrieved; (a)-(c) are then still reported and the verdict rests on them with reduced confidence.
tests.interpretation: The claim bundles a precise mathematical premise (power-of-two-step superposition for additive rules) with an informal class ('essentially nested' rules) and a non-universality conclusion. The test checks the premise exactly, checks that it discriminates additive rules from the complex rules the book contrasts them with, and cross-checks the nested single-cell patterns against externally tabulated sequences (Gould's sequence for rule 90, and the rule-150 analogue). It does not prove non-universality; a rule's universality depends on permitted encodings and no finite computation can exclude it, so 'supports' here means the premise and the discriminating contrast hold, not that the conclusion has been verified.

measured.unit: failures of the power-of-two-step superposition identity over 3696 (rule, lattice, initial condition, k) checks for the eight additive rules
measured.uncertainty: exact bitwise comparison

tests.hypothesis: Rule 54, run from each of the first N initial conditions (binary digits of n on a white background, as in NKS p. 697), produces only repetitive or nested patterns: none has the local space-time complexity characteristic of class 3 or class 4 behaviour.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Family: initial conditions n = 1..65536 (16 bits), cell values = binary digits of n placed on an infinite white background (validated against the figure: n = 1 single cell, n = 3 two cells, n = 291 nested); rule 54 run for T = 256 steps on a lattice wide enough that the light cone never reaches the edge. Classifier (frozen before the census): the number D of distinct 6 x 6 space-time tiles whose top-left corner lies in rows 128..250 and inside the light cone (plus 2 cells) of the pattern. Calibration on controls outside the family, disclosed: repetitive and nested rules give D <= 1007 (rule 90 single cell 115, random 14-bit seeds 267-395; rule 150 single 316, random seeds 804-1007; rule 22 single 119; rule 18 random 309-602; rules 250, 108, 184, 62, 41 random 1-178), while class 3/4 controls give D >= 1094 (rule 110 random 14- and 30-bit seeds 1094-1553; rule 30 6801-7166; rule 45 6338-6401), with a few class-3 rules from narrow seeds in between (rule 106: 462 and 2912; rule 126: 130-402; rule 146: 371-413; rule 73: 64-774). The eight rule-54 patterns shown in the book's figure (n = 1, 3, 75, 259, 291, 787, 803, 56549) give D = 10, 37, 315, 315, 286, 391, 391, 370, and a batch of 256 random 14-bit seeds gave max 391. Threshold: D > 1050 (geometric midpoint of 1007 and 1094) = 'more complicated'. Also recorded per initial condition: exact temporal periodicity (period <= 16) of the pattern's core over steps 128..256 ('repetitive'). The claim PASSES if 0 of the 65536 initial conditions has D > 1050. Reported, not decisive: the distribution of D, the fraction that is exactly periodic, the number with D > 700 (a stricter threshold that still clears all rule-54 book examples), and for any initial condition above threshold a re-run with T = 512.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if at least one initial condition n <= 65536 has D > 1050 and the T = 512 re-run also gives D > 1050 (sustained local complexity comparable to the class 3/4 controls). If some exceed 1050 at T = 256 but not at T = 512 the verdict is 'mixed' (transient complexity). The census is 1/1526 of the book's 10^8 initial conditions; a pass is consistent with the claim but far from exhausting it.
tests.interpretation: The claim is a finite observational statement about the first 10^8 initial conditions; the full census is beyond a few minutes of Python, so this is a scaled census (2^16 initial conditions) with the book's informal judgement 'nothing fundamentally more complicated than repetitive or nested' frozen into a local-complexity classifier. The classifier counts distinct 6 x 6 space-time tiles in the second half of the evolution: self-similar (nested) and periodic patterns have bounded tile vocabularies, whereas class 3 patterns have thousands and class 4 patterns with interacting gliders over a thousand. The threshold was set from controls outside the rule-54 family plus the book's own eight rule-54 examples; it is admittedly coarse, and the random-seed rule 150 controls (nested, up to 1007) show that nested patterns with wide seeds approach it. A failure under this classifier would therefore need the T = 512 confirmation and visual inspection before being read as a counterexample to Wolfram's census.

measured.unit: number of initial conditions n <= 65536 whose rule-54 pattern has more than 1050 distinct 6x6 tiles in steps 128-256
measured.uncertainty: exhaustive over n = 1..65535 (n = 65536 has 17 bits and was not included)

tests.hypothesis: With a single-step block-emulation scheme of the kind shown on NKS pp. 703-705 (fixed background blocks of width w between single input cells, t steps of the underlying rule, output read at a fixed offset), the underlying rules 22, 30 and 110 can realise, as the induced map from (x[i-1], x[i], x[i+1]) to the output under cell i, every one of the 256 elementary rules once w is large enough, whereas rules 90 and 184 realise only a small number of them at the same widths.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Scheme: the initial condition is periodic with period w+1: one input cell x[i] in {0,1} followed by a fixed background block B in {0,1}^w. The underlying rule f is run for t steps with w+1 <= t <= 2w+2 and the output for cell i is read at offset d in 0..w to the right of x[i]'s position. For each (w, B, t, d) the output is computed for all 32 assignments of (x[i-2], ..., x[i+2]) in a window padded on both sides with t+2 further background cells (input positions in the padding set to 0; they lie outside the light cone). If the output depends only on (x[i-1], x[i], x[i+1]) (the 4 assignments of the outer inputs agree for each of the 8 inner triples), the induced 3-input truth table is an elementary rule g that f emulates for one step at width w. E(f, W) = the set of g realised for some w <= W. Widths searched: W = 1..6. 'supports' if |E(f, 6)| = 256 for each f in {22, 30, 110} and |E(f, 6)| <= 32 for each f in {90, 184}.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if |E(90, 6)| >= 128 or |E(184, 6)| >= 128 (a 'simple' rule emulates at least half of all elementary rules), or if min over f in {22, 30, 110} of |E(f, 6)| is smaller than max over f in {90, 184} of |E(f, 6)| (the contrast is reversed). 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if neither condition holds, e.g. because 22, 30 or 110 do not reach 256 within W = 6 under this scheme: Wolfram's figure uses a scheme whose exact readout and width conventions are not fully recoverable from the online text, so a shortfall under the reconstructed scheme does not refute the claim. In every case the counts for all 256 underlying rules at W = 6 are reported.
tests.interpretation: The claim concerns one-step emulation under block encodings, which Wolfram himself distinguishes from universality. The test reconstructs the p. 703-704 scheme from its caption (fixed initial conditions except at input positions; blocks of 3 cells between inputs for the rule 30 to Xor example; blocks 5 cells wide for all 256 rules) with the output position and step count as free parameters searched over a bounded range. 'A few' is given the threshold 32 of 256 (one eighth). Positive emulations are exact finite certificates; negative counts are relative to the scheme and the searched widths. All computation is in analysis.py; there is no external download.

measured.unit: number of the 256 elementary rules emulated for one step with background width <= 6 (pre-registered range)
measured.uncertainty: exhaustive within the reconstructed scheme and searched range; none

tests.hypothesis: The 2-state, 5-colour Turing machine whose rule is drawn on NKS p. 707, started as described in the note 'Rule 110 Turing machines' (p. 1119: tape = Prepend[4 list, 0] with colour 1 to the left and colour 0 to the right, head on the first tape element in state 1), emulates rule 110: successive 'new rightmost head position' snapshots of the tape, decoded as colour 4 -> black and all other colours -> white, are successive steps of rule 110 applied to the initial list on a white background. Given Cook's published proof that rule 110 is universal, the machine is universal.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using the rule table transcribed from the p. 707 figure (10 cases; the transcription is recorded in derived/tm25-rule.json), for the single-cell initial list and for 40 random binary lists of length 10-60 (numpy default_rng seeds 0..39), with a fixed integer offset c determined once from the single-cell run and then held fixed, the k-th new-rightmost snapshot decoded as above equals rule-110 iterate k-c of the initial list for every k from c to c+199, on every cell of the window spanning the full rule-110 pattern (100% of 41 x 200 snapshot comparisons). 'Supports' if this holds.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if for any initial list some snapshot differs from the corresponding rule-110 iterate, or if no fixed offset makes the single-cell run match; 'inconclusive / not-operationalizable' if the rule table cannot be read unambiguously from the published figure.
tests.interpretation: The claim has two parts: (i) the 2-state 5-colour machine emulates rule 110 one step per complete sweep, which is tested directly by simulation; (ii) universality follows from (i) and the universality of rule 110 (Cook 2004, Complex Systems 15(1), doi:10.25088/ComplexSystems.15.1.1), which is taken as a published premise and not re-proved here. 'Complete sweep' is operationalized as the moment the head reaches a position further right than ever before (the convention of Wolfram's compressed picture). The rule table is only published as a picture; it was transcribed from the figure's grey levels and arrow orientations (white=0, lightest grey=1, ..., darkest grey=4; the head arrow pointing down is state 1 because that is the state in which the published initial condition yields rule 110, pointing up is state 2). The number of states and colours in the table (2 and 5) is also checked.

tests.hypothesis: Every one of the 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colours (Wolfram's convention: each (state, colour) maps to (new colour, new state, move left/right); no halt state) has behaviour that from every finite initial condition becomes eventually periodic, possibly with a drifting head (a 'glider'), after a short transient. Since a universal machine must have initial conditions whose evolution is not eventually periodic (otherwise every question about its evolution is decidable), such a classification is strong evidence that none is universal.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For each of the 4096 machines and each initial condition in the set I = {every binary tape string of length 1-7 with the head on each of its cells, in each of the 2 states} (1284 initial conditions per machine) plus 100 random tapes of length 16-32 per machine (seeded), simulate on an infinite blank (0) tape for up to 10000 steps and classify the evolution exactly as (A) eventually periodic modulo translation: the head-relative configuration (state, tape between the outermost non-zero cells, head offset) recurs exactly, which implies periodic evolution forever; or (B) escaping: the head is beyond all non-zero cells, moving outward over blank cells, and the same state occurs twice during that outward run, which implies it moves outward forever. 'Supports' if 100% of the (machine, initial condition) pairs are classified as (A) or (B) within 10000 steps, and the largest period found is at most 1000 steps. The symmetry-reduced count of distinct machines (state relabelling, colour swap, reflection) is also computed and compared with Wolfram's 560 as a consistency check on the enumeration.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The test cannot establish universality, so 'refutes' is not reachable by this computation alone. 'Mixed' if any (machine, initial condition) pair is unclassified after 10000 steps (unbounded non-periodic behaviour within the tested inputs, which would be at least consistent with the complexity universality needs) or if periods above 1000 steps occur. 'Supports' otherwise.
tests.interpretation: 'Too simple to support universality' is operationalized as: every tested evolution is provably eventually periodic (with or without drift), established by exact recurrence detection rather than by visual inspection. This is necessary-condition evidence: universality requires some input with a non-eventually-periodic evolution, and the tested inputs cover all short tapes exhaustively plus random longer ones, but not all inputs; a proof for all inputs would need a per-machine argument. The convention follows NKS p. 78 and the note 'Turing machine enumeration' (p. 1120): machines never halt, and all 4096 = 8^4 rule tables are counted. The search program is in C (compiled by analysis.py with gcc) for speed; this tooling deviation is recorded.

measured.unit: fraction of the 13,008,896 (machine, initial condition) runs classified exactly as eventually periodic (A) or escaping (B) within 10000 steps (pre-registered threshold 1.0)
measured.uncertainty: exact for A and B; C, D and E are heuristic pattern fits (see caveats)
