tests.hypothesis: Under Wolfram's evaluation scheme (one Mathematica-style /. pass of the S and K rules per step), the size-7 expression s[s[s]][s][s][s][s] grows exponentially in leaf count without reaching a fixed point, a small number of the 109,824 size-8 expressions also grow without bound, and the combinator w given in the note 'Cellular automaton combinators' (NKS p. 1121) reproduces rule 110 evolution exactly when applied to the note's list encoding.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (A) Growth: evolve s[s[s]][s][s][s][s] for 40 steps, each step = one ReplaceAll pass of {s[x][y][z] -> x[z][y[z]], k[x][y] -> x} (outermost subexpression first, no re-scan of replaced parts, heads and arguments visited); PASS-A if no fixed point is reached and a least-squares fit of log2(LeafCount) against step over steps 10..40 has slope in [0.45, 0.55] (book: growth like 2^(t/2)) with R^2 >= 0.99. (B) Census (reported, not decisive): evolve all 109,824 size-8 S/K expressions for up to 60 steps or until LeafCount > 20,000; record how many reach a fixed point, how many exceed 20,000 leaves (unbounded/exponential candidates), and the remainder; the book reports 49 with exponential growth. (C) Emulation: implement ToC bracket abstraction, p, num, inc, cr and w exactly as printed in the note; encode every binary list of length 3, 4 and 5 (56 lists) with p[num[Length]][Fold[p[Nest[s,k,#2]][#1]&, p[k][k], list]] fully normalised; apply w once, twice and three times (full normalisation by iterated ReplaceAll after each application); decode by applying the pair selectors (p[a][b][s[k]] -> a, p[a][b][k] -> b) and normalising; PASS-C if for all 56 lists and all t in 1..3 the decoded list equals t steps of rule 110 applied to the list padded with one 0 on each side per step (length n + 2t). The claim PASSES if PASS-A and PASS-C both hold (the growth and the emulation components, which are what the book presents as evidence); the census (B) and any descriptive statistics of internal structure are reported only.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if the size-7 expression reaches a fixed point or its growth is not exponential (slope outside [0.45, 0.55] or R^2 < 0.99), or if the published w combinator does not reproduce rule 110 for every tested list and step count. If w cannot be transcribed unambiguously from the note (the HTML lost the rule arrows) the emulation component is inconclusive (other) and the verdict rests on (A) as 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: The claim has three parts: simple rules (two rewrite rules), highly complex behaviour (illustrated by exponential growth of a tiny expression and irregular size sequences), and the ability to emulate rule 110. The first two are tested through the book's own exhibit (the shortest unboundedly growing expression) and the exhaustive size-8 census; 'seemingly random internal structure' is not given a decisive statistical test here because the structures involved have at most a few hundred steps, too short for the compression-based criteria used elsewhere; it is reported descriptively. The emulation is tested as an exact computational reproduction of the published construction. Evaluation order follows the book's note 'Combinator properties' (expr /. crules per step); fixed points do not depend on order (Church-Rosser) but intermediate sizes do.

measured.unit: pre-registered components A and C (C under the pre-registered reading and under the alternative reading of 'padding with 0 on either side')

size7_validation.book_values: all but 2 of 16,896 reach fixed points in at most 12 steps; largest fixed point 41

tests.hypothesis: For elementary rules 60 and 188 started from a single black cell, the colour of the cell at position x after t steps is a 2-automatic function of (t, x): a fixed finite automaton reading the base-2 digits of t and x in parallel (one digit pair per step, hence about log2(t) steps) outputs the colour, and this automaton can be constructed from the pattern and reproduces it exactly, including at times not used in its construction.
tests.pass: Pre-registered, for each of rules 60 and 188: (i) the number of distinct 2-kernel elements A(2^k t + r, 2^k x + s), compared on a 64 x 64 window, saturates: the cumulative count over levels k <= 5 equals the cumulative count over all levels k <= K - 6 of a 2^K x 2^K pattern with K = 11 (i.e. no new element appears beyond level 5), and that count is at most 64; (ii) the finite automaton whose states are those kernel elements and whose transitions on a digit pair (dt, dx) go from element (k, r, s) to (k+1, r + 2^k dt, s + 2^k dx) is consistent (every representative of a state yields the same target state for each digit pair) and, run on the least-significant-first binary digits of (t, x), reproduces 100% of the cells of an independently evolved 2^12 x 2^12 pattern (t < 4096), three quarters of which lie outside the K = 11 construction range; (iii) the number of automaton steps for a cell at time t equals the number of binary digits of t, i.e. floor(log2 t) + 1.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: for rule 60 or rule 188 the kernel count keeps growing beyond level 5 (no saturation) or exceeds 64, or the automaton is inconsistent, or any cell of the 2^12 x 2^12 pattern disagrees with the automaton's output. Control rules 30 and 110 (not nested) are expected to fail (i) and (ii); if they passed, the test would be too weak and the verdict would be 'inconclusive' with reason 'not-operationalizable'.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's statement (p. 744) is that the colour of a cell of rule 60 or rule 188 after t steps can be found by a cellular automaton acting on the base-2 digit sequences of the cell's coordinates (6 colours for rule 60, 12 for rule 188) in about log2(t) steps instead of t steps. The finite-automaton formulation used here is equivalent: a two-dimensional pattern computable from the binary digits of (t, x) by a finite-state device is a 2-automatic double sequence, whose characterization (Cobham, Salon) is finiteness of its 2-kernel; the automaton's step count is the number of digit pairs, floor(log2 t) + 1. The exact state counts Wolfram quotes (6 and 12) refer to his particular digit-CA encoding and are not tested; only the existence of a finite digit automaton and its logarithmic step count are. Rules 60 and 188 both grow only to the right from a single black cell at x = 0, so A(t, x) is defined for 0 <= x <= t and taken as 0 for x > t. For the controls, the right half (x >= 0) of rule 30, 90 and 150 and the mirror image of rule 110 are used. The clause 'nested patterns generally' is addressed only through rules 90 and 150 as further nested examples.

measured.unit: cells (of 2 x 16,777,216) where the digit automaton disagrees with direct evolution, rules 60 and 188
measured.uncertainty: exact

extra.automaton_steps_per_cell: bitlen(t) = floor(log2 t) + 1 digit pairs (12 for t = 4095) versus 4095 direct evolution steps

tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, when all 4096 two-state two-colour Turing machines are run under the book's one-sided convention on every input x with up to 10 binary digits, the maximum halting time T(n) over inputs of length n is, for every machine (and every distinct function/time pair), either constant, linear, quadratic or exponential in n, and every function computed with exponential T(n) is also computed by some two-state two-colour machine with constant T(n).
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Conventions from NKS pp. 761 and 1143: tape cells i = 1, 2, ... hold the binary digits of x with the least significant digit at i = 1 (x = 0 is the single digit 0), all other cells 0; head starts at i = 1 in state 1; a step applies the rule (new state, new colour, displacement d) and moves the head to i - d; the computation is complete at the first step t at which i = 0; the output f(x) is the tape read as a binary number. Machines are numbered with the NKS scheme (p. 888). Inputs x = 0..1023 (lengths n = 1..10). Non-halting is established by (i) a cycle of states that keeps moving left on blank cells once the head is left of every visited cell, (ii) exact repetition of the configuration (Brent's algorithm), or (iii) a cutoff of 20000 steps. For each machine and each distinct (f, t) pair over x = 0..1023, T(n) = max t(x) over halting x of length n. Growth class on n = 3..10, requiring halting inputs at >= 5 of these lengths (otherwise 'insufficient'): exact fit (max residual < 1e-9) tried in the order constant, linear a+bn (b>0), quadratic a+bn+cn^2 (c>0), exponential a*2^n+b (a>0); if none is exact, the lowest-complexity of linear, quadratic, exponential (a*c^n+b, c in {2,3,4}) whose relative RMS residual over n = 3..10 is <= 0.15; else 'other'. PASS (supports) if (a) no (f, t) pair with sufficient data is classed 'other', and (b) for every exponential pair the same function f (as a map on x = 0..1023 including where it is undefined) is computed by at least one machine whose pair is classed constant. The book's census numbers (748 never halt / 3348 sometimes / 1683 always; 351 functions, 149 total; 492 (f,t) pairs; 164 constant, 295 linear, 27 quadratic, 6 exponential; machines 378, 1953, 2289 exponential with total functions; the formulas for machines 3279, 1285, 3333, 261, 1447, 1953, 1969, 3517, 3246, 3374) are recorded as cross-checks of the implementation and do not decide the verdict.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if some (f, t) pair with sufficient data has a growth class other than constant, linear, quadratic or exponential and this is confirmed when the machine is rerun on x up to 2^14 - 1 with cutoff 2^20 steps (e.g. a cubic or super-exponential fit is best), or if some exponential pair has no constant-time partner computing the same function. MIXED if 'other' pairs exist but on the extended inputs fit one of the four classes within tolerance, or if the cross-check numbers disagree with the book in a way that indicates a convention mismatch.
tests.interpretation: The claim is a census statement under a specific computational convention (head leaves the right end), which the book's notes state precisely and which is implemented literally. 'Rate of growth' is finite-sample: classes are assigned from n = 3..10 by exact or near-exact fits, which cannot prove asymptotics but follow the book's own method of reading growth from short inputs. 'The same function' is tested on the same finite input range including the halting/non-halting pattern.

measured.unit: distinct (function, halting-time) pairs with exponential maximum halting time, of 493 pairs over 4096 machines
measured.uncertainty: exact enumeration up to the 20000-step cutoff (224573 of 4194304 machine-input pairs hit it and are counted as non-halting)

remaining_other_under_parity_fit.2242: T(odd n) = 29, 53, 89, 129, 181, 237; T(even n) = 17, 41, 73, 113, 165, 221: quadratic growth with a period-4 modulation
remaining_other_under_parity_fit.2439: T = 15, 51, 39, 87, 71, 127, 111, 179, 163, 235, 219, 303 for n = 3..14: quadratic growth with a period-4 modulation

tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, then for every length-preserving involution 'negation' on binary strings and every set S of strings of a given length that a multiway system could eventually generate, S is complete (every string or its negation is in S) and consistent (no string together with its negation is in S) if and only if |S| is exactly half of all strings of that length; in particular more than half implies inconsistent and less than half implies incomplete.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Part 1 (sets): for length n = 3, enumerate all 764 involutions of the 8 strings and all 256 subsets S; for n = 4, take 300 pseudo-random involutions of the 16 strings (numpy seed 20261031, including the complement map, reversal and the identity-on-some-strings cases) and all 65536 subsets. For each (involution, S) record complete, consistent, |S| versus half. Part 2 (multiway systems): enumerate all multiway systems over {A,B} with one or two rules lhs -> rhs, |lhs| in {1,2}, |rhs| in {|lhs|, |lhs|+1} (length-non-decreasing so that the set of generated strings of each length <= 6 stabilises and can be computed exactly), started from the string 'A' taken to represent true; for each system and each length n = 2..6 record the exactly generated set, under negation = complement and under negation = reversal. PASS (supports) if in Part 1 and Part 2 there is no counterexample to either direction of the biconditional (complete and consistent <=> exactly half) for any involution.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the biconditional fails in both directions, or if either of the book's two directional arguments (more than half => inconsistent; less than half => incomplete) has a counterexample. MIXED if the three implications the book argues for (more than half => inconsistent; less than half => incomplete; hence complete and consistent => exactly half) hold without exception but the converse (exactly half => complete and consistent) has counterexamples both among arbitrary sets and among stabilised generated sets of actual multiway systems. The number of counterexamples and the role of involution fixed points are reported.
tests.interpretation: The book (pp. 796-797) states the criterion as an equivalence ('the criterion for whether a system is complete and consistent is simply that exactly half ... are eventually generated') but argues only the two contrapositive directions. 'Negation' is taken as the book says: any operation that preserves length and gives back the original when applied twice (a length-preserving involution), including ones with fixed points (strings equal to their own negation), for which the test records separately what happens. 'Complete' = for every string, it or its negation is generated; 'consistent' = for no string are both generated (a fixed point that is generated counts as both). 'Eventually generated' is made exact by restricting to length-non-decreasing rules so that the generated set at each length is a finite closure.

measured.unit: stabilised (multiway system, length, negation) cases that generate exactly half of the strings but are not complete and consistent
measured.uncertainty: exact enumeration

multiway_counterexample_complement_lengt.generated: the 32 length-6 strings with an even number of B's (exactly half); contains both AAAAAA and BBBBBB (inconsistent) and neither ABAAAA nor BABBBB (incomplete)

multiway_counterexample_complement_lengt.note: exactly half, both a string and its complement present, AA and BB both absent

tests.hypothesis: Among the simplest equational axiom systems for one binary operator (single equations with at most four operator occurrences), the large majority admit several non-isomorphic finite models (operator forms) on 2 and 3 elements, and only a small minority force a single form.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all single-equation axiom systems lhs == rhs where lhs and rhs are terms built from one binary operator and variables, with a total of n = 1..4 operator occurrences in the equation, variables named canonically in order of first occurrence (a, b, c, ...) reading lhs then rhs, excluding equations with lhs identical to rhs, and identifying an equation with its side-swapped twin (so each unordered pair of sides is counted once). For each axiom system and each k in {2, 3}, enumerate all k^(k^2) operator tables (16 and 19,683), keep those satisfying the equation for every assignment of the variables, and count the models up to isomorphism (relabelling of the k elements by any permutation): m2 and m3. Definitions: 'many forms' = m3 >= 3; 'single form' = m2 <= 1 and m3 <= 1 and m2 + m3 >= 1; 'no non-trivial form' = m2 = m3 = 0 (only the one-element model). The claim PASSES if the fraction of axiom systems with 'many forms' is >= 0.80 and the fraction with 'single form' is <= 0.05. Reported, not decisive: the same fractions restricted to n = 4; the list of 'single form' systems; the systems whose k = 2 model set is exactly {Nand, Nor} (operators 7 and 1 in Wolfram's numbering) or {Xor, Xnor} (6 and 9); and, as a validation of the model-finding code against the note 'Properties of operators from axioms' (p. 1171), the k = 2 model sets of all lhs == a systems with up to 6 operators under this canonical labelling, listing how many allow only {6, 9} and only {1, 7} (the note reports 32,004 and 964 for its family of 274,499 systems; the family definition in the note is not fully specified, so this is a plausibility check, not a decisive comparison).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if fewer than 50% of the axiom systems have 'many forms', or if more than 20% force a 'single form'. Between those bounds and the pass thresholds the verdict is 'mixed'. If the enumeration cannot be completed for k = 3 within the run-time budget the verdict is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's pictures (pp. 804-805) show, for a sequence of simple axiom systems, the operator forms (multiplication tables) allowed with 2, 3 and 4 elements, inequivalent under relabelling; his claim is that the vast majority of systems allow many forms and are 'not really about operators of any particular form', while a few (logic, i.e. Nand; junctional, equivalential and implicational calculi) force essentially a single form. This test reproduces that model enumeration for k = 2 and 3 only (k = 4 would require 4^16 tables per axiom, beyond the budget) over an explicit, exhaustively enumerated family of the simplest single-equation systems. 'Vast majority' is read as >= 80%, 'only a few' as <= 5%. Multi-axiom systems (e.g. group theory) are outside the enumerated family and are not needed for the majority statement.

measured.unit: fraction of axiom systems with >= 3 non-isomorphic 3-element models ('many forms')
measured.uncertainty: exhaustive enumeration, no sampling; 1900 of 4692 systems

datasets.name: All single-equation axiom systems for one binary operator with 1-4 operator occurrences, canonical variable labelling (generated by analysis.py)

tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, the published six-Nand single axiom ((a.b).c).(a.((a.c).a)) = c has exactly the models that Nand-logic has on small domains (on 2 elements only Nand and Nor, on 3 elements none, on 4 elements only the 12 operation tables isomorphic to the Nand of the four-element Boolean algebra); no shorter single axiom of the form X = variable passes even the 2- and 3-element screens; and in a natural enumeration of axiom systems by number of Nands a system passing all screens appears within the first few thousand.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Enumerate all Nand expression trees X with k Nands (k+1 leaves) over variables a, b, c and consider (I) single axioms {X = a} for k <= 6 (34488 systems for k <= 5, 288684 for k = 6, plus the 16896 two-variable systems for k = 6) and (II) two-axiom systems {X = a, a.b = b.a} with k = 4 (3402 systems, 6 Nands in total). Screen each system against all 16 binary operations on {0,1}, all 19683 on {0,1,2} and, by backtracking search, all operations on {0,1,2,3}; a system 'works up to n values' if its models on each domain of size <= n are exactly the operation tables isomorphic to the Nand (or, on 2 elements, Nand or Nor) of a Boolean algebra of that size, i.e. {Nand, Nor} on 2, none on 3, the 12 tables isomorphic to Nand_4 on 4. PASS (supports) if (a) the published axiom works up to 4 values; (b) no single axiom {X = a} with k <= 5 over <= 3 variables works up to 3 values; (c) at least one system of family (II) works up to 4 values, and the number of systems of forms (I) and (II) with at most 6 Nands in total that precede it in the enumeration (fewer Nands first) is below 10000. The book's counts (0 of 16896 two-variable six-Nand systems up to 3 values; 296 of 288684 up to 3 values and 100 up to 4 values; 32 of 3402 in family II) are recorded as cross-checks and do not decide the verdict. If the 4-value search over all 3-value survivors of (I) exceeds 20 minutes it is applied only to the published axiom and to family (II), and the 100-count cross-check is dropped and reported.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if the published six-Nand axiom has a model on 3 elements or a non-Boolean model on 4 elements (then it does not axiomatise Boolean logic), or if no system with at most 6 Nands in total passes the screens up to 4 values (then nothing 'among the simplest few thousand' is a candidate). MIXED if (a) holds but (b) fails (a shorter single axiom survives the screens, undermining 'as short as possible'), or if (c) fails only on the count bound.
tests.interpretation: Finite-model screening is a necessary condition for axiomatising Boolean algebra (every Boolean algebra is a model, and no 3-element algebra is), not a sufficient one; the sufficiency of the six-Nand axiom rests on the equational proof the book presents on pp. 810-811 (found with automated theorem provers) which standard tooling here cannot re-run. The test therefore checks everything about the claim that is checkable by enumeration: that the published axiom is consistent with being an axiom for logic on all domains up to 4 elements, that six Nands is the minimum passing even the weakest screens, and that a screen-passing system appears within the first few thousand systems of the book's own enumeration. 'Simplest few thousand' is read against the book's own ordering (by total number of Nands, systems {X = a} and {X = a, a.b = b.a}).

measured.unit: six-Nand three-variable single axioms {X = a} (of 288684) whose models on domains of size 2, 3 and 4 are exactly those of Boolean Nand
measured.uncertainty: exact enumeration

datasets.name: Enumeration of Nand equational axiom systems with up to 6 Nands over 3 variables, with finite-model screening on domains of size 2, 3, 4, generated by analysis.py

threads.title: Physics of the flying fish: glide data and Thompson's flight envelope
threads.headline: Closed (stale, no update since 2026-10-31T21:50:00Z). TFF v2 (HYPOTHETICAL co-design map, no bird data): with Lean's C14 binding, a truly-flying 60 g fish is a region, not a point: feasible pairs of wing loading and aerobic O2 capacity shrink with altitude on both axes, but within the troposphere to 5 km the boundary moves by about 30 percent while the real fish sits 30x below it, so the gap is O2 delivery, not wings. The TFF point (12 N/m2, 1.31 W aerobic) reaches a 1000 m target (bat reference) only with a cardiac output 36x the sourced fish maximum or an air-breathing surface taking up 450 ml O2/min/kg in air, which no fetched source sizes; its map ceiling is 2.7 km; in the sim it climbs at 0.15 m/s. Winged zebrafish (0.51 g, v_min 6.1 m/s = 205 body lengths/s): could glide if launched, cannot launch itself. Co-evolution of wings and O2 processing: no comparative evidence found either way (logged search); stays a hypothesis. Launch drag threshold on chain power: body Cd <= 0.01 and lobe Cd <= 0.1. Earlier results unchanged: real fish inside Thompson's envelope; sustained aerobic flight eliminated by Lean C14; 13 unsigned nanopub drafts; birds excluded throughout.
